records.speaker: Mr. Grattan
records.sentence: they do art act unparalleled in the annals of history, such as nor envy, nor time, nor malice, nor prejudice, nor ingratitude can efface—they give to his subjects liberty, and to himself life and royalty.

records.speaker: Lord Morpeth
records.sentence: With an inflexible integrity and ardent attachment to liberty, Mr.

records.speaker: Lord Auckland
records.sentence: He did not admire the precedent, and he thought the circumstance that rendered the suspension less hateful than it would otherwise be, was, the right of action reserved to those who might be deprived of their personal liberty by its means.
records.haiku_rationale: The right of legal action to challenge deprivation of personal liberty—that is, the capacity to contest interference through courts—is a procedural safeguard enabling people to maintain or recover freedom from arbitrary detention.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdown

but he knew also with what circumspection, with what self-examination, it behoved those to proceed who were about to put away from them the sa-

cred ark of their country's freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Canning
records.sentence: Further, it appears, from what has been stated by the gallant admiral behind me (sir John Beresford), in anticipation of a question which I might perhaps have taken the liberty to put to him, that not only had the royal family really entertained that intention, but that the disposition to carry it into execution survived the report of its abandonment;
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "taken the liberty to put" is a formulaic parliamentary expression meaning "presumed to ask" or "ventured to ask"—it does not invoke liberty as a value but rather as procedural courtesy. The speaker is not claiming freedom from interference with questioning.

records.speaker: Lord Redesdale
records.sentence: That was the sort of freedom coveted by persons of that description.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence lacks sufficient specificity about what freedom is being referred to or whether it is freedom from interference or freedom to act, making the substantive liberty claim unresolvable from the text alone.

records.speaker: The Earl of Liverpool
records.sentence: In the name of internal peace, in the name of morals, in the name of good order, in the name of security and liberty, he called upon their lordships to adopt this measure.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked here rhetorically as a value opposed to disorder and insecurity—the speaker appeals to liberty as a cause supporting a particular measure, without specifying what is being freed from or enabled to do.

records.speaker: Mr. Curwen

records.haiku_rationale: The poacher risks loss of his liberty (freedom from state interference/detention) as a cost of poaching; liberty is being constrained through potential arrest or imprisonment.

records.speaker: Lord Castlereagh

To this honourable and liberal, but animated and determined contest of parties, was, he would repeat, to be attributed the envied
 
 271 
superiority of this country in public happiness, and wisdom, and liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty here is cited as an outcome of inter-party political contest and debate—a consequence of the freedom that such competitive deliberation safeguards. It names an overall condition of the nation rather than a specific freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. Canning
records.sentence: friend, but I have never felt myself at liberty to call in question the independency of his opinions.

records.speaker: The Earl of Darnley
records.sentence: If this argument was useful for any thing, it tended to show, that in reducing the army, we had violated the constitution, and that a standing force was the only safeguard of our freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: A standing military force is presented as a safeguard of freedom itself—the freedom being protected from violation of the constitution and threats to national order. The "freedom" invoked is freedom from constitutional violation and disorder, defended through state military power.

records.speaker: Mr. William Smith
records.sentence: He had heard, that when a man of the name of Winterbottom was some years ago confined in Newgate, the manuscript had been sent to him, with liberty to print it for his own advantage, if he thought proper;
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "with liberty to print it for his own advantage" grants permission/capacity to a confined person to print a manuscript for profit—this is empowerment to act despite confinement, a positive liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Canning
records.sentence: and I trust it will go forth to the world that this conviction has been avowed and supported chiefly by those who, on other occasions, are the open antagonists of ministers, and the professed advocates of the liberty of the subject.
records.haiku_rationale: The "liberty of the subject" is a rhetorical invocation of freedom from ministerial tyranny and arbitrary power—freedom from interference with the rights and person of the subject.

records.speaker: Mr. P. Moore
records.sentence: The constitution rested on two great pillars: property and liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes liberty as a foundational constitutional value (one of two pillars supporting the constitution), in opposition to tyranny or arbitrary rule, without specifying what particular freedoms or capacities are at stake.

records.speaker: Lord Castlereagh
records.sentence: and learned gentleman, with the peculiar feelings which he displayed on several occasions, had stated, that all personal liberty had been invaded;
records.haiku_rationale: Personal liberty (freedom from detention/state interference) has been invaded—this is negative liberty, the freedom from interference with the person and bodily autonomy.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: Yet as justices of the peace claim this power rather by connivance than any express warrant of law, and since the undue execution of it may prove highly prejudicial to the reputation as well as the liberty of the party, a justice of peace cannot well be too tender in his proceedings of this kind," &c.
records.haiku_rationale: The liberty at stake is freedom from unwarranted interference by a justice of the peace with the reputation and personal standing of the party being proceeded against—a negative liberty of non-interference with civil status.

records.speaker: Lord Holland
records.sentence: But it would be, I think, a matter of deep regret, if the investigation of the practices alluded to in the Prince Regent's message, should, at this period, lead, in the judgment of your lordships, to the enactment of any law that may tend to abridge the liberty of the subject.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is the "liberty of the subject" (general personal liberty); it is being freed from government interference through law that would abridge or restrict it.

records.speaker: The Hon. J. W. Ward
records.sentence: But in a country where freedom is already established upon an immovable basis—where an organ for expressing the public opinion already exists, which has never yet failed of the purpose to which it was destined—there I object to innovation.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes freedom as an already-established value (non-interference with existing institutions and public expression), contrasted against unwanted innovation/change, grounding an argument for political conservatism.

records.speaker: Sir Egerton Brydges
records.sentence: In 1662 was passed the Licensing act, with a view to suppress seditious writings, and indeed to destroy the liberty of the press.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence identifies "liberty of the press" as the object of freedom, and describes the Licensing Act as having the intent to destroy it—that is, to suppress freedom from governmental interference with publishing. This is a core negative liberty claim.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdown
records.sentence: but when it was confessed that the great body of the people was sound, and when it was remembered with what fortitude they had supported their difficulties and privations, he felt himself justified in requiring for them the full enjoyment of that freedom which was their birth-right, and of those constitutional advantages which could not be surrendered without some hazard of losing them altogether.
records.haiku_rationale: People are freed to the full enjoyment of constitutional advantages (civil and political rights) that are their birthright—this names empowerment to exercise rights and participate in governance, not mere absence of interference.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Buckingham
records.sentence: Allow it to be stript of all respect in the eyes of the people—allow it to be vilified and degraded at public meetings, and it would soon lose its energy, and with its energy the power of prolonging its own duration or securing public liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses the power of government (presumably) to maintain its capacity to secure public liberty—the object being freed is "the public" and the freedom is from unspecified threats/harms that erode over time if government loses respect and energy.

records.speaker: Earl Grey
records.sentence: Where were they to seek for that liberty, and that independence, of which the noble earl boasted?
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: liberty and independence of a nation or polity. From-or-to what: the sentence poses a rhetorical question about where to seek/find that which the noble earl claimed, framing liberty as something to be sought or pursued—presenting it as an empowering ideal or capacity the speaker questions whether exists.

records.speaker: Lord Cochrane
records.sentence: He would prefer undisguised despotism to the condition of this country, deprived of the bulwark of its freedom, and exposed to the petty vexations of magistrates;
records.haiku_rationale: The country is being deprived of "the bulwark of its freedom" — the object is freedom from interference by magistrates ("petty vexations"), rhetorically contrasted with despotism as a loss of protection against arbitrary power.

records.speaker: The Marquess Wellesley
records.sentence: The wisest patriots had ever felt, that true liberty has its basis in public order— pax est tranquilla libertas.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty (freedom from interference and coercion) has its basis in public order, which provides security—what is being freed is the capacity for individuals to exercise their will without disruption, and it is freed through the stable conditions that order provides.

records.speaker: The Lord Mayor
records.sentence:
and if they would exa-

mine them, he should be happy to procure, by such means, liberty to the people of England to breath one day in freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The people of England are being empowered/enabled to breathe freely—to enjoy a respite from oppression or constraint. The object of freedom is the capacity to exist without interference or suffering, framed as an enabling opportunity.

records.speaker: Sir Francis Burdett
records.sentence: they looked upon it as a new era, that was to produce freedom and prosperity.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from constraint/oppression is being freed from the old conditions to a new era, but the sentence does not specify what freedom consists of or from what precisely people are being freed—only that they anticipated it would be produced by something.

records.speaker: Mr. Speaker
records.sentence: The riches that will result from this augmented industry will engender a spirit of independence, and give birth to liberty, and be the means of removing those fetters which despotism seems, from the transactions of the last twenty years, to have rivetted more strongly.
records.haiku_rationale: Industry and resulting riches will remove fetters of despotism and give birth to liberty — the speaker is describing the capacity/empowerment of the people to achieve independence and break free from oppressive state constraints, not merely describing freedom from interference.

records.speaker: The Lord Chancellor
records.sentence: he was now in the decline of life, and he declared that he should feel deep regret in his retirement, if he could think that the measures which he had deemed it his duty to advise or support, had trenched upon the just liberties of the country: but, on the contrary, he believed sincerely that they had been essential to the preservation of a constitution, under which more practical liberty and happiness was enjoyed by the subject than any other under the canopy of heaven.
records.haiku_rationale: The Lord Chancellor invokes "liberties of the country" (freedom from government interference/infringement) and contrasts this with "practical liberty" as capacity for happiness under a constitution—mixing freedom from restraint with empowered enjoyment, but the primary substantive claim concerns whether measures "trenched upon" (restricted) the citizenry's freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Sir John Nicholl
records.sentence: It produces more freedom, more security, more prosperity, more glory, more happiness, to those who have the fortunate lot to live under it than any government that ever existed in any other country.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asserts that a particular government produces "freedom" as an outcome—increased freedom and prosperity as a capacity or state of flourishing, rather than freedom from a specific interference. This is freedom as an empowered condition of well-being.

records.speaker: Sir Samuel Romilly
records.sentence: and the suspension having once taken place, magistrates were at liberty to disregard all law, to exercise what arbitrary acts of power they thought proper, spies and informers were to be busily employed to betray the rash and inconsiderate, who were labouring under the pressure of penury and distress, to their destruction, and under colour of an indemnity, a total denial of justice was to prevail, for those who d suffered the most grievous wrongs.
records.haiku_rationale: Magistrates were enabled to act arbitrarily without legal restraint—freedom to exercise power without constraint—but the speaker opposes this as enabling tyranny and denying justice to suffering citizens.

records.speaker: Mr. Brougham
records.sentence: The experience, he thought, might have been spared, that they rested this cause on numbers alone—that relying on the eloquence of votes, they deemed all other eloquence superfluous —that the persons who had been deprived of their liberty under the suspension of the Habeas Corpus act, were to be deprived of all legal redress, because such was the will and pleasure of his majesty's ministers, who did not think it even necessary to condescend to give any reasons in justification of such a measure.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence protects persons deprived of liberty under the Habeas Corpus suspension and seeks to restore their legal redress against arbitrary government detention—freedom from unlawful imprisonment and arbitrary power.

records.speaker: Mr. Bathurst

records.speaker: Mr. Holme Sumner

records.speaker: Mr. Wilberforce
records.sentence: gentleman was mistaken if he supposed that the intention had been to give them nominal freedom without providing for their future protection.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdowne
records.sentence: This writer proceeded to state, what he (the Marquis of Lansdowne) would have hesitated to say, that "every state has a right to give liberty of raising, troops in its dominions, and marching them through the country, and may grant to one state what it refuses to another, in war and in peace, without infringing its neutrality.
records.haiku_rationale: A state is empowered to grant another state the capacity to raise troops and march them through its territory, or refuse this permission; the object of freedom is a state's governmental authority to conduct military operations, and the freedom is to act (be granted permission to do so).

records.speaker: Mr. Croker
records.sentence: Nor is it surprising, that on the accession of William and Mary—when, as I have stated, the new government was struggling for existence—when the delay or procrastination of an hour might have defeated the whole object of king William and the friends of civil and religious liberty, that these safeguards should be re-enacted, and brought into such immediate operation, that not the smallest postponement could be allowed.
records.haiku_rationale: Civil and religious liberty refers to freedom from interference with conscience, religion, and civil rights—specifically the freedoms that the new government (William and Mary) was defending against the threat of defeat or tyranny.

records.speaker: Mr. Granville Vernon
records.sentence: The principle of liberty is of a diffusive and communicative nature.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence presents an abstract, philosophical characterization of liberty as a principle with diffusive and communicative properties, but does not specify what is being freed, from what interference, or to what capacity—it is a general maxim without concrete object or direction.

records.speaker: Mr. Hume
records.sentence: Why should not the holder of money have equal freedom?
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: the holder of money. From or to what: the capacity to use money without unequal restrictions compared to other asset-holders; a claim for equal empowerment/treatment in economic agency.

records.speaker: Mr. Gratton
records.sentence: The objection that they have not a love for a liberty I despise also.

records.speaker: Earl Grey
records.sentence: The principle of the Revolution being, that the government of the country was not only Protestant but free, nothing seemed so essential to the security of that freedom as the preservation of purity in parliament.

records.speaker: Mr. Wilmot
records.sentence: and while we are appointed to watch the Hesperian fruit of liberty with a dragon's eye, be ourselves the only slaves of the whole community?

records.speaker: The Lord Advocate
records.sentence: In this charter, the king sets forth, "That his progenitors had, by their charters, granted to our citizens of London ( civibus nostris civilatis prœdictœ ) liberty to choose a mayor and aldermen among themselves;

records.speaker: Mr. F. Robinson
records.sentence: It had been charged, that ministers were acting in hostility to the principles of liberty: it was very easy to make general accusations, and very difficult to answer them but by a general denial;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "liberty" as a rhetorical principle opposed to ministerial hostility, but does not specify what is being freed or from-or-to what; this is a bare, general invocation of liberty as a cause in debate without substantive specification of negative or positive liberty.

records.speaker: The Chancellor of the Exchequer
records.sentence: All that the executive government had considered itself at liberty to do, was, to apply any part of the sums granted by parliament for any service, and which might remain unexhausted, to that particular service, beyond the time for which it had been voted.
records.haiku_rationale: The executive government considers itself "at liberty to" reallocate unexhausted parliamentary grants across services beyond their original voting period—this is parliamentary procedure language describing what the executive is permitted to do, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Canning
records.sentence: and that instead of tearing each other to pieces with a waste of blood, such as few wars have occasioned, some compromise could have been effected, favourable at once to rational principles of liberty, and to the peace of the old world and the new!
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "rational principles of liberty" as an abstract ideal opposed to warfare and bloodshed, which is a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause favored over tyranny and violence.

records.speaker: Mr. Granville Vernon
records.sentence: For instance, the liberty of the press in this country, the freedom of debate in this House, is probably very injurious to Spain, and to every other despotic government;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence identifies freedom of the press and freedom of debate as negative liberties—freedoms from interference with public expression and parliamentary speech—and notes their value as a check against despotic government.

records.speaker: The Earl of Liverpool
records.sentence: He had no objection, therefore, to strike out the word "thereupon," which would, at all events, leave the committee completely at liberty to make such observations as they should deem meet.
records.haiku_rationale: The committee is being freed from a procedural constraint (the word "thereupon") that would have restricted their capacity to make observations as they see fit.

records.speaker: Mr. Granville Vernon
records.sentence: but is she therefore entitled to call upon us to stifle that freedom, and to abrogate that liberty?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is objecting to being called upon to restrict ("stifle") freedom and abrogate liberty — opposing interference with unspecified freedoms, a rhetorical invocation of liberty as something to be defended against suppression.

records.speaker: Mr. Serjeant Copley
records.sentence: Was there any civilized country in the world which did not entrust such a power to some public body, and was it not essential to liberty that it should be so entrusted.
records.haiku_rationale: A power (to regulate some matter) is being entrusted to a public body; this is framed as essential to liberty—i.e., liberty requires empowerment of public institutions to govern.

records.speaker: Mr. Wynn
records.sentence: Under these circumstances, he proposed by the bill which he meant to bring in, that a general board of inspection for mad-houses should be appointed, and that the members of that board should be at liberty to visit such houses throughout the country at different and uncertain times, so as to ascertain the manner in which they were conducted, and to report any existing evil to the board, which should be invested with powers to enforce their correction.
records.haiku_rationale: Members of the inspection board are freed from restrictions preventing their visits to mad-houses (negative liberty from impediment), but the substantive purpose is to empower the board to conduct oversight and enforce corrections—the "liberty to visit" enables their capacity to fulfill a regulatory function (positive liberty to act).

records.speaker: Mr. Brand
records.sentence: This privilege of appointing game-keepers, with liberty, under these deputations, to kill game where they pleased, was the only manorial right that he desired to attack or to affect.

records.speaker: Sir Francis Burdett

records.speaker: Mr. Gratton
records.sentence: the revolution, properly understood, is the victory of civil and religious liberty, not over a sect, but over a tyranny.
records.haiku_rationale: Civil and religious liberty is being freed from tyranny—a rhetorical invocation of liberty as freedom from oppressive rule and state interference with conscience and civil matters.

records.speaker: Mr. Marryat

records.speaker: Lord Sidmouth

records.speaker: Mr. Cooper
records.sentence: What was liberty?

He believed, indeed, that, according to the ordinary rules of courts of justice, the liberty now claimed would be allowed to

counsel, and he had also understood it to be their lordships intention on Saturday last to grant it.

records.speaker: Lord Castlereagh
records.sentence: Every facility of access was then granted, and he was at liberty to enjoy in its full latitude the hospitality of this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is at liberty in the sense of being permitted or allowed (parliamentary procedure); this is not a substantive claim about freedom as a value—it is procedural language meaning "he was able to" or "he was permitted to" enjoy hospitality.

records.speaker: Mr. Brougham

records.speaker: Unknown

records.speaker: Mr. Hobhouse
records.sentence: he maybe received with hollow smiles and pretended deference, but would he not be in reality a thousand times more important with the ministers of foreign states, if he still continued to represent a people true to their ancient character, jealous of their ancient institutions, the uncompromising protectors of the oppressed of all nations, and the resolute patrons of liberty in every quarter of the globe?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes liberty as a cause and value that Britain should champion globally—defending oppressed peoples and protecting liberty everywhere. records.speaker: Mr. Garston
records.sentence: When any of the crew slept when they were at liberty they went into the hold, did they not?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty" here is parliamentary procedure language meaning "able/permitted" (were they permitted to sleep in the hold?), not making a claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. J. R. S. Graham
records.sentence: He thought it unnecessary to make any observations as to the known advantages of the liberty of the press, or as to its being the palladium of freedom, and a tower of strength to resist military force or despotic ambition.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of the press is being invoked as protection against interference—specifically as a safeguard against military force and despotic ambition, making it a freedom from external constraint and oppression.

records.speaker: The Earl of Darnley
records.sentence: The only objection which he was prepared to make to this bill he should take the liberty of throwing out at present, for the consideration of the noble lord opposite.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning "permit oneself to" or "venture to do something," not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Lord Erskine
records.sentence: But no such case appears from the papers before us, whilst the agitation of the public mind upon a transaction so visible and public, made known to us by petitions from so many quarters, affords a strong presumption of an invasion of public liberty, which it is the duty of parliament to resist and to punish.
records.haiku_rationale: Public liberty (understood as freedom from arbitrary government power) has been invaded; Parliament's duty is to resist and punish this invasion—a defensive operation against governmental overreach.

records.speaker: The Earl of Liverpool
records.sentence: and he thought it important to call their lordships' attention to the opinion which that great lawyer (judge Foster) a man whose disposition led him to favour public liberty, had expressed on this very statute.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes a judge's disposition to favour public liberty as a rhetorical authority against statutory restriction, without specifying what particular freedom (from what interference) is at stake.

records.speaker: The Earl of Liverpool
records.sentence: but he trusted that, in the interval before the time arrived when he should be at liberty to state the reasons of the course which had been pursued, then-lordships would give him credit for not having shrunk from offering any advice that appeared necessary, either for the honour of the Crown, the advantage of the country, or the particular interests of the case.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to state" is parliamentary procedure language meaning "permitted" or "able" to speak/explain, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Mr. Scarlett
records.sentence: Was it necessary that such publications should be tolerated, to afford a pretext for the introduction of coercive measures and restrictions on the liberty of the subject?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is objecting to restrictions on the liberty of the subject—i.e., freedom from coercive interference with individual persons. This invokes negative liberty as a value to be protected against state constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Attorney-General
records.sentence: I mention this to show the degree of familiarity which existed between them—the assumption which this man naturally took in consequence of the familiarity of manners which he thought himself at liberty to assume, considering himself of equal rank with her majesty, and entitled to assume dominion over persons serving her majesty.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to assume" is parliamentary procedural language indicating what someone felt permitted to do, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value or non-interference with a recognized right.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdowne
records.sentence: while we enjoyed amid our distresses a great portion of practical freedom, while we had an equal administration of wise laws, and while we possessed a constitution, which, though it might contract blemishes or acquire defects by time and neglect, might by its own operation be brought back to its first principles of purity, without shock or commotion, and which constituted our present happiness and future security.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "practical freedom" as a cause of national happiness and security, referring to the capacity to live under a stable constitutional system with equal administration of wise laws—a condition enabling the nation to act on itself and maintain social order without shock or commotion.

records.speaker: The Earl of Liverpool
records.sentence: A greater extension of liberty than was ever before known in any part of the world, had, grown with the increase of knowledge.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty (absence of oppressive constraint) has grown alongside increased knowledge—a claim about expanding freedom from interference as enlightenment progresses.

records.speaker: Sir J. Mackintosh
records.sentence: It was rather surprising that the noble lord had not had recourse to the editor of the "Cap of Liberty," the "Medusa," and other journals equally respectable.
records.haiku_rationale: "Cap of Liberty" is a proper noun referring to a journal/publication title; the sentence makes no substantive claim about liberty as a value or constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Bright
records.sentence: There was another provision which he would take the liberty of suggesting, namely, that in any case in which a judge might think it necessary, he should be empowered to have a jury called in to assist his inquiries.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of suggesting" is parliamentary procedural language (rhetorical courtesy), not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value. The sentence's content concerns empowering judges to call juries, which is administrative/institutional, not fundamentally about freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Williams
records.sentence: The Solicitor General submitted, that the witness was at liberty to state all the circumstances, whether in other respects evidence or not, that induced her to write that letter, and the statement of which was necessary for the purpose of explaining it.
records.haiku_rationale: The witness is permitted (at liberty) to state circumstances in a courtroom context; "at liberty" is a procedural phrase meaning "allowed" or "permitted," not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Brougham
records.sentence: As that, however, might still be doubted, he should take the liberty to read another passage, to show that assassination had been unequivocally recommended.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty to read" is parliamentary procedure language meaning "I proceed to read"; it is not making a claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Tierney
records.sentence: But to return to the motion—trusting to the moderation of his noble friend, he took the liberty of advising him to withdraw it, in consequence of the declaration of the noble lord.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of advising" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning he ventured or dared to offer advice; liberty here is used as a polite formula for action undertaken, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Earl Grey
records.sentence:
Could their wearing caps of liberty, or their being

accompanied by music be said to be illegal?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "caps of liberty" is a symbolic reference to revolutionary insignia; the sentence asks whether wearing such symbols or being accompanied by music could be made illegal, treating "liberty" as a rhetorical political symbol opposed to legal restriction rather than making a substantive claim about a freedom-value itself.

records.speaker: Mr. Shepherd
records.sentence: The revolutionary demagogues wished for a description of liberty, which would deprive every individual of his rights.
records.haiku_rationale: Revolutionary demagogues seek a description of liberty that would deprive individuals of their rights — a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a value opposed to tyranny and deprivation of rights, framing liberty as freedom from interference with individual rights.

records.speaker: Mr. Wilmot
records.sentence: even our virtues might, by their excess, approximate to vice, nor is it otherwise with liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a virtue that, like others, can become excess and approach vice—a rhetorical observation about liberty as a value to be balanced, not a specific claim about freedom from or capacity to do something substantive.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: What sort of freedom, what do you mean by freedom?
records.haiku_rationale: This is a meta-linguistic question asking for clarification about the meaning of the word 'freedom' itself, without specifying what is being freed or from-or-to what.

records.speaker: Mr. Hobhouse
records.sentence:
" 
In those days, however, this trait was one of the features of a rude, suspicious liberty—now, it will be only one of the many signs of degradation and slavery.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" as a contrast to "degradation and slavery," characterizing it as something valued and threatened—a rhetorical claim about freedom from tyrannical control and oppression.

records.speaker: Lord Morpeth
records.sentence: But it is that liberty, and only that liberty I mean which is connected with order, and that not only exists with order and with virtue, but cannot at all exist without them.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a foundational political value that depends on order and virtue, without specifying either what activity is freed or from what constraint, making this a rhetorical assertion of liberty as an ideal rather than a claim about freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. J. R. S. Graham
records.sentence: It was, in fact, a species of censorship, which, if adopted, must tend to destroy that liberty of the press, the preservation of which had hitherto been considered the great bulwark of our liberties.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence identifies "liberty of the press" as freedom from censorship, presented as a fundamental protection ("bulwark") against tyranny—a classic negative liberty claim about freedom from governmental interference with the press.

records.speaker: Mr. Ellice
records.sentence: and he was sure that the States of America would require protection in any negotiation with Spain, for maintaining the freedom they had acquired.
records.haiku_rationale: The States of America are freed to self-govern and maintain their independence from Spanish rule; this is empowerment to conduct their own affairs as a sovereign entity.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdowne
records.sentence: By such conduct, by a careful attention to the distresses or the people, and a zealous endeavour to reduce their burthens, the ministers and the legislature would do more to recall them to their duty, to allay their discontents, to secure their obedience, and to ensure their cordial co-operation in maintaining peace and tranquillity, than all the restrictive measures which the House could enact, than all the privations or suspensions of liberty which they could inflict.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence explicitly contrasts positive measures (reducing distresses and burdens) with "privations or suspensions of liberty"—meaning restrictions on freedom from interference. The object of freedom is the people's liberty (from state interference), and the sentence argues against its curtailment.

records.speaker: Earl Grey
records.sentence: It is stated, my lords, in the preamble to the bill, that her royal highness whilst the said Bartolomeo Bergami was in her said service, conducted herself towards the said Bergami, and in other respects, both in public and private, with indecent and offensive familiarity and freedom, and carried on a licentious, disgraceful, and adulterous intercourse with the said Bergami, which continued for a long period of time, during her royal highness's residence abroad;
records.haiku_rationale: The word "freedom" here appears as an incidental legal term describing alleged improper conduct (indecent familiarity and freedom), not as a value-laden claim about liberty-as-freedom-from-interference or empowerment-to-act. This is a statement of formal charges in parliamentary procedure, not a substantive argument about what ought to be freed or from what.

records.speaker: Mr. Plunkett
records.sentence: He would take the liberty of reading a short extract upon this point from Burnet's "History of the Reformation.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is using "take the liberty of" as a parliamentary courtesy phrase to request permission to read an extract—this is procedural convention, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Marryat
records.sentence: and this I am at full liberty to do, it having been communicated to us by message from the Lords, and reprinted by order of this House.
records.haiku_rationale: This is parliamentary procedure language: "at liberty to do" is an idiomatic expression meaning "permitted" or "allowed under procedure," not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Lord Erskine
records.sentence: ) did not mean to offer a decided opinion upon this point, but he thought the same liberty ought now to be allowed to the counsel for the Queen.
records.haiku_rationale: Counsel for the Queen should be allowed the same liberty (procedural permission to act) as others in debate or argument—freedom to participate equally in parliamentary/legal proceedings.

records.speaker: Mr. Huskisson
records.sentence: but that time having elapsed, his opinion had changed, and he was at liberty fully to state to the House how much he regretted that the agitation of the country had been excited in consequence of that measure.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker describes being "at liberty" to state his regrets to the House—a parliamentary phrase indicating procedural permission to speak, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Mr. Canning
records.sentence: The price at which political liberty is to be valued, and the cost at which it is to be obtained, constitute the nicest balance, and one which only those immediately interested in the calculation are competent to decide.
records.haiku_rationale: Political liberty is being valued and obtained at a price/cost, framing freedom as a good to be weighed in cost-benefit calculation, rather than a freedom from interference or a specific enabling capacity.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdown
records.sentence: No, the word liberty is carefully excluded from the vocabulary of the allies.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking "liberty" as a political value that has been deliberately excluded from discourse by the allies—a rhetorical claim that liberty (freedom from oppressive control) is absent from their vocabulary and presumably their governance.

records.speaker: The Marquis of Lansdown
records.sentence: In former times Great Britain had acquired deserved glory by the policy she adopted, as the fosterer of every nascent spark of liberty which was struck out of any of the nations in the world.
records.haiku_rationale: Great Britain is praised for fostering "every nascent spark of liberty" in other nations—understood as nurturing the emergence of freedom from interference (including independence movements and resistance to tyranny) across the world.

records.speaker: Earl Grey
records.sentence: That paper he had read with disgust, as it contained those principles of arbitrary power, which were more consistent with a conspiracy of kings against liberty than with an alliance deserving the name of "Holy".
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty (understood as freedom from arbitrary power and conspiracy by kings) is being opposed to arbitrary power and monarchical conspiracy—a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause against tyranny.

records.speaker: Mr. Plunkett
records.sentence: He knows that the same principle gives him and us life, liberty, and property;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes liberty as an abstract foundational principle (grouped with life and property) that is bestowed or possessed, without specifying a particular domain of freedom from interference or capacity to act; the principle itself is the object of discussion.

records.speaker: Mr. Horace Twiss
records.sentence: I answer, at the point which completes to every man the greatest share of freedom and of franchise which he can enjoy, consistently with the general good;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker seeks to identify the point at which individuals can enjoy "the greatest share of freedom and of franchise...consistently with the general good"—balancing individual liberty (negative: non-interference in exercising rights/franchise) against collective welfare constraints.

records.speaker: The Lord Chancellor
records.sentence: He took the liberty to point out to their lordships that it would be quite competent for them, provided they felt confident that the whole or part of the charges were substantiated in evidence, to alter the preamble of this bill, so as to assert or deny, first, every thing which they believed to be true, and which might be retained;
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty to point out" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning he was permitted to make a remark; "liberty" here is not substantively about freedom-as-a-value but rather parliamentary permission/procedural convention.

records.speaker: Mr. Hobhouse
records.sentence: And what was his first effort in favour of freedom?
records.haiku_rationale: What was being freed: it is unclear from this rhetorical question alone. The sentence invokes "freedom" as a cause (presumably opposed to tyranny or oppression) but does not specify the concrete object or mechanism—freedom of what, or freedom from what. Requires broader context to classify definitively.

records.speaker: Mr. Nolan
records.sentence: They all live under the same constitutional law—receive the, influence of the same governing system—enjoy the same freedom, and may, boast, that the upper ranks of life in all assimilate as much as possible to each other in knowledge, manners, ants, and civilization.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom as a shared constitutional benefit ("enjoy the same freedom") without specifying what people are freed from or empowered to do; it functions as a rhetorical claim about the excellence of the constitutional system rather than making a substantive argument about either freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. Hobhouse
records.sentence: Peel) would raise liberty to a pitch to which it had never before been fexalted—that he would do much more for freedom than ever had been done by gentlemen on that (the Opposition) side of the House.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" and "freedom" as values opposed to the actions of the Opposition, suggesting Peel would advance freedom in a general sense, but without specifying whether this means removing constraints on action (negative liberty) or enabling new capacities (positive liberty).

records.speaker: Lord John Russell
records.sentence: In the 7th year of king William, was passed the act well known by the name of the Treating act: the preamble of that act he should take the liberty of reading to the House, because, with some variations, he had taken the words of it for the first Resolution which he should propose.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of reading" is parliamentary procedure language—a conventional idiom meaning "took it upon myself to" without substantive claims about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Speaker
records.sentence: For my own part—and I am sure I may take the liberty of saying, on the part of the author of this bill—there is no human authority which would avail with us in any thing like the same degree as a conviction that the principles of that bill are at variance with that incomparable standard;
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of saying" is parliamentary procedure language meaning "permit myself to say" or "venture to say"—not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Brougham
records.sentence: ] The noble lord, after making the extraordinary observation on which he had just taken the liberty of offering a few comments, proceeded to make another, which, if possible, was still more extraordinary.
records.haiku_rationale: This is parliamentary procedure language: "took the liberty of" is a formulaic phrase meaning "ventured to" or "presumed to speak," not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Sir James Mackintosh
records.sentence:
A modern poet of great celebrity had so indulged his fancy, when speaking of the Holy Alliance of his time, and the inroads made upon national liberty—
 "while European freedom still withstands 
 The encroaching flood which drowns her lessening lauds, 
 She sees fir off, with an indignant groan, 
 Her native plains and empires once her own.
records.haiku_rationale: European freedom (national liberty) is being threatened by external encroachment and erosion—this is freedom from interference with nations' independence and self-governance, described as being lost to invasive political forces.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennard
records.sentence: It was the energy, the boldness of a man's mind, which prompting him to speak, not in private, but in largo and popular assemblies, that constituted the principle of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom consists in the capacity and empowerment of a man's mind to prompt him to speak boldly in public assemblies—not freedom from interference, but the positive ability or energy to act.

records.speaker: Sir James Mackintosh
records.sentence: In the second place, it accustomed the subjects of a free state to the spectacle of slavery, and by inuring them to the sight of rights infringed and injuries unredressed gave a dangerous example of slavish suffering, and lessened the habit and love of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom as a civic virtue and habit—the capacity and disposition of free citizens to resist oppression and value their rights. It contrasts "the habit and love of freedom" with "slavish suffering" and the spectacle of rights infringed, making this about citizens' empowered capacity to maintain and exercise their autonomy, not merely absence of interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Brougham
records.sentence: but, taking it altogether, the country enjoys as much practical liberty, and parliament is really as independent, as in any former reign.
records.haiku_rationale: The country and parliament are described as enjoying/possessing "practical liberty" and independence in their own governance—a capacity-based, empowered state of self-determination rather than freedom from specific interferences.

records.speaker: The Lord Chancellor
records.sentence: and he would say, that if they were at liberty to do that which was now proposed, the parliament of Scotland had made a bargain with the legislature of this country, so exceedingly foolish, that he knew not how to designate it by any appropriate epithet.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to do" is used in a parliamentary procedural sense—to describe whether a body (the parliament of Scotland) would be permitted or able to undertake an action. This is not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value but rather incidental parliamentary language about what a body is allowed to do procedurally.

records.speaker: Mr. Ricardo
records.sentence: ) had stated his opinions in the committee, and for the sake of his own character and consistency, he would take the liberty of restating them to the House.
records.haiku_rationale: Mr. Ricardo is using "take the liberty of" as an idiomatic parliamentary phrase meaning he permits himself to restate his views; this is procedural language about what a speaker may do in the House, not a substantive claim about freedom from constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Haldimand
records.sentence: With regard to the circulation of Bank paper, he would take the liberty of making one remark;
records.haiku_rationale: Parliamentary procedure: "took the liberty of" is an idiom meaning "ventured to" or "proceeded to," not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. T. Wilson
records.sentence: he, therefore, might be pardoned if' he took the liberty of throwing out another for the consideration of parliament.
records.haiku_rationale: Parliamentary procedure: "took the liberty of" is a formulaic phrase meaning "ventured to" or "permitted myself to," used to introduce a proposal without substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennard
records.sentence: It was that principle which gave life to liberty;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes liberty as a foundational principle in opposition to constraint or death (slavery/tyranny), using it as a general political value without specifying what concrete freedoms or capacities are at stake.

records.speaker: Mr. Wilmot
records.sentence: As to the freedom which they enjoyed, he must remind the hon.

records.speaker: Mr. Grant
records.sentence: It had revived a conviction in the minds of the lower classes of Irishmen, that the law wasp upon principle, hostile to them, and that their governors in England felt themselves at liberty to resort to unconstitutional measures for the administration of Ireland, to which they dared not resort for the administration of England.
records.haiku_rationale: English governors felt themselves at liberty (empowered) to resort to unconstitutional measures against Ireland, describing their capacity to act without constitutional restraint—a positive liberty of governmental power.

records.speaker: Mr. Hobhouse
records.sentence: five caps of liberty!
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes liberty as a symbol/cause against restraint, using the rhetorical image of caps (Phrygian caps) worn in revolutionary and anti-tyranny contexts, expressing aspiration for freedom from oppression.

records.speaker: Lord Folkestone
records.haiku_rationale: A bare reference to "liberty" in the abstract without specifying what is being freed or from-or-to what; the sentence merely notes that a definition of liberty was given, but does not articulate that definition or its normative content.

records.speaker: Mr. Plunkett
records.sentence: Whilst freedom is true to itself, every thing becomes subject to it, and its very adversaries are an instrument in its hands.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom itself—conceived as an abstract principle or force—is being invoked as a cause that subordinates everything to its logic; what is being freed is an ideological or philosophical concept, not a person or group from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Hume
records.sentence: Looking at the advantages which resulted from the freedom of discussion, and the part which able men were always ready to take in behalf of true religion, he thought it would be doing equal injustice to that religion and to the community, to adopt any other means of arriving at the truth than by fair discussion.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of discussion (discourse without interference) is the object being protected; it is freedom from suppression or constraint in pursuit of truth within the community and religion.

records.speaker: Mr. Stuart Wortley
records.sentence: de San Miguel a dignity, as if the spirit of liberty had given him at once a superiority over those to whom he was opposed.
records.haiku_rationale: The spirit of liberty is portrayed as conferring superior capacity or empowerment on de San Miguel over his opponents—a capacity-based or enabling notion of freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Bright
records.sentence: and from these returns I will take the liberty of submitting certain results.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "liberty" as a formulaic parliamentary courtesy phrase meaning permission to proceed with an action (submitting results), not as a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Lord Ellenborough
records.sentence: Was it for our interest that France should be placed at liberty to march an army from her frontiers, to smother every ember of liberty in Germany and Italy?
records.haiku_rationale: France is being freed (given capacity) to march an army and suppress liberty in other nations; the second use of "liberty" refers to negative liberty (freedom from foreign oppression) being extinguished in Germany and Italy.

records.speaker: Mr. Wynn
records.sentence: but it was that principle which had been found to give the greatest support to civil liberty that was ever known at any period of time.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "civil liberty" as a value being supported by a principle, without specifying the object of freedom (freedom from what interference, or capacity to do what). The sentence is a rhetorical affirmation of liberty as a cause but does not disambiguate whether the freedom at issue is freedom from interference or empowered capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. Bolett
records.sentence: He would now take the liberty of submitting the result of some very careful calculations which he had made in relation to the subject before the House.
records.haiku_rationale: This is parliamentary procedure: "took the liberty of" is a formulaic expression meaning "ventured to" or "proceeded to", not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Marryat
records.sentence: for he thought that its operation had the effect of restraining the liberty of the subject.
records.haiku_rationale: The subject (citizens) is being freed from restraint/restriction; the sentence discusses freedom from governmental constraint on liberty itself.

records.speaker: Lord Palmerston

for in this very Spain, in support of these very

records.speaker: Mr. Grey Bennet

and this, too, while your petitioner has to pay a part of those county-rates and those poor-rates which are occasioned by the prosecutions and punishments for the preservation of game:

records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "liberty and property of Englishmen" as a rhetorical appeal to traditional political principles opposed to arbitrary power, without specifying any particular freedom from interference or capacity being granted or constrained.

records.speaker: Mr. S. Rice

records.haiku_rationale: Religious liberty is being freed from state interference and coercion in matters of conscience and religious practice.

records.speaker: Mr. Hume
records.sentence: — At perfect liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a parliamentary procedural phrase meaning the speaker is permitted to speak; it does not articulate a substantive claim about liberty as a value or political concept.

records.speaker: Mr. C. Ellis
records.sentence: No mode of arguing can be more fallacious, nor, I must take the liberty of saying, more un-fair, than to cite the bad state of morals in the West Indies as a reason" for the enfranchisement of the slaves.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of saying" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning "permit myself to say" or "venture to say," not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Lord Nugent
records.sentence: Remember that the office of a magistrate gives power in many cases over the property and liberty of our fellow subjects.
records.haiku_rationale: A magistrate's power "over the liberty" of subjects invokes liberty as a status or condition vulnerable to interference by state authority—the object of freedom is personal liberty itself, and the concern is protection from power's incursion.

records.speaker: Sir James Mackintosh
records.sentence: He was ashamed to hear it said that the constitution of England was unfit for Scotland, at the very time when they were reproving other nations for not bringing their constitutions nearer to the great model of justice and liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of liberty is unspecified ("liberty" stands alone); the sentence invokes liberty as a positive value/ideal that constitutions should embody and approach, in the context of national constitutional design—a rhetorical appeal to liberty as a foundational principle opposed to injustice.

records.speaker: Mr. C. Ellis
records.sentence: I entreat the House to recollect that liberty, though the greatest of all political blessings, is a blessing capable of being abused, if conferred on persons not fitted to receive it;
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a political blessing that can be granted to (or withheld from) persons based on their fitness—a rhetorical claim about freedom as a value that depends on the recipient's capacity to use it wisely, touching on both the non-interference aspect (liberty as a blessing) and the conditional empowerment (conferring it on those fitted to receive it).

records.speaker: Mr. Canning
records.sentence: —If we were at war with France upon any question such as I must again take the liberty of describing by the term "external" question, we should not think ourselves—(I trust no government of this country would think itself)—justified in employing against France the arms of internal revolution.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of describing" is parliamentary procedural language (a conventional expression allowing the speaker to use terminology), not a substantive claim about freedom from interference or empowerment to act as a political value.

records.speaker: Sir James Mackintosh
records.sentence: Even in Cornwall, the very home and holy land of borough mongering, the feelings of freedom were not extinct.
records.haiku_rationale: The "feelings of freedom" refer to the sentiment or disposition of the people—their sense of being free from tyranny or oppressive control; this invokes liberty as a rhetorical cause opposed to the borough-mongering system that constrains political autonomy.

records.speaker: Lord Nugent
records.sentence: Sir, the idea of freedom is closely interwoven with that of privilege.

records.speaker: Mr. Fowell Buxton

records.speaker: Mr. Baring
records.sentence: So fixed were his opinions on that subject, that were he an inhabitant of Ireland he should infinitely prefer a despotic government, one in which the judges alone should have the power to decide upon his case, to that constitutional form so favorable to the liberty of the subject, in which the aid of the people themselves was called in.

records.sentence: In recommending the government to pursue that course, he was not seeking to create any new system, but merely to bring back the old— that system under which our ancestors had lived free, and under which they had distinguished themselves, not only as the patrons of liberty, but as the generous dispensers of it to others.

The use of "facility" and "enjoyed" suggests a legal status or privilege rather than freedom from a specific interference or freedom to exercise a specific capacity.

records.sentence: It was undoubtedly the practical efficiency which it had hitherto shewn in cherishing all the various interests of the community, and which had tended so much, not only to the maintenance of the great principle of the security of property, combined with general freedom, but also to the increase of the wealth and industry of the people, and the power and greatness of the State.

records.speaker: Mr. Grote
records.sentence: I know that there are some who dispute whether secrecy really will bestow this freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. O'Connell
records.sentence: He would not waste the time of the House by declaiming on the merits of Jury Trial, he would only say, that he pitied the man, who, calling himself a lover of freedom, did not estimate highly this mode of trial.

records.speaker: Mr. Alderman Thompson
records.sentence: In order to show the feeling which prevailed among, British merchants upon this subject, he would take the liberty of reading to the House an extract from a letter written by Mr.

records.speaker: Lord Althorp
records.sentence: That was not what he called liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Lord Althorp is disputing someone else's definition or application of the term "liberty" itself without specifying what is being freed or from-to what.

records.sentence: The Ministers were not only taking away the protection from life and property, but were actually robbing the people of their liberty, by this Bill, which, he again asserted, was to facilitate the collection of tithes.

records.speaker: Lord John Russell
records.sentence: He was convinced that by subduing insurrection, while they maintained, as they ought, the authority of the laws and the dignity of the Crown, it would be confessed in the end, even by those who were averse to own it now, that they had been the best friends to the peace, the liberty, and the prosperity of Ireland.

records.speaker: Mr. Henry Grattan
records.sentence: Certainly the hope that she would participate fully in the freedom of the British Constitution.

records.speaker: Mr. Henry Lytton Bulwer
records.sentence: " After mentioning various things that the Diet would do in the grant of particular rights and privileges, it went on to say: "That the Diet will occupy itself, at its first re-union, with a uniform law respecting the liberty of the press, and the measures to adopt for guaranteeing authors and editors against the piracy or counterfeiting of their works.

records.speaker: Sir Francis Burdett

records.sentence: that which he proposed, would secure to the people of Ireland the free liberty and power of originating a petition to the King in Parliament at a public meeting, while, if they gave to the Lord Lieutenant ten days' notice of such meeting, he might be prepared with all his civil and military force to put it down, should it turn out to be an illegal one, or be perverted to any other purpose.

records.sentence: and ingenuous persons who, though lovers of liberty themselves, yet respected the character of Whig, to remind the House of the great debt of gratitude which Ireland owed to that party.

records.speaker: Mr. Cobbett
records.sentence: For my own part I will resist it to the last gasp of my existence—to the last drop of my blood—and when I feel the hour of my dissolution approaching, I will like the father of Hannibal, take my children to the altar, and swear them to eternal hostility against the invaders of their country's freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Baring
records.sentence: But if they could not give such a hope—if they proceeded with reckless impetuosity—if what was called freedom proved to be freedom from labour—then the result would, he apprehended, be, that the white men would be obliged to leave the islands, and we should be compelled to take an article of extensive commerce from foreign colonies which employed slave-labour, while the price of sugar would be doubled or trebled in Jamaica.

records.speaker: Mr. Godson
records.sentence: The principal feature of the plan was, that the slaves should work out their own freedom, receiving certain debentures, the probable amount of which would be five millions, at three distinct periods of five, ten, and fifteen years.
records.haiku_rationale: Slaves are enabled to acquire freedom (liberation from bondage) by working and earning debentures over time—this describes empowerment to achieve a state of freedom rather than protection from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Thomas Attwood

records.speaker: Mr. Stanley

records.sentence: "—"The absolute rights of man, considered as a free agent, endowed with discernment to know good from evil, and with power of choosing those measures which appear to him to be most desirable, are usually summed up in one general appellation and denominated the natural liberty of mankind.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "natural liberty of mankind" as an inherent capacity—the power of choosing measures that appear desirable based on discernment. records.speaker: Mr. Baring
records.sentence: Why, freedom was associated in his mind with images of idleness and neglect of labour;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker describes "freedom" negatively through association with idleness and neglect of labour — treating freedom as absence of constraint or obligation to work, a characterization of negative liberty (freedom from compulsion to labour).

records.sentence: The Act of 1782, was the Irish charter of liberty—it was not given up by the people.

records.speaker: Mr. Macaulay
records.sentence: For, in the first place, our freedom and our high civilization render this improvement, desirable as it must always be, less indispensably necessary to us than to our Indian subjects: and in the next place our freedom and civilization, I fear, render it far more difficult for us to obtain this benefit for ourselves than to bestow it on them.
records.haiku_rationale: Macaulay invokes "freedom and high civilization" as conditions that make improvement less necessary for Britain but harder for Britons to obtain for themselves—the object of freedom is left unspecified, but it is presented as a general state or condition enabling Britain's superiority, neither clearly freedom from interference nor freedom to do something specific.

records.speaker: Mr. Buckingham
records.sentence: He would begin, then, with the objections to immediate emancipation, which were raised by the noble Lord, the member for Stirling (Lord Dalmeny), which embraced the three following assertions:—That the slaves were too ignorant to be admitted at once to the enjoyment of freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Roebuck
records.sentence: Freedom in itself is not a good thing—it is only good when it leads to good—if it lead to evil, it must be, it is every day, restrained by the most stringent and coercing bonds.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (general capacity/state of non-restraint) is being evaluated instrumentally: it is good only when it leads to good outcomes, and when it leads to evil it must be restrained through coercive bonds. records.speaker: Mr. Ward
records.sentence: Secretary of State delayed the arrival of entire freedom, it delayed it only that freedom might be more valuable and secure.

records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberality and freedom" as guiding principles for conducting an undertaking successfully, without specifying either what is being freed from or what capacity is being enabled.

records.speaker: Mr. Sergeant Woulfe
records.sentence: and learned Member for Bandon had put a question with regard to this circumstance which he would take the liberty to answer, after the fashion of his country, by putting another.
records.haiku_rationale: This sentence uses "take the liberty to" as a colloquial parliamentary phrase meaning simply "he would proceed to" or "he would venture to" answer a question. It is not making a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value but rather using liberty as a formulaic expression of procedural intent.

records.speaker: Mr. C. Lushington
records.sentence: With the permission of the House, he would take the liberty of reading to them the passage to which he referred.
records.haiku_rationale: This is parliamentary procedure language where "took the liberty of" is an idiom meaning "allowed myself to" or "was permitted to" read a passage—not a normative claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Lord J. Russell
records.sentence: that there should be full freedom of choice of occupation or profession;
records.haiku_rationale: Individuals are freed to choose their own occupation or profession; this is an enabling capacity to pursue one's chosen work.

records.speaker: Mr. Harvey
records.sentence: It has, therefore, from the beginning of the discussions upon this subject, appeared to me that whilst I should be most prompt to confer these great and responsible powers upon the noble Earl who has, I think, been most happily selected by her Majesty's Government—cheering, as he does, the friends of freedom wherever he goes—I should at the same time be little disposed to fetter him in the exercise of the mighty authority with which he is clothed.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom here is from fetters/constraints on the exercise of authority—the speaker values not restraining the Earl's power, invoking "freedom" as a rhetorical appeal against impediment to governance.

records.speaker: Lord Brougham
records.sentence: But linger not on the islands where the gift of freedom has been but half bestowed—look to Antigua and Bermuda, where the wisdom and the virtue has been displayed, of at once giving complete emancipation.
records.haiku_rationale: Enslaved people are being freed from bondage through the action of emancipation; this is freedom from the constraint of slavery, achieved by the removal of legal restrictions on their persons and labor.

records.speaker: Mr. O'Connell
records.sentence: Make the best of your way to the common place of execution—walk under it—bow your heads to it—and then, forsooth, when you have rendered yourselves as contemptible as degradation can make you, when you have satisfied us of your unmanliness and worthlessness, then we will consider you fit objects of conciliation, and entitled to participate with us in the enjoyment of rational liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "rational liberty" as a right/capacity that the addressed group will be "entitled to participate in" once they cease their alleged degradation—this frames liberty as an empowered status or condition to be granted to those deemed worthy, not as freedom from a specific interference.

records.speaker: Lord Brougham
records.sentence: "you cannot emancipate the negro apprentices now, because you have not given them time to be prepared for the enjoyment of complete freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The negro apprentices are being freed to the capacity of enjoying complete autonomy/self-governance; the claim is that they lack preparedness for this positive capacity, not that they are being interfered with.

records.speaker: Mr. Bannerman
records.sentence: But if that wish should be indulged in, it will be ridiculous, or worse than ridiculous, to arm ourselves with the terrors of privilege, to guard against ridicule or invective, while we take no means to secure ourselves against a repetition of this gross and dangerous attack on the freedom of our debates, and the independence of so many of our Members.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of debates—the freedom from interference with parliamentary debate itself—is being asserted as under attack, and the Member argues that privileges should not guard against criticism while leaving this freedom unprotected.

records.speaker: Sir J. C. Hobhouse
records.sentence: Friend said, they would have the advantage of this palladium of British liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "palladium of British liberty" as a protective emblem/safeguard against interference or tyranny, treating liberty as a value to be defended from encroachment—a rhetorical invocation of negative liberty.

records.speaker: Lord Glenelg
records.sentence: He did not believe that this was the necessary consequence of bestowing freedom on the negroes;
records.haiku_rationale: Bestowing freedom on negroes means granting them freedom from enslavement and unfreedom—empowering them to act as autonomous agents rather than property.

records.speaker: Lord Brougham
records.sentence: they have been fervent in their prayers for perfect equal liberty and exception from all taxes, which they cannot pay, conscientiously pay—you will deeply disappoint the hopes of those millions who regard their principles more than the pressure of the amount, and who would object on principle to the tax, were it only a farthing, because they feel that the principle is a violation of their consciences.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is conscience and principles (specifically, freedom from taxation that violates one's moral convictions). The freedom sought is freedom FROM compulsory taxation that conflicts with conscience, not empowerment TO do something new.

records.speaker: The Earl of Mansfield
records.sentence: He had taken the liberty, when the Roman Catholic Relief Bill passed, of stating in his place, in their Lordships' House his opinion, that it would be difficult, upon the grounds on which that bill was passed, if not impossible, to support the religion of the minority as the established religion of the state in Ireland.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "taken the liberty" is a conventional parliamentary expression meaning "took the opportunity" or "ventured"; it refers to procedural permission to speak, not to a substantive claim about freedom as a value or about freedom from constraint or empowerment to act.

records.speaker: The Marquess of Sligo
records.sentence: "I said nothing of any division in the Cabinet, of which, not having been a member of it, I probably should not have been aware, and which, if I had known it, I should not have thought myself at liberty to mention.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "at liberty to mention" as a parliamentary courtesy phrase—not making a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value but rather following procedural decorum about what one is permitted to discuss in debate.

records.speaker: Mr. Wyse
records.sentence: He took the liberty to enter on subjects of that kind, because imputations had been thrown out against him, or rather his objects had been impugned by the Church party.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty to" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning "ventured to" or "proceeded to"; it does not advance a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value but rather describes the speaker's action in beginning to discuss a topic.

records.speaker: Sir William Molesworth
records.sentence:
" 
Their object, according to resolutions adopted by them at Caledon, on the 14th of August, 1837, is "to establish a settlement on the same principles of liberty as those adopted by the United States of America, carrying into effect, as far as practicable, their burgher laws.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being sought is freedom to establish a settlement governed by principles of liberty (self-governance and burgher laws) modeled on the United States — an empowerment to institute self-governing institutions, not merely freedom from external interference.

records.speaker: Lord John Russell
records.sentence: Baronet, as well as every other Member, is fully at liberty to declare his dissent, if he think proper, to any proposition contained in the estimates.
records.haiku_rationale: A Member is freed from impediment to declare dissent to propositions; this invokes the right to voice disagreement without interference—a classic negative liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Sergeant Jackson
records.sentence: It would be in the recollection of the House, that last year he took the liberty to bring in a bill to remedy these evils, and that after the bill had been read a second time  pro formâ,  it went into committee, so as to enable him to give the details of the measure the fullest consideration, and he had since taken all the pains in his power to render the bill perfect.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty to" is parliamentary procedure language referring to the speaker's procedural prerogative to introduce a bill—not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. C. Buller
records.sentence: Baronet, for the part which, with his station, interest, and character, he had taken on himself in commencing the debate, and giving to it a tone of calm deliberation and perfect freedom from party favour which he hoped would be adopted by every body as successfully as he should do his utmost to imitate it.
records.haiku_rationale: The clause "perfect freedom from party favour" specifies freedom from interference by partisan bias in debate—a constraint on deliberation to be removed.

records.speaker: The Attorney-General
records.sentence: Now, the House must either give up its powers altogether, or interpose at once, because if an attorney's clerk could carry on an action in his master's name, and remain at liberty, the object of the House would be defeated.
records.haiku_rationale: An attorney's clerk remaining "at liberty" to conduct litigation in another's name without oversight or restriction; the freedom is from procedural constraint on who may act in legal proceedings.

records.speaker: Lord Lurgan
records.sentence: He said this confidently, because though the Roman Catholics might have been admitted in some boroughs to the freedom, they were everywhere altogether excluded from the governing body;

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: Capital will be withdrawn, the negro population may enjoy freedom and repose, but cultivation will have ceased, Jamaica will indeed remain, but she will remain only as a memorial, to tell you what the bounty of God had done for man, but what man's own folly and recklessness had prevented him from enjoying.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: I say, whatever abstract notions may be entertained by some, I have no difficulty in reconciling prerogative and freedom, dependency and independency.

records.speaker: Lord Brougham
records.sentence: it was full of objectionable provisions, and it was quite enough to say, that it would extirpate every vestige of the liberty of the press.
