records.speaker: Lord Mahon
records.sentence: Let it not be said, that after all our past labours and struggles in the cause of constitutional freedom—after having won the Habeas Corpus—and the Bill of Rights—after tyranny had been expelled from the castles of the feudal barons, and the palace of the Stuart kings—that she had found her last refuge and shelter within the walls of a reformed House of Commons.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: Britain/constitutional order from tyranny and arbitrary rule (Habeas Corpus, Bill of Rights explicitly named as protections against executive/feudal interference). From: executive oppression and feudal/monarchical despotism.

records.speaker: Lord Stanley

records.speaker: Sir J. Graham
records.sentence: he (Sir James Graham) had adduced the opinion of Lord Althorp after the close and settlement of the question, and Lord Althorp had then, in terms as explicit as he could possibly have used, declared that, as a Member of Lord Grey's Government, he was not at liberty to support the ballot, though he had supported that question on a previous occasion.

records.sentence: Therefore, although it might not be an open question on the other side, he conceived that the real difference between them was, whether they should put the whole education of the country into the hands of the Established Church, or admit that liberty of education, what was sanctioned by his late Majesty, and by his Royal Highness the Duke of Kent, and which certainly the present Ministers were disposed to think was the only principle upon which education ought to be supported.

records.speaker: Lord Brougham

but I shall live to see the Parliament of England perform, at length, its too long-delayed and most sacred duty, of giving instruction to all classes, of all descriptions, all ranks, and all sects of

people, upon the broad, universal, and eternal principles of religious as well as of civil liberty.

records.speaker: The Earl of Clarendon

records.speaker: Lord John Russell
records.sentence: and I hope that this may be done in such a manner as to conduce, in the end, to the freedom and the happiness of those colonies.
records.haiku_rationale: Lord John Russell hopes colonial policy will conduce to the freedom and happiness of the colonies—empowering them toward self-governance and flourishing.

records.speaker: Mr. Hume
records.sentence: I was very sanguine respecting the working of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker expresses optimism about "the working of freedom" without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what. The bare use of "freedom" with only an optimistic sentiment is insufficiently specified to determine whether the reference is to freedom from interference (negative) or capacity/empowerment to act (positive).

records.speaker: Mr. O'Connell
records.sentence:
He knew that it had great evils, but the people had worked themselves out a certain degree of freedom under it, and while he would desire to alter it, in order that its operation might

be made more unembarrassed, he would still adhere to it in preference to the noble Lord's bill, especially as that bill had not a proper basis.
records.haiku_rationale: The people worked themselves out "a certain degree of freedom" referring to increased capacity and empowerment to act within a system they have shaped, contrasted with reform that would remove constraints on operation—a positive capacity that has been achieved through their own effort.

records.speaker: Lord John Russell
records.sentence: and that, in order to attain and maintain their freedom, they should exercise their ancient constitutional right of providing themselves with the arms of freemen.
records.haiku_rationale: Freemen exercising their constitutional right to provide themselves with arms in order to attain and maintain freedom — the object is the capacity/empowerment of citizens to possess arms as a means to securing freedom against tyranny.

records.speaker: Mr. Macaulay
records.sentence: but the worst was that which worked with the machinery of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to something that "worked with the machinery of freedom" but does not specify what is being freed, from what, or to what. The phrase "machinery of freedom" is too vague and metaphorical in isolation to determine whether this concerns freedom from interference (negative) or empowerment/capacity (positive).

records.speaker: Mr. Law
records.sentence: said, that there was not an infringement upon the liberty of the subject which might not be extracted from some local act.

records.sentence: Was it the case with respect to that which was, perhaps, the highest privilege the House possessed, namely, the privilege of liberty of speech within the walls of Parliament?

records.speaker: Lord Glenelg
records.sentence: The noble and learned Lord had told them that liberty had retrograded in consequence of the law which had been established, but he was bound to dissent from that opinion, because, whatever might be the defects of the ordinance, when he looked to the previous state of Malta, he could not but feel that a sensible advance in improvement had taken place since the ordinance had been framed.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty (in the form of improvements to Malta's governance) is being freed from or advanced beyond a previous state of oppression/defects, moving toward a more improved constitutional condition.

It must be clear to all who had any experience of the business of the House of

records.sentence: It did appear to him, if arguments in favour of privilege were allowed to have a preponderance, that the safety and liberty of the people—of every individual in the kingdom—would be entirely at the mercy of the House of Commons.

records.speaker: The Lord Chancellor
records.sentence: The object of this clause was to assimilate the law in Ireland to what it was in England, and to provide that no man should have a right to the freedom, who did not derive through some one who was a freeman previously to the 31st of March, 1831, or through some person who, since that time, should have become, or should hereafter become, a freeman in respect of servitude.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses legal rights to "freedom" (the status of being a freeman) that are contingent on genealogical descent from prior freemen or future attainment of freeman status — this concerns empowerment to hold a legal status and its prerequisites rather than freedom from interference with action or belief.

records.speaker: Lord Lyndhurst
records.sentence: Transmission by birth or marriage would give the freedom generally to Protestants, but by servitude a lower class of freemen was introduced, the greater portion of whom would be Catholics.
records.haiku_rationale: This sentence discusses freedom granted to Protestants through transmission by birth or marriage, versus a restricted status ("lower class") for Catholics through servitude. The object being freed is eligibility for a particular social/legal status (Protestant freemen), and what is being imposed or withheld is that status itself based on religion. This is positive liberty in the sense of enabling/empowering a group to enjoy elevated legal standing.

records.speaker: Mr. Halford
records.sentence: We knew that he could not speak on the subject in connexion with political liberty without risking the imputation of vague and puerile declamation;

records.sentence: Such a declaration, coming from such a quarter, was well calculated to excite the jealousy and suspicion of the Chinese Government, and to induce them immediately to take the most effectual measures to put an end to a system which manifestly tended to the destruction of the liberty and independence of the Chinese empire.

records.speaker: The Chancellor of the Exchequer
records.sentence: They had represented to him that they were obliged to keep post-chaises and carriages, on which they paid a heavy tax, but from which they derived little remuneration, and suggested, that if they were at liberty to keep different classes of carriages at a reduced rate of duty, they might, by opening fresh lines of trade, receive some compensation for the injuries they had sustained.

records.speaker: Mr. W. Gladstone
records.sentence: When, therefore, complaints were made of the want of labour in the West Indies, it was most unjust to charge it upon the labourers themselves No one who had seen the excitement that had existed, the inaptitude of all classes to enter upon a state of freedom, no one who knew the difficulties that presented themselves on entering upon negro emancipation, could deny that the result, upon the whole, had been highly honourable to the class of men whom it affected.

records.sentence: That measure ought to apply to railways as well as to canals, for it would be unfair to restrain canal companies from carrying goods on Sunday, if railway companies were to be at liberty to do so.

The object of liberty is not specified (no "freedom of X" or "freedom from Y"), making the sense of what is being freed ambiguous between capacity to act under law versus freedom from interference.

records.speaker: SIR R. H. INGLIS
records.sentence: and if we cannot be members of the same holy faith, would to God that we could concede full liberty to all, yielding in a generous spirit to the dictates of charity and justice, interpreting each other's feelings with brotherly love, seeking to put the best construction on each other's actions, and palliating each other's faults!
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "full liberty to all" in a context of religious difference, calling for mutual tolerance and charitable interpretation—a rhetorical appeal to freedom from sectarian interference and constraint, set against the backdrop of religious coercion and intolerance.

records.speaker: Unknown

records.speaker: MR. ANSTEY
records.sentence: but that she was at perfect liberty to protest, either separately or conjointly with France;
records.haiku_rationale: She is freed from interference or restriction in her ability to protest, either separately or conjointly with France.

records.speaker: Unknown

The phrase "liberty of speech" exemplifies the core negative liberty concept, protecting the capacity to speak without suppression or restriction.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence: Daily their religion was extending itself—new Roman Catholic churches were rising in all directions around us—and the Roman Catholics themselves carried on a wide system of combination, and had perfect liberty of action throughout the British empire.

records.speaker: LORD NORREYS
records.sentence: The proposition appeared to him to be a step towards that system of centralisation which, whilst it increased the public expenditure, would destroy that local government which secured the peace and tranquillity of the country, and was at the foundation of public liberty.

records.speaker: SIR G. GREY

records.haiku_rationale: The sentence claims suffrage (voting rights) is a necessary accompaniment to liberty. This expresses the positive liberty view that electoral empowerment—the capacity to participate in choosing government—is essential to freedom, rather than merely freedom from interference with voting.

records.speaker: MR. C. ANSTEY
records.sentence: and, assuming that to be the true state of the case, he affirmed that they were at liberty to rise upon their captors and put them to death.

records.sentence: But I cannot help urging this—that the plan I propose would have the effect of doing much more for the general liberty of commerce than the plan of unconditional legislation would do.

records.speaker: MR. BRIGHT
records.sentence: I honour the memory and revere the character of those who have gone before us, and who gained for us the personal and political liberty which we possess.

records.speaker: The EARL of ABERDEEN
records.sentence: They had no constitutions or constitutional liberty;

records.sentence: If that be the case, it shows that there may be some alteration in the forms of this House without injury to the essential rights of discussion, and without impediment to the freedom of debate.

records.speaker: MR. URQUHART

records.speaker: MR. O'FLAHERTY
records.sentence: and he warned the House, and English Members in particular, that they were arming Ministers with a power which would come in the end to be turned against themselves, and used to put down freedom of expression in Lancashire and Yorkshire.

records.speaker: LORD C. HAMILTON

records.speaker: MR. GLADSTONE
records.sentence: Further, it had the effect of lowering the colonial tone—it was adverse to the cherishing habits of freedom and self-dependence.

records.speaker: MR. M. GIBSON
records.sentence: It is Her Majesty's hope and belief that by combining liberty with order, by preserving what is valuable, and amending what is defective, you will sustain the fabric of our institutions, as the abode and the shelter of a free and happy people.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a cause to be "combined with order" in sustaining national institutions and enabling a "free and happy people"—a rhetorical appeal to liberty as freedom from tyranny/oppression, foundational to institutional stability.

records.speaker: SIR J. B. WALSH

records.speaker: LORD DUDLEY STUART
records.sentence: and now they spoke only of the evils of the Hungarian constitution, passing wholly by the reforms established by Kossuth, to whom the country was indebted for the liberty of the peasants and of the press.

records.speaker: MR. DISRAELI
records.sentence: They maintain that all those considerations to which I have referred respecting the maintenance of order, of liberty, and of the stability of States, are mere superstitions;

records.speaker: MR. BRIGHT

records.speaker: LORD D. STUART

records.speaker: MR. ADDERLEY
records.sentence: He could not agree with the other plans which had been laid down, or with the premises upon which they had been laid down, nor could he agree with the noble Lord in the historical sketch upon which he seemed to rest his policy and his statesmanship, when he stated that it had always been the policy of this country to give freedom to the colonies.

records.speaker: LORD J. RUSSELL
records.sentence: He said, if such grounds were laid before him as he thought were sufficient, he would have proceeded in that course, and felt at liberty to summon the witnesses;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker would feel "at liberty to" summon witnesses—this is procedural language describing permission to act within parliamentary/legal procedure, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: The EARL of ESSEX
records.sentence: Having thanked their Lordships for the patience with which they had hitherto heard him, he would conclude by expressing his fullest concurrence in the last sentence of Her Majesty's Speech, namely, that by combining liberty with order, by preserving what was valuable, and amending what was defective, their Lordships would sustain the fabric of our institutions as the abode and the shelter of a free and happy people.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a foundational value to be combined with order in sustaining institutions; the speaker references liberty as a general political ideal opposed to defect and disorder, not specifying a particular freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: LORD J. RUSSELL*
records.sentence: But there was another and a most remarkable characteristic attending these colonies, and this was, that wherever Englishmen have been sent, or have chosen to settle, they have carried with them the freedom and the institutions of the mother country.
records.haiku_rationale: Englishmen are freed from foreign interference and empowered with self-governing institutions (characteristic of the mother country); the specific object of freedom is political self-governance and the civil liberties systems of England.

records.speaker: LORD R. GROSVENOR
records.sentence: and he felt sure that, rejoicing in their own liberty, it would be a matter of gratification to them to see the business of Parliament so conducted as not to inflict pain and discomfort upon those sitting upon the same bench and engaged in the same arduous duties as themselves.

records.speaker: The EARL of ESSEX

records.haiku_rationale: Individual Italian States are empowered to exercise municipal liberty—self-governance and local autonomy—a capacity being fostered and valued as a source of national greatness.

records.speaker: EARL RUSSELL
records.sentence: But if the Russians once come into the enjoyment of greater privileges and greater freedom, so far from that feeling of hostility to the Poles existing, they will then be glad to see them also in the enjoyment of civil and religious liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Russians gaining capacity to enjoy "greater privileges and greater freedom" and subsequently allowing Poles to enjoy "civil and religious liberty" (freedom from interference with conscience and belief).

records.speaker: SIR JAMES ELPHINSTONE
records.sentence: Henley) the question of which he had given notice, he felt pretty sure what the answer would be, and he would therefore take the liberty of making some remarks in respect to that matter.

records.speaker: LORD JOHN RUSSELL:
records.sentence: Within a very few years we have seen great changes in several of the nations of Europe in the direction of representative Constitutions, of greater freedom of person, greater freedom of the press, and greater encouragement of those powers which bad Governments take away, and which good Governments take away, and which good Governments are delighted to see their subjects enjoy.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom of person" (protection from interference with bodily integrity) and "freedom of the press" (freedom from government censorship/interference), both classic negative liberties. The reference to "powers which good Governments are delighted to see their subjects enjoy" reinforces a negative liberty framing: capacities protected from government suppression rather than government-enabled capacities.

records.speaker: MR. ROEBUCK
records.sentence: Similar liberty to change a name had not been given by the War Office in a recent case.

records.speaker: LORD FERMOY
records.sentence: If in concert England, France, and Austria were to come to the resolution to insist that Russia should either take the alternative of adhering honestly to the Treaty of Vienna, or be prepared to see them come to the support of Poland in the endeavour to win her freedom, we might depend upon it that there would be no war—that Russia would either do justice to Poland or she would be set altogether free;
records.haiku_rationale: Poland's freedom here refers to national independence and self-determination—the capacity to govern itself free from Russian domination; this is positive liberty (empowerment to act as a sovereign state) rather than merely freedom from interference.

records.speaker: MR. M'MAHON
records.sentence: It was absurd to maintain that the Legislature, having been tricked into the passing of such an Act as that of 1842, which he must characterize as a job, was not now at liberty to retrace its steps.
records.haiku_rationale: The Legislature is freed from constraint—it is empowered to retrace its steps and reconsider prior legislation, overcoming a past act that tricked it. This is about capacity and self-governance to act.

records.speaker: THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER

Under freedom of competition the amount of a duty must go to the man who buys, and not to him who produces.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence: He had only risen to protest against the House being deceived, conceiving that by any hasty action of their own in the case of Poland, they might be hurrying the Government into that which might become a most serious complication, without being likely to advance in Poland the cause of true freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "the cause of true freedom" in Poland rhetorically as an abstract value opposed to hasty, complicating action. The "true freedom" being advanced is not further specified—it is not freedom from a concrete interference, nor freedom to perform a particular action, but a general appeal to freedom as a political ideal that the Government should not undermine through rash intervention.

records.speaker: VISCOUNT PALMERSTON

records.speaker: THE EARL OF CARNARVON

records.speaker: EARL RUSSELL
records.sentence: Would they allow as much freedom of opinion as the  Ammonia  and other newspapers publish now?

records.speaker: MR. DISRAELI
records.sentence: But the principle of religious liberty is impugned if you pass a law by which the Dissenters may say to the followers of the Church:—We will invade your sacred places, and will enforce our claims to keep your consecrated ground for the interment of our dead according to our conditions and regulations.
records.haiku_rationale: Religious liberty (freedom from state interference with religious practice and conscience) is being impugned by a law that allows Dissenters to enforce burial in consecrated Church ground against the Church's conditions—infringing the Church's freedom from interference in its sacred religious practices.

records.speaker: MR. MAGUIRE
records.sentence: The result was, that the noble Lord was enabled to lift up the veil that hid the atrocities practised in the name of liberty, and under the government of a constitutional King, and which would be odious under the worst imaginable despotism;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" as a cause under which atrocities have been justified and perpetrated; the freedom being discussed is freedom from restraint on governmental action, which enabled harm.

records.speaker: MR. HORSMAN
records.sentence: and when she professes now to march with France and England in the cause of justice and freedom, she has not only her antecedent history to redeem, but her current actions to confront.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "cause of justice and freedom" invokes freedom as an abstract value opposing tyranny or injustice; freedom is what is being fought for in alignment with France and England, presented as a cause or ideal rather than a specific capacity being granted or interfered with.

records.speaker: MR. SCULLY
records.sentence:
The noble Lord at the head of the Government talked in a strain of great liberality of mixed education, and would not countenance anything exclusive, although he took the liberty of reminding him that in the public schools of Eton, Harrow, Rugby,
 144 
and at the University of Oxford, the system was exclusive and carried on exclusively by Protestant clergymen.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of reminding him" is parliamentary procedural language indicating the speaker exercised his right to speak, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value being constrained or enabled.

records.speaker: EARL RUSSELL
records.sentence: But the Emperor of Russia, seeing that the interests of humanity were involved in the question, and that millions, not only of the present race, but of those yet unborn, would derive benefit from the proclamation of freedom, has not hesitated—with due deliberation, but at the same time with the utmost boldness—to declare the freedom of the serfs throughout the wide extent of his dominions.
records.haiku_rationale: The serfs are being freed from the condition of serfdom (servitude/legal bondage); this is freedom FROM a state of unfreedom, exemplifying negative liberty as liberation from constraint.

records.speaker: MR. O'REILLY
records.sentence: and although in France and other countries a contrary system was adopted, it had always been held in England that the individual freedom of the citizen would thereby be compromised.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual citizens are being freed from external constraints on their choices and autonomy; the speaker opposes systems that would compromise this non-interference with personal liberty.

records.speaker: MR. DALGLISH
records.sentence: and I will take the liberty, with the permission of the House, to read the opinion given by the lute Sir James Graham—an opinion which must have great weight on all subjects connected with the Admiralty.

records.speaker: MR. LAYARD
records.sentence: Another was from the Protestants of Austria, asking the Catholic Queen of Spain to grant the same liberty of conscience which they enjoyed in Austria under a Calholic Government.

records.speaker: MR. GRANT DUFF
records.sentence: If they inscribe "absolute toleration" and "unlimited freedom" upon their banners, they will succeed;

records.speaker: MR. HORSMAN
records.sentence: Their war has been not against freedom, but civilization;
records.haiku_rationale: Bare rhetorical invocation of "freedom" (presented as a cause opposed to barbarism/"civilization"), without specifying what is being freed or from what; the sentence gestures toward freedom as a value opposed to the enemy's aims but does not articulate a concrete conception of liberty.

records.speaker: MR. CAVENDISH BENTINCK
records.sentence: We have neither personal nor political liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker asserts absence of both personal liberty (freedom from state interference in private affairs) and political liberty (freedom to participate in governance/exercise political rights), framing these as fundamental freedoms from constraint.

records.speaker: THE EARL OF SHAFTESBURY
records.sentence: and, my Lords, I do hope, and I am sure it is the hope of this country—nay more, it is the earnest prayer of every true man within these realms, that we may yet live to see the time when this down-trodden and long-oppressed people shall enter again upon their ancient rights, and after so much experience and bitter sorrow shall inaugurate a noble career of civil and religious liberty, of humanity, and of justice.
records.haiku_rationale: A people are freed from oppression and restored to their "ancient rights" and enabled to exercise "civil and religious liberty" (freedom from interference in civil and religious matters).

records.speaker: MR. FINLAY
records.sentence: I trust that the Chancellor of the Exchequer will turn his powerful and logical mind to the question, and that having been instrumental in removing many restrictions to free trade, he will support freedom in banking.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom in banking" as an analogue to free trade—freedom from restrictions/regulations on banking activity. This is negative liberty: freedom from interference with banking operations.

records.speaker: MR. DISRAELI
records.sentence: What, then, can we expect in a country where, instead of infallibility, religion is founded upon the principle of free inquiry—and where, though that religion has, generally speaking, been supported by the Civil Power, that Civil Power has yet been established on the principle of civil liberty?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes civil liberty as the foundational principle governing the Civil Power's authority—he is framing "civil liberty" as a constitutional constraint limiting power, not as an enabling capacity. This is negative liberty: freedom from arbitrary exercise of Civil Power.

records.speaker: MR. KIRKMAN HODGSON
records.sentence: It would give greater freedom to contract, which meant greater freedom to industry, and would confer upon honest, deserving, and excellent men opportunities of reaping the fruits of their industry which they had not hitherto enjoyed.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to contract is freedom from legal/regulatory interference with agreements, which is negative liberty; but the sentence's ultimate focus is on enabling opportunities and capacity to reap rewards, which is positive liberty. The passage presents both a removal of constraints (freedom of contract) and an empowerment to act and benefit, making it mixed.

records.speaker: MR. MAGUIRE
records.sentence:

records.speaker: MR. KINGLAKE

records.sentence: I call it the development of that true principle of liberty which is the basis of our constitution.

records.speaker: MR. BLACK
records.sentence: He denied that banks ought to be intrusted with freedom in paper issue as there was freedom in other departments of business, because while the latter was an affair of trade, the former would in reality be nothing more or less than coining money.

records.sentence: He thought, therefore, that the Queen ought not to be placed in the position in which she would be placed if called upon to assent to this measure The Queen had made herself personally responsible to protect the Protestant Constitution, The Roman Catholics were sincere men, but they recognized as part of their religion that liberty of conscience was not the right of any man, and that it was monstrous heresy to suppose the civil power supreme over the spiritual power of the Pope.

records.sentence: They consider that the purpose to be attained is good government, the freedom of the people within the State and their security from without, and that the best mode of attaining these ends is the problem to be solved.

records.speaker: MR. GREGORY
records.sentence: … The best resistance to be offered to Russia is by the strength and freedom of those countries that will have to resist her.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns the capacity of countries to resist Russian dominance through their collective strength and autonomy—it names an enabling empowerment (the freedom of nations to govern and act independently) necessary to withstand external power, not freedom from specific interference.

records.speaker: SIR GEORGE BOWYER
records.sentence: said, he approved the Bill, on the ground that constituencies ought to have the fullest freedom of choice in the selection of representatives, and that restriction by disqualification was opposed to the policy which ought to govern our legislation.
records.haiku_rationale: Constituencies are enabled to exercise the capacity to choose their own representatives without disqualification restrictions.

records.speaker: MR. MAGUIRE
records.sentence: but in the name of the public at large, whose dearest interests are involved in the question of the fitness and competency of the Judge who is to try questions of property, of liberty, and of life.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty here is mentioned as a substantive interest of the public—a domain of law (alongside property and life) on which judicial competency bears—rather than as a freedom-from or freedom-to a particular constraint or capacity. The sentence invokes liberty as a collective value without specifying what interference is forbidden or what capacity is enabled.

records.speaker: MR. WALPOLE
records.sentence: The desire of Parliament was to give liberty to labourers to act in combination when their object was legitimate and reasonable, and to restrain them from combining to abuse the liberty accorded to them.
records.haiku_rationale: Labourers are being freed to act in combination (positive empowerment to engage in collective action), but simultaneously restrained from abusing that granted liberty (negative constraint on interference protection).

records.speaker: LORD CAMPBELL
records.sentence: And can such deliberations take effect if the action of the consulting body is forestalled, and if its liberty is stifled by an engagement nine months before that, come what may, a certain subject shall be forced upon the country?
records.haiku_rationale: A consulting body's liberty—its freedom to deliberate and decide on matters—is being stifled or constrained by a prior engagement that removes its capacity to act freely.

records.speaker: MR. HORSMAN
records.sentence: I believe, Sir—however much it may shock the Gentlemen below the gangway—that there is an irreconcilable enmity between democracy and freedom, but I know of no irreconcilable enmity between freedom and an hereditary House of Lords.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is invoked rhetorically as a value opposed to democracy on one hand and compatible with hereditary aristocracy on the other; no specific object of freedom (e.g., "freedom of speech") or enabling capacity is identified, making the referent of "freedom" too under-specified to determine whether negative or positive liberty is intended.

records.speaker: COLONEL BARTTELOT
records.sentence: But it was the sole occasion, save that of invasion, in which they ought to be at liberty to act as a military force.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is saying that a military force ought to be free from restriction to act militarily — empowered to perform military action — except in cases of invasion. This describes a capacity or empowerment to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: MR. DARBY GRIFFITH
records.sentence: It was not creditable that Members of that House should come forward as champions of the freedom of populations, and then, when in an official position, adopt a different style of language.
records.haiku_rationale: Members claiming to champion freedom of populations while contradicting that position when in office—freedom here refers to freedom from interference with populations' self-determination, a negative liberty value invoked as a principle of consistency.

records.speaker: MR. GATHORNE HARDY
records.sentence: There is no man to whom I would refer a question concerning my own honour with greater frankness, freedom, or unreserve than him;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "freedom" as a personal quality characterizing candor and openness in discussion ("frankness, freedom, or unreserve"), not as a normative claim about liberty-as-a-value from interference or empowerment.

records.speaker: THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER
records.sentence: and it is this hold upon the Executive which is the best, ay, the only security for our freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being protected (secured) FROM executive overreach through parliamentary hold upon the Executive—a negative liberty claim about non-interference with rights.

records.speaker: THE ATTORNEY GENERAL
records.sentence:
says—
 "The realm of England, recognizing no superior under God, but only the King, hath been and is free from subjection to any man's laws, but only to such as have been devised, made, and obtained within this realm, for the wealth of the same, or to such others as by sufferance of the King, the people of this realm have taken at their free liberty by their own consent to be used among them.
records.haiku_rationale: England is free from subjection to external laws—an absence of constraint or domination by foreign authority, defending negative liberty as non-interference with the realm's self-governance.

records.speaker: EARL RUSSELL
records.sentence: in short, in selecting men on whom the conduct, power, faith, and freedom of this country depend for many years—if you give them that advantage freely and fairly, and to a proper extent, then you may hope to settle this question.
records.haiku_rationale: The "freedom of this country" (as one of the qualities/capacities on which national conduct and power depend) is being empowered or secured through proper selection of men and giving them advantage freely and fairly—this is about enabling the nation's capacity to act and endure, not removing external interference from a pre-specified activity.

records.speaker: MR. ADDERLEY
records.sentence: Disunion saps their liberty as well as their power, and paralyses their self-reliance.
records.haiku_rationale: Disunion is presented as sapping the capacity for self-reliance and autonomous action—it removes the ability (positive sense) to act independently, not merely the absence of interference from an external authority.

records.speaker: COLONEL EDWARDS
records.sentence: He would take the liberty of reading the letter which had been addressed to him by the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: Parliamentary procedural usage: the speaker is claiming permission to perform a parliamentary action (reading a letter), a formulaic courtesy phrase with no substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: MR. W. E. DUNCOMBE
records.sentence:
As he believed that this measure was an attempt to change the Constitution of England—that Constitution which had lasted so long, had brought such prosperity and happiness to the people of this country, and had given them an amount of public liberty such as never had been enjoyed by
 72 
any other nation in the world—he should give his support to the Amendment.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "public liberty" as a historically valuable characteristic of England's Constitution that has enabled "prosperity and happiness" for the nation—framed as a constitutional gift and source of national good rather than freedom from a specific interference.

records.speaker: MR. HIBBERT
records.sentence: The whole system of public works prisons was based on the convict gaining his liberty at some future time by good conduct and industry.
records.haiku_rationale: The convict gains liberty (freedom from imprisonment/confinement) at a future time through good conduct and industry—freedom from the constraints of prison, not empowerment to do something.

records.speaker: MR. BRUCE
records.sentence: Gentleman (Sir John Pakington) that such districts should be at liberty to levy rates to defray the cost of schools.
records.haiku_rationale: Districts are granted the capacity/empowerment to levy rates to fund schools—enabling them to act independently in raising funds for education.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence: Whether there is anything in the position of the Papacy, whether there is anything in the position of the Roman Catholics, in respect to their liability to the spiritual influence of the Papacy, which should make us sweep away the safeguard of having a majority of this House bound not to disturb the supremacy of the law, that supremacy being essential to the freedom of this Protestant, and, therefore, wholly and really independent country.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes the "freedom" of the nation (a "Protestant, and, therefore, wholly and really independent country") as freedom from external spiritual/papal interference and disturbance of the supremacy of law — a negative liberty argument against removing safeguards.

records.speaker: MR. CHICHESTER FORTESCUE
records.sentence: It would depend on themselves to retain their liberty;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence presents liberty as something the subjects themselves have capacity or agency to retain through their own actions—framing it as an empowerment or self-sufficiency rather than freedom from external constraint.

records.speaker: MR. WALPOLE
records.sentence:
Hume's Committee runs as follows:—
 "That it is the opinion of this Committee that
 184 
masters and workmen should be freed from such restrictions as regard the rate of wages and the hours of working, and be left at perfect liberty to make such agreements as they may mutually think proper.
records.haiku_rationale: Masters and workmen are freed from restrictions on wages and hours, and left at liberty to negotiate freely — this is freedom from interference with contract and economic negotiation.

records.speaker: THE MARQUESS OF CLANRICARDE
records.sentence: There were only two reasons why railways could not be constructed without a Private Act with the same freedom of trade as other branches of industry were carried on—one being, that railway companies required compulsory powers to take private property, and the other that validity must be given to their bye-laws, by which their business, as public carriers, and other transactions might be beneficially carried on.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is discussing the exceptional reasons why railways cannot operate with the same freedom of trade (freedom from restriction/interference) as other industries—specifically, they need compulsory powers and legal validity for bye-laws, implying railways lack the standard freedom of trade that other commercial branches enjoy.

records.speaker: LORD CLARENCE PAGET
records.sentence: It was certainly desirable that we should go on constructing those iron-clads, and constructing them regularly, and the Government were responsible for this—not to allow other nations to build more powerful armour-plated ships, or ships of any other description to an extent which, compared with our own force, might endanger the liberty, the honour, or the dignity of this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The liberty being protected is the nation's freedom from foreign military domination or constraint—the capacity to act independently without being endangered by other nations' superior naval power.

records.speaker: LORD MONCK
records.sentence: trusted that in any measure that might be framed upon this subject we should not throw overboard in matters of an ecclesiastical nature the principle which had been adopted with such eminent success in civil matters—namely, that of leaving the colonists the most perfect liberty to manage their own affairs.
records.haiku_rationale: The colonists are freed to manage their own affairs (empowered to self-govern) without interference in both ecclesiastical and civil matters; this is positive liberty—the capacity to govern oneself granted by leaving them alone.

records.speaker: GENERAL PEEL
records.sentence: but no doubt a liberal and paternal Government has had its attention directed to the promotion of the liberty and the welfare of the country.
records.haiku_rationale: The Government promotes "liberty and welfare" of the country — this invokes liberty as a general cause or value that a paternal government directs attention toward, without specifying freedom from what interference or freedom to do what. The object of freedom is not clearly articulated.

records.speaker: THE EARL OF CARNARVON
records.sentence: Colenso's request, and to curtail the clergy of Natal of any liberty which the recent judgment of the Privy Council had conferred upon them, either in acknowledging or in not acknowledging Dr.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses curtailing clergy of Natal of liberty (freedom) that the Privy Council had conferred upon them — freedom from state interference in ecclesiastical judgment (whether to acknowledge or not acknowledge Dr. Colenso). This is freedom FROM interference with their discretionary authority.

records.speaker: MR. BRIGHT
records.sentence:
From the hour of their freedom until this hour it has been merely the freedom
 322 
granted by Parliament.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (of a people or entity) granted by Parliament - positive liberty, as it refers to empowerment or authority bestowed by a legislative body, enabling self-governance or autonomous action.

records.speaker: MR. TORRENS
records.sentence: said, he wished to ask the Secretary to the Treasury, Whether it is the fact that the clerks of the Inspector General of Imports and Exports have applied to the Board of Customs for liberty to forward a Petition to the Lords Commissioners of Her Majesty's Treasury, praying for a re-consideration of a Petition presented in May last, with a view to giving them a more substantial benefit than was afforded by the recent Treasury Minute upon Customs Salaries;
records.haiku_rationale: The clerks have applied for liberty to forward a petition—a parliamentary procedure sense where "at liberty to" means "permitted/allowed to" perform an administrative action, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: SIR E. BULWER-LYTTON
records.sentence: Not that the middle class has not as many faults of its own as any other class above or below, but that, on the whole, it the most faithfully represents all the interests and opinions which constitute the mind and welfare of a nation, and the most felicitously reconciles the securities of order with the demands of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as a political value that must be reconciled with "securities of order," framing it as a demand the middle class addresses—freedom from constraint/oppression in the context of political order, characteristic of negative liberty rhetoric.

records.speaker: MR. COLERIDGE
records.sentence: All, then, that we ask to be done with the Colleges is that the State should remove restrictions on their freedom of action which the State itself imposed.
records.haiku_rationale: The State is asked to remove restrictions on colleges' freedom of action—this is freedom from state-imposed interference, negative liberty.

records.speaker: MR. M'CULLAGH TORRENS
records.sentence: It is, indeed, an essential part and parcel of international freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "international freedom" as a value without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what. It is a bare rhetorical assertion about freedom as a cause or principle, without the substantive detail needed to determine whether the underlying claim concerns freedom from interference or freedom to act.

records.speaker: MR. COLERIDGE
records.sentence: As to the Universities, it enacts, and so to say it compels, freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Universities are compelled to grant freedom (an empowering capacity), suggesting positive liberty — the enabling of Universities to act freely or the empowering of persons within them.

records.speaker: THE BISHOP OF LONDON
records.sentence: I do not mean that liberty should be altogether constrained — that the whole Church of England must be reduced to absolute uniformity, so that there should not be the slightest difference between the mode of performing Divine worship in one church and the mode of performing it in another—but that liberty shall be legally secured, not licence seized by individuals in the hope that they may escape in immunity from the consequences of their licence.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty (freedom of action in religious practice and worship modes) is being constrained versus legally secured, distinguishing legitimate liberty from unregulated licence—this is about freedom from arbitrary interference and unlawful constraint on how churches may conduct worship.

records.speaker: MR. GATHORNE HARDY
records.sentence: Member would not be at liberty to move that the Riding should be divided into two divisions with three Members each, because the clause said distinctly that it should be in three divisions with two Members each.
records.haiku_rationale: A member is constrained from making a particular procedural motion because a clause explicitly forbids it; "at liberty to move" here means having procedural permission or lack of constraint.

records.speaker: MR. G. MORRIS
records.sentence: but about the year 1842 a change was made, by which Roman Catholics were admitted to the freedom of the town.
records.haiku_rationale: Roman Catholics were admitted to the freedom of the town—granted the right to participate in municipal privileges and self-governance (a capacity/empowerment).

records.speaker: MR. M'LAREN
records.sentence: I will take the liberty of reading two sentences from a petition which I have presented to-day from Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a procedural phrase ("took the liberty of") used as a colloquial softener before reading parliamentary business, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: MR. GLADSTONE
records.sentence: and learned Gentleman will see that there are real barriers in our way which restrict very much the liberty of choice we must possess when we are here dealing with one of those questions of which this House is entirely master, and on which the country has formed a distinct and decided opinion.
records.haiku_rationale: Restrictions on the liberty (capacity) of choice available to Parliament when legislating on matters where the country has formed a decided opinion—an obstruction to Parliament's ability to act freely.

records.speaker: LORD COLCHESTER
records.sentence: whereas now an attempt was made to control the course of action of those who only used their liberty to maintain the rates.
records.haiku_rationale: A group is being freed from control/interference in their action of maintaining the rates (their chosen course of conduct).

records.speaker: MR. GRAVES
records.sentence: and the tendency of legislation was to limit still further their freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom of persons (implied: merchants or traders) is being limited by legislation—freedom from legislative interference or restriction of their capacity to act commercially.

records.speaker: MR. REARDEN
records.sentence: : Am I at liberty to move the latter part of the Amendment?
records.haiku_rationale: Mr. Rearden is asking whether he is permitted to make a procedural motion under parliamentary rules; "at liberty to" is a parliamentary idiom meaning "permitted" or "allowed" in a procedural sense, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: THE EARL OF DERBY
records.sentence: I have already said that the seats are not vacant, and it is proposed to take only four of the seven that were at liberty for disappointed candidates;
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty" here is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning "available" or "not yet assigned," not a substantive claim about freedom as a value. The sentence concerns allocation of parliamentary seats, not liberty from interference or capacity empowerment.

records.speaker: VISCOUNT ENFIELD
records.sentence: they are judges in cases of life and death, in cases which concern property, liberty, character, and life itself.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence lists liberty as one of several important legal interests or stakes that judges decide in cases (alongside property, character, and life), without specifying whether this concerns freedom from interference or empowerment to act. The context is purely descriptive of judicial scope.

records.speaker: MR. THOMAS CAVE
records.sentence: He asked him why he did not free himself from slavery, having the means and knowing the desirability of freedom;
records.haiku_rationale: The person is being freed from slavery, which is removal of an unjust constraint on liberty itself.

records.speaker: MR. STEPHEN CAVE
records.sentence: If a guard was informed that something was going wrong, was he to be at liberty to stop the train or not?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is asking whether a guard has the power/authority to stop a train when informed of danger—a question about empowered capacity to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: MR. GATHORNE HARDY
records.sentence: Has it interfered with ordinary freedom of intercourse?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is asking whether something has interfered with freedom of intercourse—the freedom from obstruction in ordinary social and commercial interaction.

records.speaker: MR. WINTER BOTHAM
records.sentence:
The argument used by Milton in his  Plea for the Liberty of Unlicenced Printing , was applicable to this question—
 "Where there is much desire to learn, there of necessity will be much arguing, much writing, many opinions;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes Milton's "Plea for the Liberty of Unlicenced Printing" to argue that freedom of the press (unlicenced printing) enables intellectual inquiry and debate—where people are free from censorship of printing, there arises much arguing and writing.

records.speaker: MR. GLADSTONE
records.sentence: Gentleman with reference to our freedom of future action upon the state of affairs he has made known to us.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of future action—capacity to act without constraint based on new information; empowerment to choose future policy responses

records.speaker: THE BISHOP OF PETERBOROUGH
records.sentence: Still there is one great encouragement I feel —it is a thought that has been present to my mind all through this debate— that is that I have the privilege of addressing an assembly in which freedom of speech is still permitted to its members.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech is the specific object—the Bishop is celebrating that members of Parliament are free from interference in their ability to speak.

records.speaker: SIR CHARLES W. DILKE
records.sentence: The despatches of Lord Carnarvon showed that the policy of the present Government was adopted at the Colonial Office a long time ago, and the Duke of Buckingham, in a despatch last year, while deploring the fresh disturbances which had arisen, stated that the Government did not feel at liberty to assume the control of native affairs or undertake the duty of defending the colony from native disburbances.
records.haiku_rationale: The Government is constrained from acting—it did not feel at liberty to assume control or undertake defence—describing their inability or non-empowerment to intervene in native affairs; this reflects freedom from a duty or obligation they declined to assume, a negative liberty regarding constraint from governmental action.

records.speaker: MR. BERESFORD HOPE
records.sentence:
and to show to the House what is the nature of the views contained in that pamphlet, which has brought down the dissent of the Rector of Lincoln, I will read the passage which he singles out for criticism—
 "I venture very earnestly to urge the conviction that the intellectual freedom for which Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is "intellectual freedom," which refers to freedom from interference with intellectual inquiry and thought. This is negative liberty—the absence of restraint or constraint on the exercise of mind.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence: Gentleman lectured upon equality and liberty until he (Mr.

records.sentence: Moved, That a Select Committee be appointed, "to inquire into the present modes of conducting Parliamentary and Municipal Elections, in order to provide further guarantees for their tranquillity, purity, and freedom" ( Mr.

records.speaker: MR. BRIGHT
records.sentence: It is notorious that in many countries the freedom is perfect;

records.speaker: MR. WHALLEY
records.sentence:
Despite the Resolution of last Session, personal interests were ignored, and a grant was to be made to the Trustees of Maynooth College—Bishops of the Church of Rome, who from the time they got possession of

records.speaker: MR. W. M. TORRENS
records.sentence: Before this Bill was in being, before the General Election, before the memorable Resolutions of last year were framed, I took the liberty of submitting to the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of submitting" is parliamentary procedural language indicating the speaker is making a request or proposal; no claim about freedom-as-a-value is being made.

records.speaker: THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER
records.sentence: Gentleman opposite thinks so necessary, and with absolute freedom to regulate her own affairs in her own way, in a country like Ireland, with no other check except such as might be imposed by a court of law—not by an ecclesiastical court.

records.speaker: VISCOUNT CRICHTON

records.speaker: MR. PIM
records.sentence: Such a  quasi  Establishment, without freedom, without the power of managing her own affairs, would be the most fatal thing that the House could do in respect to the Church.
records.haiku_rationale: The Church is being freed to manage her own affairs — empowerment to self-governance, not merely freedom from interference.

records.speaker: EARL GRANVILLE
records.sentence: Of course, the noble Duke would be at liberty to move his Amendments at any stage of the Bill;

records.speaker: THE MARQUESS OF HARTINGTON
records.sentence: He denied that there was any ground for saying that in the negotiations between the Government and the Companies there was anything which in the slightest degree diminished the freedom of action of the Government with regard to the contracts in Parliament.

records.speaker: Unknown

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence: The Bill, in fact, proposed to extend the privilege of a small section of the community at the expense of freedom of speech at present enjoyed by the public.

records.sentence: I need not say it is a matter of great regret to the Government that the proceedings of this meeting should have been interrupted in the manner stated, and that there is every desire on our part to maintain freedom of meeting and discussion in Ireland.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence: It might be right to give a new Church entire freedom;

records.speaker: MR. T. CHAMBERS
records.sentence: And all this was done, forsooth, in the interests of religious liberty!

records.speaker: EARL GRANVILLE
records.sentence: : I must appeal to the words I used, and what I stated was this, that the course the House has pursued, both with regard to the Royal lands and the alteration of the Amendment, leaves the Government at liberty to deal with it as they think fit;

records.sentence: The plan of the Bill amounted to this, that the owner was to be rated, and that at the option of the occupier, because the tenant was to be at liberty to deduct the rate from his rent.

records.speaker: MR. G. O. MORGAN

records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is referring to compulsory bye-laws as an interference with the liberty of Englishmen — a constraint on non-interference with individual conduct or choice, specifically regarding what regulations can be imposed.

records.speaker: MR. GREENE
records.sentence:
The simple question was, whether persons who were incarcerated and who were unable to protect themselves, should have opportunities of expressing their desire to come out into the world again to those who would see that their right to liberty
 
 1011 
should be vindicated.
records.haiku_rationale: Imprisoned persons are freed from incarceration (given opportunities to express their desire for release and to have their "right to liberty" vindicated), addressing their capacity to regain agency and exit confinement.

records.speaker: LORD WAVENEY
records.sentence: In their loyalty to a Sovereign who was a great lover of liberty they saw no need of foreign intervention.
records.haiku_rationale: The Sovereign's love of liberty is invoked as a value opposed to foreign intervention; this is a rhetorical reference to freedom from external interference/control.

records.speaker: SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT
records.sentence: The law should not interfere with the personal liberty of the individual—he should have free power to dispose of his property as he wished;
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from legal interference with personal liberty in property disposition; negative freedom established by removing constraints on disposal.

records.speaker: MR. P. J. SMYTH
records.sentence: Slavery may be imposed on a people—liberty cannot be, she must be won—and as a rule the greatness of the effort made to win her is the measure of the fitness to receive her, the best preparation for her enjoyment, and the surest guarantee of her permanency.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty as a collective capacity that a people must achieve and earn through their own effort — emphasizing empowerment and self-governance as something gained rather than something merely freed from interference.

records.speaker: MR. BLENNERHASSETT
records.sentence: If I were asked to name the fundamental cause of their discontent, I would say that it arises from the conviction they entertain that, although they may have Constitutional freedom in theory, they are without it in fact, and that the essential conditions which make goverment through a Representative Assembly, freely chosen by the people, the highest type of ordered liberty, do not exist in Ireland.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker identifies government through a freely chosen Representative Assembly as "the highest type of ordered liberty" — this refers to the capacity (empowerment) of a people to govern themselves through democratic self-determination, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: MR. GIBSON
records.sentence: but it was rather too much to ask the House to adopt clauses which would absolutely sweep away freedom of contract, not only in the future but in the past, and which placed freedom of contract outside the pale of the law altogether.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with contracts: the speaker opposes clauses that would restrict the ability to enter into and enforce contracts without legal impediment.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE
records.sentence:
426 
It is gratifying to see the Radical Members of this House rising in their places to defend great constitutional principles, which secure the freedom of the people of this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being invoked is constitutional liberty securing the people from interference—a protection against tyranny, not an empowerment to do something specific.

records.speaker: DR. KENEALY
records.sentence: " Such freedom as was asked for by the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and does not specify what freedom is being discussed or whether it involves liberation from constraint or empowerment to act, making classification impossible.

records.speaker: LORD ELCHO

When he found Gentlemen whose views on this question of interference with contract were diametrically opposed to his own, supporting the Bill on the very ground that it did interfere with freedom of
 
 789 
contract, he thought there was  ipso facto  good ground that the enemy was in the right, and that this unsound policy did exist in the Bill.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with contract—that is, non-interference with the liberty to make agreements freely—is a paradigmatic negative liberty.

records.speaker: THE EARL OF CARNARVON
records.sentence: we have looked to freedom of government as our ultimate object, and we have been rewarded by an almost immeasurable freedom of growth.
records.haiku_rationale: People are freed from interference in governing themselves (negative liberty), which enables them to experience freedom to grow (positive liberty); the sentence conflates these two aspects.

records.speaker: THE LORD CHANCELLOR
records.sentence: He took the liberty of stating on a former occasion what he found to be the fact—namely, that since the Union, so far was the minority from being unrepresented, there were actually made out of the Irish Peerage no fewer than 61 Peers of the Realm.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of stating" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning "ventured to say" or "permitted himself to say"; it does not concern freedom-as-a-value or constraints on human action.

records.speaker: SIR HENRY JACKSON
records.sentence: but he does this with due subordination of the case to his conviction of the rights of the matter and the law bearing upon it, to considerations as to public time, and to the feelings of others, and he considers himself at liberty entirely to disregard, if necessary, the instructions with which clients too often hamper him as to the manner in which he shall conduct the case.
records.haiku_rationale: A barrister is freed from constraint—specifically, from being bound by clients' instructions—to conduct his case according to his own professional judgment and the law.

records.speaker: SIR ALEXANDER GORDON
records.sentence: As things now stood, a Militia officer was at liberty to go where he pleased;
records.haiku_rationale: A Militia officer has freedom from restriction on his movement/whereabouts—he is free from interference in choosing where to go.

records.speaker: EARL GRANVILLE
records.sentence: But do your Lordships believe that if absolute freedom were given to Convocation the Tests Acts would have been repealed long since?
records.haiku_rationale: Convocation is being freed from constraints (the Tests Acts implied restrictions) to govern itself and make its own legislative decisions—an empowerment to act, not merely absence of interference.

records.speaker: SIR GEORGE BOWYER
records.sentence: It was a model for municipal freedom and good government;
records.haiku_rationale: Municipal bodies are being empowered (granted capacity) to govern themselves—positive freedom to self-govern, not freedom from external interference.

records.speaker: MR. COWPER-TEMPLE
records.sentence:
" 
His object was to preserve to school boards a liberty which many of them had lost through a misunderstanding of the Act of 1870.
records.haiku_rationale: School boards are being restored/preserved in their capacity to act (exercising powers under the Act of 1870) after losing that capacity through misinterpretation—positive liberty as empowerment.

records.speaker: LORD FREDERICK CAVENDISH
records.sentence: Did the Scotch value liberty less than Englishmen did?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" as an abstract value or cause, comparing national groups' commitment to it without specifying freedom from or to what particular constraint or capacity.

records.speaker: LORD FREDERICK CAVENDISH
records.sentence: The constitution of the past might have been considered satisfactory in the days of slavery, but it was unfitted to the days of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contrasts a constitutional arrangement suited to "days of slavery" with one suited to "days of freedom," invoking freedom as the absence of the constraint of slavery.

records.speaker: MR. LOWE
records.sentence: Wilson as an inquisitor to get information, which might be used greatly to the injury of the Government of Egypt, but, as I understand the matter, it was a very considerable liberty to send him out, unless they had made up their minds to some definite policy.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: The utmost liberty should be given to seamen before the voyage commenced, but coupled with such discipline as would be necessary for safety.
records.haiku_rationale: Seamen should be freed from (before voyage) restrictive constraints, but disciplined during voyage for safety—both non-interference (liberty) and enabling conditions (discipline for ordered action) are present, making this ambiguous between negative and positive liberty.

records.speaker: MR. RITCHIE
records.sentence: If he had had the opportunity, on previous occasions, of taking the opinion of the House on the subject, he should not have thought himself at liberty again to trouble the House with it;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "at liberty" in the parliamentary procedural sense, meaning "entitled" or "permitted" to bring a matter before the House again—a formulaic expression about parliamentary privilege, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: MR. JOHN BRIGHT
records.sentence: and if, in consequence of the political character of the Church, these Church questions come into the political arena, it is almost certain they will be discussed very much with the same kind of freedom with which other political questions are discussed.
records.haiku_rationale: Church questions will be discussed with freedom (from interference/censorship) in the same manner as other political questions in the political arena.

records.speaker: MR. E. JENKINS
records.sentence:
and, for his own part, he was prepared to divide the House unless the Chancellor of the Exchequer was able to give the assurance that in no case would the money be used in any way to limit the

records.speaker: MR. ASSHETON CROSS
records.sentence: Why, practical self-government and local liberty are the growth of years.

records.speaker: MR. NEWDEGATE

records.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
records.sentence: That was the freedom they enjoyed.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers generically to "freedom" that some group "enjoyed" but provides no substantive specification of what was being freed or from-or-to what, making it too bare and context-dependent to classify definitively.

records.speaker: MR. JOHN GEORGE MACCARTHY
records.sentence: public health would be promoted, taxation would be diminished, climate would be improved, a new element of healthy Conservatism would be introduced into Irish social life by the formation of a class of peasant proprietors, whose interest in the soil and security in the enjoyment of the fruits of their own labour would render them industrious, law-respecting, and order-loving citizens—the bases of social order, civil freedom, and national prosperity.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "civil freedom" as a collective good that would flow from creating peasant proprietors with security in property rights and fruits of labour. records.speaker: MR. MULHOLLAND
records.sentence: He said he wished to interfere with freedom of contract as little as possible, and that he interfered with it in the case of small tenancies, only because, in the circumstances of Ireland, the tenant was not free;

records.speaker: LORD CAMPBELL
records.sentence: Their newly-gotten right to go to war with one another—a necessary incident of freedom—they would owe to a State which in the world has always been the patron of tranquillity and order.

records.speaker: MR. W. E. FORSTER
records.sentence: That is the good government or better government of the people of Turkey —the interest of the freedom of the Christian subjects of the Porte from the cruel bondage and the senseless tyranny which, until it ceases, makes that European peace impossible which, as the Earl of Derby rightly stated, is the chief interest of England.
records.haiku_rationale: Christian subjects of the Porte are being freed from cruel bondage and senseless tyranny—a claim about freedom from oppression and unjust rule.

records.speaker: MR. CHAMBERLAIN
records.sentence: If the Greeks had a Kingdom given to them, with boundaries equal to their legitimate aspirations, they would show themselves worthy of their ancestors, and fight again if their freedom or independence should be attacked.

records.speaker: MR. JACOB BRIGHT
records.sentence: All who had travelled in those districts would tell them, that when they stepped into a Greek town they found a place with all the signs of freedom and progress, and that the contrast between Greek and Turkish territory was as great as it possibly could be.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker observes that Greek towns exhibit "signs of freedom and progress" as contrasted with Turkish territory, using freedom as a general descriptor of the condition of Greek society rather than specifying what particular freedom or from-or-to what it consists.

records.sentence: No Englishman who went to the Channel Islands could go there without risk of his personal liberty and loss of his property.

records.sentence: The Prime Minister had stated that it was in defence of European liberty that the Government had taken up their present position.

records.speaker: LORD ESLINGTON
records.sentence: and that they would go hand-in-hand in doing their duty in the Conference by resisting a dangerous peace, and in securing for these different communities freedom and good government.

records.speaker: MR. WALTER
records.sentence: He wanted to know how far, by the expenditure of money or military operations, the Government were prepared' to curtail liberty in those parts?

records.speaker: THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER
records.sentence: We desire to promote the cause of freedom, of liberty, and of peace, upon the largest and the highest scale.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" and "liberty" as abstract causes in opposition to their contraries (implicitly: oppression, unfreedom, conflict); it does not specify what is being freed from interference nor what capacity is being enabled, making the specific object of freedom under-specified and the reading ambiguous between negative liberty (non-interference as a cause) and rhetorical flourish.

records.speaker: MR. CHAMBERLAIN
records.sentence: Every one of these things, and many others that might be named, touch personal liberty and freedom directly or indirectly;
records.haiku_rationale: Personal liberty and freedom are being recognized as something that various matters "touch" — the sentence is invoking personal liberty as a value under threat, without specifying whether the object is freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: THE MARQUESS OF HARTINGTON
records.sentence: I believe that before the outbreak of these unfortunate disturbances Servia and Roumania, at all events, were enjoying a large measure of real and constitutional freedom and of real happiness and prosperity.
records.haiku_rationale: Servia and Roumania are said to be "enjoying" constitutional freedom and happiness/prosperity—a characterization of their existing state of freedom-as-good-governance and order, not a claim about freedom from interference with a specific activity or capacity.

records.speaker: MR. GRAY
records.sentence: The House of Commons was at liberty to restrict its own privileges;
records.haiku_rationale: The House of Commons is empowered to restrict (limit) its own privileges—this concerns capacity and authority to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: LORD ESLINGTON
records.sentence: It was due to Turkey that it should be stated in the House of Commons that religious freedom was as absolute there as it was in England or in America.
records.haiku_rationale: Religious freedom (freedom from interference in matters of conscience and worship) is an absolute right in Turkey, England, and America—a statement of negative liberty protecting individuals from state coercion in religious life.

records.speaker: THE CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER
records.sentence: I observe that the Austrian Government, for instance, have explicitly declared their neutrality to be conditional, but they reserved to themselves "full liberty of action for the protection of Austrian interests.
records.haiku_rationale: Austrian interests are being freed from constraint—Austria reserves the capacity to act without prior restriction in defence of its interests; the "full liberty of action" refers to empowerment to protect itself.

records.speaker: THE MARQUESS OF HARTINGTON
records.sentence: I have not been sorry that the Government have expressed with freedom and plainness to Russia her objections to the proposals she was making;
records.haiku_rationale: The Government is freed from constraint in expressing objections to Russia—they have the capacity/ability to speak plainly and directly. This is about governmental empowerment to communicate candidly.

records.sentence: It is certain that the feelings of the Christian subjects of the Porte will be in favour of the Porto or of Russia exactly in proportion to the amount of liberty, prosperity, and order which they enjoy under the one, or are likely to obtain under the other.
records.haiku_rationale: Christian subjects' liberty is correlated with their condition of prosperity and order under political rule—a complex state encompassing both freedom from oppression and capacity for flourishing, not reducible to either single dimension.

records.haiku_rationale: Each State is being freed to retain its capacity to take independent action (retire from Congress) and not be bound by majority decisions—positive liberty understood as empowerment or self-governance.

records.speaker: MR. PEASE
records.sentence: One prisoner was set at liberty, three were sent to penal servitude.
records.haiku_rationale: A prisoner was released (set at liberty) from detention, describing a change in legal status from confinement to freedom from constraint.

records.speaker: MR. PARNELL
records.sentence: The absolute knowledge that the visitors were Government officials would procure for them much greater freedom of access and fuller facilities for performing their duties than would otherwise be the case.
records.haiku_rationale: Visitors (Government officials) are being empowered with greater freedom of access and facilities to perform their duties — this is freedom TO do something (access, perform duties), not freedom FROM interference.

records.speaker: MR. P. J. SMYTH
records.sentence: Will that man be disposed to look kindly on the class legislation that thus abridges his liberty?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes "class legislation" for abridging someone's liberty—restricting their freedom from interference. The liberty being constrained is general freedom from discriminatory legal constraint.

records.speaker: MR. P. J. SMYTH
records.sentence: It would be a war against nationality, liberty, and law, and in support of despotism, slavery, and crime.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked here as a rhetorical cause opposed to despotism and slavery—freedom from tyrannical oppression and the domination of slavery, contrasted with the speaker's opposition to war against nationality and law.

records.speaker: LORD ROBERT MONTAGU

records.speaker: MR. GOLDSMID
records.sentence: There were two kinds of freedom—one which relied on the intelligent co-operation and choice of an active population, and was regulated alone by their just regard for each other's right;

records.speaker: MR. GLADSTONE
records.sentence: This is the field upon which were fought all our greatest and noblest battles for freedom.

records.speaker: MR. CHAPLIN
records.sentence: Writing on the 6th of May, 1856, one of the men still living who were responsible for that war pointed out the future danger of an "encroachment upon and absorption of Turkey by Russia," adding that "such a danger to the peace, liberty, and privileges of all Europe we were bound to resist by every means in our power.

records.sentence: These rules and regulations were, no doubt, of pecuniary advantage to the creditors, but were laid down because the Egyptian Government of that day was in the hands of persons whom it was impossible to trust, and who, if full liberty were allowed them, would have involved the country in the greatest possible difficulties.

records.speaker: THE FIRST LORD OF THE TERASURY (Mr. W. E. GLADSTONE)
records.sentence: It must be borne in mind that in regard to the Irish Land Act of 1870 the Government always founded themselves on the exceptional circumstances of Ireland, and the exceptional absence from freedom of contract in that country.

records.sentence: Now, my Lords, I do not think that anyone will suppose that a few weeks—not months—are too much for the consideration by Her Majesty's present Advisers of substantial measures which they may have to introduce with regard to Ireland—with regard to its social state, with regard to its crime, with regard to the fulfilment of contracts, and with regard to personal liberty of action.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "personal liberty of action" as a value to be protected/restored in Ireland alongside social improvement and crime reduction—a rhetorical appeal to freedom from interference or oppression, consistent with negative liberty as a governing principle.

records.speaker: MR. MILVAIN  (Durham)
