records.haiku_rationale: Parents have freedom from interference (the ability to opt out of religious instruction for their children without losing access to other school services), establishing freedom from coercion on the object of religious education.

records.speaker: Mr. LYNN
records.sentence: Friends on the Labour and Liberal Benches, and I am sorry there are not more present because they talked very loudly in their own country with regard to the freedom of education and taking it from under the control of clericalism, and I should have thought that they would have been here even in their attentuated battalion to support us in this attempt to establish public control over our schools.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is education: the sentence advocates removing education from clerical control and establishing public control—a freedom to pursue a particular political goal of secularization and public governance, not a claim about freedom from interference with educational choice itself.

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence: If they have the liberty to do that, they have the liberty to withhold it, and from what I know of the Belfast Corporation I say that Catholic children and Catholic teachers, if there ever were Catholic teachers in these schools, would not have that opportunity given to them.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is discussing whether the Belfast Corporation has the capacity (empowerment) to provide educational opportunity to Catholic children and teachers—freedom to grant or withhold opportunity—which concerns their ability to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Captain BENN
records.sentence: If no business of this kind can be done until the Foreign Secretary is at liberty, the position does not appear to be very important.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty" here is parliamentary procedural language meaning the Foreign Secretary is available or has opportunity to attend to business; this is not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value but rather a formulaic parliamentary usage indicating availability or scheduling status.

records.speaker: Mr. SAMUEL
records.sentence: The whole Bill, from beginning to end, is so objectionable, and so against the freedom of the individual, that I felt constrained to put down my Amendment.
records.haiku_rationale: The individual is being freed from state interference/constraint via the Bill; the speaker opposes restrictions on the individual's liberty to act without government imposition.

records.speaker: Major TRYON
records.sentence: The French Republic have extended their fiscal boundaries in their own areas to include not only the North of Africa, but even such distant places as Madagascar, and if the French may give Preference there under the League of Nations I cannot understand why we should not have equal liberty to do as we please in our own Dominions within the Empire.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker seeks freedom for the British Empire to grant trade preferences in its own dominions—an empowerment to act, analogous to French fiscal freedom in their territories, not freedom from external interference with existing action.

records.speaker: Mr. W. GRAHAM
records.sentence: I have no desire to give away any of our doings up to this stage in that important Commission, but I think I am at liberty to say that the evidence we have already taken points to the urgent need of far-reaching changes in the administrative side of the Income Tax and certainly far-reaching changes in its economic significance.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "at liberty to say" as parliamentary procedural language meaning he is permitted to speak, not making a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: General CROFT
records.sentence:
It seems to me that the only effect would be that his advisers would take scrupulous care that they did not submit any name for a title or honour unless they were quite sure that the suggested recipient was deserving, and they would thus protect not only the honour of the Prime Minister, but what is more important, the
honour of the Throne One ought to have regard to the freedom of.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and truncated mid-clause ("One ought to have regard to the freedom of..."), making it impossible to determine what specific object of freedom is being referenced or whether freedom from interference or capacity to act is at stake.

records.speaker: The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER
records.sentence: I must reserve my liberty till the last moment;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is reserving freedom to make a decision or announcement until the final moment—this is a claim about the speaker's capacity to defer action until a strategically advantageous time, not a claim about freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Sir T. WHITTAKER
records.sentence:
Is Ireland to prevent us from recovering Parliamentary freedom and efficiency here, because really all the objections taken have been taken by those who naturally have looked at the question through Ulster Are we in this Imperial
Parliament as a whole United Kingdom to be held up by a Parliament that cannot do its work because of trouble in Ireland?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "Parliamentary freedom" as a value being threatened by delay or obstruction—freedom from external constraint (Ireland's troubles) preventing the Parliament from functioning. This is rhetorical invocation of liberty as non-interference with Parliament's capacity to do its work.

records.speaker: The SECRETARY of STATE for INDIA
records.sentence: I have hardly met a critic who has not told me that it is absolutely essential for the local Governments to get more freedom from the Government of India.
records.haiku_rationale: Local Governments being freed from interference/control by the Government of India—a classic negative liberty claim to be unobstructed in their own governance.

records.speaker: Mr. ROBERTS
records.sentence: He wants people to have perfect liberty of purchasing where they will.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker wants people to have the capacity/freedom to choose where they purchase goods—this is freedom to act (to purchase where they will), not merely freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. ROSE
records.sentence: I know more than I feel at liberty to say to-night, because, as a matter of fact, I am a member of a Committee on public expenditure, and until certain matters are reported upon I do not think it would be quite within my province to make any statement concerning them.
records.haiku_rationale: A speaker says they are not "at liberty to say" certain things due to their committee membership and confidentiality constraints—this is parliamentary procedure language where "at liberty" means "permitted" or "authorized," not a claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Captain BENN
records.sentence: was right to this extent, that it is the first occasion on which any Minister of Munitions has really been at liberty to-speak freely of the work of his Department.
records.haiku_rationale: A Minister is at liberty to speak freely of departmental work—freedom from prior restraint on speech, a negative liberty.

records.speaker: Commander BELLAIRS
records.sentence:
It is the declared policy of the Labour party, and I do not know why they do not carry it into effect, because in that reform programme which the Socialist Labour party put forward Clause 4 demanded
 complete restoration of freedom of speech publication, travel, residence, and choice of occupation.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence lists "freedom of speech, publication, travel, residence, and choice of occupation" — all are protected domains where individuals should not face interference. These are classic negative liberties: freedom from state or other interference in expression, movement, and personal choice.

records.speaker: Lord R. CECIL
records.sentence: But here we arrive at a point of great importance which involves just what I am afraid of in regard to schemes of nationalisation, which, while promising to give greater facilities and greater freedom to the workmen, always end by less freedom and greater control on the part of those responsible for the management.
records.haiku_rationale: Workmen are promised greater freedom (positive capacity to act) but schemes of nationalisation actually result in less freedom (negative liberty/non-interference curtailed) and greater control by management.

records.speaker: Major TRYON
records.sentence: We cannot be certain that foreign nations may not copy the example of our own Labour party by cutting off: certain essential supplies, and for the sake of freeing ourselves from foreign control, and for the Bake of freedom of development as we wish, we must meet our Dominions and decide now and at once to go forward.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contains two liberty concepts: "freeing ourselves from foreign control" (negative liberty—freedom from interference/domination) and "freedom of development as we wish" (positive liberty—empowerment to pursue chosen development path). These are presented as complementary motivations in a single strategic argument.

records.speaker: Lord R. CECIL
records.sentence: Even if there were no waste, and everything worked well, or better than it does now, the amount that he would get as the reward for increased labour would be insignificant, and, as for freedom, his position, I am convinced, would be infinitely worse.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes freedom as a value being diminished (position "infinitely worse"), but does not specify what is being freed or from/to what—the reference to freedom is rhetorical and contextually ambiguous without clarification of the specific domain or constraint at issue.

records.speaker: Lord R. CECIL
records.sentence: I am convinced that it is a complete delusion that nationalisation will give freedom to the wage-earner, and I do not believe hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker rejects the claim that nationalisation gives "freedom to the wage-earner" — denying that a structural/economic reform empowers workers to act as autonomous agents; this concerns freedom as a capacity to exercise agency.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Colonel AUBREY HERBERT
records.sentence: John Redmond, who died fighting for the cause of his own country and the cause of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "the cause of freedom" as a rhetorical ideal opposed to oppression, in the context of fighting for one's country—a classical negative liberty formulation (freedom from foreign domination or tyranny).

records.speaker: Mr. LYNN
records.sentence: that such exercise and liberty involve extra duty on the staffs and, at the present moment, are delaying the application of the eight-hour day to the Irish warders which has been working in the English Prisons Service since 1st May;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to "exercise and liberty" granted to staffs; the liberty being discussed is the freedom/discretion exercised by staff (a capacity or empowerment to act), whose exercise is causing delay in implementing the eight-hour day policy.

records.speaker: Mr. O'CONNOR
records.sentence: Member for Duncairn in speaking for a minority was to prevent the grant of liberty to the majority.
records.haiku_rationale: The majority is being freed to act (to exercise political power), and the speaker opposes granting them this capacity or empowerment.

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence:
And this is the
hypocrisy of it all—to come here and talk about human liberty and the rights of small nationalities;
records.haiku_rationale: Human liberty and the rights of small nationalities are being invoked as values under threat from hypocrisy, representing freedom from interference in self-determination and autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. HARBISON
records.sentence: I speak as a Tyrone man and as the representative of my Constituents I shall go back to tell them that the men for whom I have fought, and for whom I will fight again, have been denied their liberty on the very night on which we hoped there was going to be universal peace in the world.
records.haiku_rationale: The men have been "denied their liberty"—specifically freedom from constraint/imprisonment on the night peace was expected, contrasting denied non-interference with a presumed right to be free from such denial.

records.speaker: Mr. WALLACE
records.sentence:
One paragraph reads as follows:
 We are of opinion that agreements restraining the liberty of the individual to buy or use the machines of other makers should be declared illegal, and any attempt by promise of bones or imposition of penalty to arrive at such a monopoly should equally be illegal.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses freedom from restraints on the individual's capacity to purchase and use machines without interference from monopolistic agreements or penalties—this is freedom FROM interference with commercial choice and action.

records.speaker: Lord H. CAVENDISH-BENTINCK
records.sentence: They really have believed that we fought this War for liberty, and for the weak and small nations.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from external interference/domination is being invoked as the cause for which the War was fought — nations being freed from aggression or imperial constraint.

records.speaker: Sir A. GEDDES
records.sentence: She is at liberty to make arrangements of that sort.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is parliamentary procedural language meaning "permitted to" or "able to"—it describes capacity or permission to act (make arrangements), not a claim about protecting someone from interference. This is incidental use without substantive reference to liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. CLYNES
records.sentence: I have already said in Committee, and I think in the House, that, personally, I would have preferred to have seen the policemen organised on voluntary lines, in harmony with the desire of the Home Office, with freedom to protect themselves in the police service as regards remuneration and pensions, whilst securing the community against the risks of collective action in the form of indulging in a strike to the public detriment.
records.haiku_rationale: Policemen are granted freedom (empowerment) to protect themselves regarding remuneration and pensions—a capacity to secure their own interests—which is positive liberty, though this freedom is immediately constrained by preventing collective strike action.

records.speaker: Mr. J. JONES
records.sentence: Gentleman consider the possibility of giving freedom and equality of opportunity to all men to become officers in the Army?
records.haiku_rationale: Men are being freed to gain the capacity to become Army officers—an enabling opportunity or empowerment, not mere removal of interference.

records.speaker: Mr. J. JONES
records.sentence: These great generals have had honours showered upon them and have received the freedom of all the great cities of the Kingdom, they have been thanked by both Houses of Parliament, they have behind them the salaries they have received and in front of them the possibility of pensions.
records.haiku_rationale: The "freedom of the cities" refers to the ceremonial honour of receiving the freedom of major cities (a civic designation), not freedom from interference or empowerment to act—it is a formal privilege/distinction conferred on military officers.

records.speaker: The CHAIRMAN
records.sentence: Perhaps I have allowed too much liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is referring to their own procedural conduct in allowing debate or discussion, using "liberty" as a colloquial term for permissiveness or latitude; this is a parliamentary procedural remark rather than a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: wish for religious liberty, those who believe in the nationality of Wales, should not be satisfied to leave the Church to carry on her work.
records.haiku_rationale: Religious liberty here means freedom of the Church and Welsh believers from state interference—freedom from interference with religion and national ecclesiastical autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. BONAR LAW
records.sentence: I believe the Committee met to-day, and I took the liberty myself of sending a letter to the Chairman pointing out that at the time the Committee was appointed the Government then said that they intended on their own initiative to do what they could.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of" is parliamentary procedure language meaning "I ventured to" or "I presumed to," not a claim about liberty-as-a-value or freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. ATKEY
records.sentence: I feel all the more at liberty to make that observation because I have heard it stated that party feeling in this House makes criticism from the Opposition, official or otherwise, to a certain extent, discounted by the Government.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is using "at liberty to" as a parliamentary procedural phrase meaning he is permitted or feels free to proceed with making an observation. This is not a claim about liberty-as-a-value but rather idiomatic parliamentary usage of the word liberty as procedural permission.

records.speaker: Major HILLS
records.sentence: Unless he does, we are left in this position, that we have carried freedom all through the world except in our own home, and we shall be the only white race holding down another white race by the sword.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is invoked as a value (what Britain claims to export) that is being denied to "another white race" in Ireland—freedom from foreign military domination and the capacity for self-determination.

records.speaker: Mr. O'CONNOR
records.sentence: When they are assured by men like myself, who have lived fifty years among the English people in amity and affection, that the masses of the British people are honourable, fair-minded, generous, and liberty-loving;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty-loving" as a character trait of British masses in a rhetorical context about national honour and shared values—freedom from external domination or constraint is the substantive reference here.

records.speaker: Colonel WEDGWOOD
records.sentence: All these people have had four or five months of liberty and equality and fraternisation, which always follows any form of revolution.
records.haiku_rationale: Bare invocation of "liberty" (paired with equality and fraternisation) in a rhetorical description of a post-revolution state, without specification of what freedoms from interference are being discussed or what capacities are being enabled.

records.speaker: Mr. WATERSON
records.sentence:
I am convinced in my own mind that until we are prepared to give self-determination to Ireland—and also self-determination to India—you will have unrest, because it is in accordance with the principles of freedom, and the natural outcome of every nation to govern itself, that it should wish for self-determination—to have that freedom of action
and freedom of thought which is the cause of the aspirations and deep inspiration of a freedom-loving people.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is championing self-determination and the capacity for nations (Ireland and India) to govern themselves—empowerment to act, not mere freedom from interference. "Freedom of action" and "freedom of thought" here are presented as enabling capacities that nations should possess to determine their own affairs.

records.speaker: Sir E. WILD
records.sentence: I invite the Committee, in the interests of freedom of the subject, to carry this Amendment of my hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom of the subject" — a classical negative liberty concept meaning protection from arbitrary state interference, set against a background of "interests" in carrying an amendment, emphasizing non-interference with the rights of citizens.

records.speaker: Sir E. WILD
records.sentence:
Friend will be advised and meet the sense of the Committee in trying to preserve
some signs of British liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: British liberty (implicitly the nation's political independence and freedoms from external/internal constraint); from-to what: preserved against threats or erosion. This is a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause opposed to loss of independence and state autonomy.

records.speaker: Lord R. CECIL
records.sentence: That is my conception of the principles upon which we have gone in erecting the whole structure and fabric of liberty in this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking "liberty" as a foundational political principle underlying the nation's institutional structure—freedom (from interference with fundamental rights and protections) upon which the country's institutions are built.

records.speaker: Mr. O'CONNOR
records.sentence: He spoke of the glories of restored liberty and of the contributions to the history, literature, and progress of the world made by the small nations and of all the emotions that rose in his bosom at that sight, and at the end of it all he made no mention of Ireland.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty here refers to restored national independence and self-governance—the freedom of Ireland (a small nation) from external constraint/colonial rule, which is invoked as a value opposed to subjection.

records.speaker: Mr. JOHN DENNIS
records.sentence: whether any valid reason exists for the restriction of trade liberty in the importation of this fertiliser;
records.haiku_rationale: A speaker questions restrictions on "trade liberty"—the freedom from interference with importing fertiliser. The liberty in question is freedom from constraint on commercial activity (trade).

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: " I am in favour of the fullest freedom;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes freedom as a bare, unspecified value without naming what is being freed or from-or-to what, making the specific object of liberty unclear.

records.speaker: Mr. BONAR LAW
records.sentence: Gentleman really suggest that the Prime Minister or I, as Leader of the House acting for him, may not be at liberty to consult any Member of the House we like?
records.haiku_rationale: This is a rhetorical question asserting the right not to be prevented from consulting Members of the House—a freedom from obstruction in the conduct of parliamentary business.

records.speaker: Mr. SHORTT
records.sentence: According to a census taken in July, 1918, the alien enemies at liberty in this country numbered 10.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty" here is used in the parliamentary procedural sense meaning "present" or "residing," describing a factual state of alien enemies in the country. It is not making a normative claim about liberty as a value or freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. BONAR LAW
records.sentence: Friend the Prime Minister is not at liberty to disclose the proceedings of the Council of Four and the Council of Ten.
records.haiku_rationale: The Prime Minister is not permitted to disclose Council proceedings; "at liberty to" describes his permitted scope of action under parliamentary/diplomatic constraints.

records.speaker: Mr. SEDDON
records.sentence: I believe policemen should be given the fullest liberty of association and opportunity for dealing with any complaints or grievances they may have.
records.haiku_rationale: Policemen are being freed from restrictions on association and given the capacity to address complaints—both absence of interference (negative) and empowerment to act (positive).

records.speaker: Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY
records.sentence: Goode was afterwards set at liberty?
records.haiku_rationale: Goode is being released from detention or captivity; "set at liberty" means freed from restraint or confinement.

records.speaker: Mr. A. WILLIAMS
records.sentence: If it is not the Church of the whole nation, then it has every right to enjoy its freedom and to be ruled by those who are in its strictest sense its own members, and, therefore, this Bill in asking for the practical government of Church affairs to be put into the hands of the Church organisation and to be left with only the most shadowy control of the State over it, is, I say, asking a very large concession indeed.
records.haiku_rationale: The Church is being freed from State control and empowered to govern itself through its own members—this is self-governance capacity, not mere freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Major BARNES
records.sentence: Nobody in this House is more in sympathy with the desire for self-government and freedom than those who are supporting this Motion.
records.haiku_rationale: Self-government is being freed from external control; the speaker is invoking liberty as a value opposed to foreign or external interference in governance.

records.speaker: Mr. EDWARDS
records.sentence: I sympathise with the generating purpose of the Bill in securing more liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker sympathises with a Bill's purpose to secure "more liberty"—an abstract invocation of liberty as a general value/cause, without specifying what is being freed or from-or-to what.

records.speaker: Mr. G. THORNE
records.sentence: I contend, therefore, that the-ruling you have given and rightly given this afternoon makes this Bill, which has no regard for the liberties of Parliament and the traditions of freedom which we have always had before us, one which we have no right to consider, much less accept.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberties of Parliament" and "traditions of freedom" as constraints being violated—Parliament's freedom from interference with its procedures and prerogatives is being threatened by the Bill.

records.speaker: Mr. BONAR LAW
records.sentence: You cannot have a State Church and yet have the absolute freedom which applies to a non-State church.
records.haiku_rationale: A church's absolute freedom (from state interference) cannot coexist with state church status, which necessarily constrains that independence.

records.speaker: Mr. CLYNES
records.sentence: I know there is a good deal of freedom in it, but when it is coupled with the process and procedure of inquiry, there are elements of compulsion which I am sure the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker acknowledges freedom (from procedural constraint) but identifies elements of compulsion within an inquiry process—a mixed statement presenting both freedom from interference and mandatory elements.

records.speaker: Mr. R. McNEILL
records.sentence: As long ago as February this year I asked that this State should be given freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: The state is being empowered to exercise choice; "freedom of choice" refers to the capacity to choose among options, not freedom from interference with a specific activity.

records.speaker: Mr. HARMSWORTH
records.sentence: He has truly said that on more than one occasion I have taken the liberty of asking him not to press questions in relation to Montenegro, and he has always most willingly agreed, although he takes a far greater interest in this question than perhaps any other private Member of the House claims to take.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "taken the liberty of asking" is a parliamentary courtesy expression referring to procedural permission to make a request, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Colonel WARD
records.sentence: I have assumed office in order to establish in the country, justice and freedom, and to give security and bread to the harassed and famine-stricken population.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being promoted is freedom from want (famine, lack of security and bread), and the speaker positions himself as empowered to establish this state of affairs. This is capacity—positive liberty—to create conditions of material security and sustenance.

records.speaker: Sir E. POLLOCK
records.sentence: Those persons most nearly and closely interested will put their points with the utmost freedom, and the greatest knowledge of the facts.
records.haiku_rationale: Persons are freed from interference in presenting their points; they speak with freedom (absence of constraint or inhibition).

records.speaker: Mr. NEAL
records.sentence: There is none of their staff who would consider himself capable of taking part in a controversy of this kind, and employers go before an Arbitration Court very badly handicapped, If you want a recent experience of how desperately unfortunate it is to limit the right of skilled advocacy, you have an instance in the Coal Commission, where there was no freedom of advocacy.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of advocacy is being freed from restrictive limitations on the right to employ skilled legal representation in proceedings; this is negative liberty—freedom from interference with the capacity to present one's case effectively.

records.speaker: Sir PETER GRIGGS
records.sentence: We should give him more freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is unspecified; the sentence does not clarify whether "him" should be freed from interference or empowered to do something specific, making it impossible to distinguish between negative and positive liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. CHARLES EDWARDS
records.sentence: First, I would give more liberty to local authorities by interfering less.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being freed from government interference (negative liberty component), but the speaker frames this as "giving...liberty to local authorities," emphasizing empowerment of a body to govern itself without external constraint (positive liberty framing).

records.speaker: Mr. N. MACLEAN
records.sentence: whether they were at liberty during the period of war or in internment camps;
records.haiku_rationale: The question asks whether certain individuals were "at liberty" (i.e., free from detention/confinement) during wartime, as opposed to being held in internment camps. This concerns freedom from physical restraint and confinement.

records.speaker: Sir E. POLLOCK
records.sentence: It was pointed out that in the case of a woman it might be very necessary to give them the liberty to be excused in certain circumstances.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses granting women the capacity/right to be excused (exempted) from certain obligations or duties in specific circumstances—an empowerment or enabling of discretion.

records.speaker: Mr. GRAHAM
records.sentence: I would respectfully submit, on that point, that the Clause is designed to confer a certain freedom as regards auxiliary or subsidiary occupations.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being conferred to engage in auxiliary or subsidiary occupations—this is empowerment to act, granting capacity for occupational choice.

records.speaker: Mr. WATERSON
records.sentence: I wonder if, in reality, his great objection is to the young men who may be installed into these positions, and who, possessing different ideals and greater aspirations, will bring that larger freedom to India that India is seeking for!
records.haiku_rationale: India is seeking "larger freedom" — empowerment and capacity for self-governance, not merely freedom from interference. This references liberation/independence enabling India to govern itself, a positive liberty concept.

records.speaker: Sir THOMAS BRAMSDON
records.sentence: and, if so, what is the reason for this treatment, and will these men be set at liberty?
records.haiku_rationale: The men are to be freed from detention/imprisonment ("set at liberty")—a claim about freedom from wrongful restraint, which is negative liberty.

records.speaker: Colonel WEDGWOOD
records.sentence: There is complete freedom, as explained in the Joint Committee's Report.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asserts the existence of "complete freedom" but provides no context about what is being freed, from what, or to what—the specific object of freedom is left unspecified and must be inferred from a separate document (the Joint Committee's Report).

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence: Gentleman the Minister for War has now arrived, with a red box—a symbol of British freedom—from the War Office.
records.haiku_rationale: The red box is invoked as a "symbol of British freedom" in a ceremonial context, referring rhetorically to the concept of freedom as a national ideal, without specifying what is being freed or from/to what constraint or enabling capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. MONTAGU
records.sentence: I think it is only right, if India is to possess any key industries, that she should have the liberty of revising her own tariffs in what she considers to be the best way.
records.haiku_rationale: India is being freed/empowered to revise her own tariffs according to her own judgment, not constrained by external interference—this is about capacity to govern economic policy.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Colonel W. GUINNESS
records.sentence: loan, or freedom to local authorities to raise the money at the best rates they can without any State guarantee.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are empowered (granted capacity) to raise money independently at competitive rates without state guarantee—this is freedom to act autonomously, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Colonel GUINNESS
records.sentence: There was great liberty and variety in these various baronial guarantees.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is observing that historical baronial guarantees contained great scope and diversity of provisions—describing an existing plurality of guarantees, not claiming anyone is freed from something or empowered to do something.

records.speaker: Mr. T. THOMSON
records.sentence: I submit that that case is also met in the original Act, because under Section 12 (3), the local authority may agree to take over from the builder, when he has built the house, that house at an agreed price, leaving the builder the same freedom which the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The builder is freed from the obligation to retain ownership of the house he has built—he has the freedom to sell it to the local authority at an agreed price, a capacity to dispose of his property.

records.speaker: Mr. MOLES
records.sentence: Members, and I think I understand precisely what freedom means quite as well as they do.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is making a bare assertion about understanding the meaning of "freedom" without specifying what freedom from or to what is at stake, rendering the substantive liberty-claim indeterminate.

records.speaker: Mr. MacVEAGH
records.sentence:
and gallant Friend, because it will tend to remind our people at home that there are still in this country friends of Ireland, and friends of liberty, who will raise their voice in protest against the outrages which day by day are being com-
mitted in Ireland by the authorities.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "friends of liberty" in rhetorical opposition to government outrages/tyranny in Ireland—a classic negative liberty appeal to freedom from state oppression and interference.

records.speaker: Mr. MOLES
records.sentence: I think they had better begin and get a lexicon and see what freedom really means.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is questioning what "freedom" itself means—calling for clarification of the concept itself—without specifying any particular freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY
records.sentence: It fought for the freedom of the slaves.
records.haiku_rationale: Slaves are being freed from the condition of slavery and bondage—a negative liberty claim about freedom from enslavement and forced servitude.

records.speaker: Mr. PRETYMAN
records.sentence: There must be a certain amount of liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence uses bare "liberty" without specifying what is being freed, from what constraint, or to what capacity—insufficient context to determine whether "liberty" denotes freedom from interference or empowered capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. LEWIS
records.sentence: I am quite ready to accept the Amendment on the understanding that those in charge of the Bill are at liberty to put it, perhaps, in a slightly altered form.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker grants permission to others to alter the Bill's form; "at liberty" here is a procedural phrase meaning permitted or allowed to act, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. ADAMSON
records.sentence: Its outlook was civilian and its conception of freedom and right was civilian.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "conception of freedom" in abstract terms without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what; the sentence names only the philosophical outlook without addressing particular constraints or capacities.

records.speaker: Mr. JELLETT
records.sentence:
I take the liberty of saying that the interests of Ireland are as dear to me as to any Gentleman on the opposite benches, but I take a different
view of what are the real interests of Ireland from what they do.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "take the liberty of saying" as a parliamentary courtesy phrase—a formulaic expression that permits the speaker to make a statement. This is procedural/conventional usage, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. O'CONNOR
records.sentence: It is only a strong sense of public duty that induces me to interrupt the business of the House with this Motion, but I have that duty laid upon me in this case, because in Ireland we are rapidly approaching an abyss and a disaster the consequences of which will not be confined to Ireland, but affect beyond the liberty and interests of the British Empire.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" as a value at stake in the context of Britain's imperial interests being threatened by the approaching crisis in Ireland—a rhetorical invocation of liberty as opposed to disaster and imperial loss, signifying freedom from interference with British imperial power.

records.speaker: Mr. JELLETT
records.sentence: I have heard the word "liberty" mentioned more than once tonight.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence reports an observation about the word "liberty" being mentioned in debate; it makes no claim about what freedom is or should consist of.

records.speaker: Mr. BONAR LAW
records.sentence: There is a difference between liberty and licence.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asserts a conceptual distinction between "liberty" and "licence" without specifying what either freedom-value is being freed from or empowered to do. It is a bare philosophical claim about terminology that lacks sufficient context to determine whether the liberty being invoked refers to freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. JELLETT
records.sentence: The liberty that some hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and does not specify what liberty is being discussed, from what it is freed, or to what it is empowered. Without the completion, no substantive claim about liberty can be assessed.

records.speaker: Mr. SHORTT
records.sentence: It gives greater freedom to the advisory committee, and I think in every way it is possibly an improvement, therefore I ask the House to accept it.
records.haiku_rationale: The advisory committee is given freedom to (act with fewer constraints), enabling it to exercise greater discretionary capacity—a positive liberty.

records.speaker: Lord H. CAVENDISH - BENTINCK
records.sentence: Gentleman that in order to secure the liberty and happiness of the world, Great Britain must be strong and prosperous.
records.haiku_rationale: Britain is empowered/enabled to secure (bring about) liberty and happiness of the world through being strong and prosperous—a capacity for action, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. HENDERSON
records.sentence: this respect the responsibility for that increased demand must rest with those who have so resolutely resisted the claim of the Irish mission to freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Irish nation being freed from colonial rule and empowered to self-govern (positive liberty); the speaker frames resistance to Irish "freedom" as obstruction of the Irish claim to freedom—understood as national independence and self-determination.

records.speaker: Mr. HENDERSON
records.sentence: After all, we remember, for we were so often told by all the Allied statesmen, that one of the primary objects of the War was to secure the freedom of small nationalities, and statesmen everywhere, including the members of the present Government, reiterated over and over again the right of people to the principle of self-determination.
records.haiku_rationale: Small nationalities are being freed to exercise self-determination—empowerment of peoples to govern themselves, not mere non-interference.

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence:
When you get these sabred and rifled gentlemen coming in to interfere with civil affairs, with the rights and liberties and freedom of the people, we know what the consequences are, and it is because the military are
ruling in Ireland now that a condition of affairs exists in that country which is causing so much pain and torture to the soul of the whole nation and which is raising a spirit of indignation and hostility towards you on the part of lovers of freedom all over the world.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking freedom and civil liberties as freedom from military interference with "the rights and liberties and freedom of the people" and from the oppression ("pain and torture") caused by military rule in Ireland—a rhetorical appeal against tyrannical interference.

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence: Gentleman that we won this claim for national justice and freedom long before you trippingly talked about the freedom of small nations or the right to satisfy the aspirations of a civilised nation to live its own life and work out its own destinies, and we won it by thirty-five years of constitutional effort.
records.haiku_rationale: National self-determination and self-governance: the object of freedom is a nation's capacity to "live its own life and work out its own destinies," describing empowerment to govern oneself rather than freedom from external interference.

records.speaker: The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of EDUCATION
records.sentence: Baronet and the other noted apostles of human liberty who support it, have been longing for a funeral that has not taken place.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "human liberty" as a cause/value opposed to something (implied: constraint or oppression), in a rhetorical and abstract manner characteristic of liberty as freedom from interference with fundamental human autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. BONAR LAW
records.sentence: The question was never answered, nor did they give any reply as to the substitute which they would have for the control which the freedom of the Straits would, give over the Government in Constantinople.
records.haiku_rationale: The "freedom of the Straits" refers to freedom from Ottoman control over navigation through the Turkish Straits—a negative liberty concerning freedom from interference with passage and commerce.

records.speaker: Captain BENN
records.sentence: That is the freedom which the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and does not specify what object of freedom is being discussed or whether it involves freedom from interference or empowerment to act.

records.speaker: Sir H. CRAIK
records.sentence: We have one thing we prize beyond all others, and that is our liberty!
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked here as a rhetorical ideal prized as a cause—the object is freedom from external domination or oppression, characteristic of negative liberty.

records.speaker: Dr. MURRAY
records.sentence:
I take the liberty first, however, to congratulate him upon his
appointment to the important office of President of the Board of Trade, and on his passage from the troubled waters of the Labour Ministry to the more placid waters of that Board.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty to" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning to permit oneself to speak or act; it does not advance a claim about liberty-as-a-value but is a conventional rhetorical device for claiming the right to address someone.

records.speaker: Mr. HARBISON
records.sentence:
The solution is the granting of liberty to Ireland, and by that I mean that the liberty that was given by the Statute of 1783, which was taken away by a deed as dark as any that blackens the pages of the
history of any country, by the Act of' Union.
records.haiku_rationale: Ireland is being empowered to govern itself—the Statute of 1783 granted self-governance that was then removed by the Act of Union. The speaker seeks to restore that capacity for self-determination.

records.speaker: Sir E. CARSON
records.sentence:
Listen to what he said:
 I believe that almost every Irish Protestant will recognise that in the present conditions it is the duty of Ulster Members to take this opportunity of trying to secure for their constituents freedom from this iniquitous measure.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is constituents' exemption from ("freedom from") an iniquitous legislative measure—a classic negative liberty claim of freedom from unwanted state interference.

records.speaker: Sir CHARLES SYKES
records.sentence: If you find you want the money, by all means raise it by proper methods, but let us revert to pre-War conditions—let us have freedom, and know where we stand.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from government interference with pre-War economic/commercial conditions; the speaker opposes wartime constraints and wants restoration of unrestricted operation ("know where we stand").

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence: Every Irishman who loves his country, who desires freedom and the order that should spring from freedom, must feel the tragedy of the whole situation.
records.haiku_rationale: An Irishman "desires freedom" in the context of national independence and self-governance—the capacity to govern oneself and one's country free from external domination, a positive sense of empowerment and self-determination.

records.speaker: Mr. BOTTOM LEY
records.sentence: sorry to be a pessimist in these circumstances, but as one who has expressed these views on many occasions in other places I take the liberty of doing so to-day, and I respectfully commend them to the attention of the House.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "took the liberty of" to mean he permitted himself to express views; this is parliamentary procedure language indicating he ventured to speak, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Viscount WOLMER
records.sentence: Friend in his most interesting memorandum calls it an Imperial memorial for the freedom of man.
records.haiku_rationale: Man is being freed from what is implicitly oppressive or tyrannical (the sentence invokes "freedom of man" as a cause opposing some constraint or domination), which is a rhetorical invocation of negative liberty—freedom from interference or subjection.

records.speaker: Sir F. BANBURY
records.sentence: I have received a letter from the Women's Freedom League.
records.haiku_rationale: This sentence merely reports a procedural action (receipt of correspondence) and uses "Freedom" as part of an organization's proper name; it makes no substantive claim about liberty as a value.

records.speaker: Sir W. JOYNSON-HICKS
records.sentence: Are these representatives of Great Britain provided with full information as to our naval and military plans, and at liberty to communicate it to other members of the League of Nations?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to communicate" is a procedural or legal idiom meaning "permitted/authorized to do X," not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. BALDWIN
records.sentence: Friend wish to carry this matter to a Division now, of course he is at liberty to do so;
records.haiku_rationale: Mr. Baldwin states that his Friend "is at liberty to do so" (call a Division) — this is a procedural declaration that someone has the capacity/permission to take a parliamentary action, not a substantive claim about liberty as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. KIDD
records.sentence: One can understand the policy of combining the minimum wage with freedom on a tonnage rate for every man with greater ability to make more money.
records.haiku_rationale: Men of greater ability are freed (enabled) to make more money through a flexible tonnage rate system, rather than being constrained by a rigid wage ceiling—freedom to earn according to capacity.

records.speaker: Sir J. D. REES
records.sentence: Member for the City and myself were wrong in-the attitude we took were entirely wrong themselves, and the House, the Government, and the nation do not part in any respect with their freedom in this connection by being parties to the Treaty of Peace.
records.haiku_rationale: The nation does not give up its freedom (capacity for self-governance/autonomy) by being a party to the Treaty of Peace—it retains the ability to govern itself and make decisions.

records.speaker: Sir D. MACLEAN
records.sentence: that is where the menace comes in, and that is where the freedom of the Press, and as I venture to say, and the protection of the public comes in.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with the Press's ability to report and publish, a key civil liberty opposed to state control and censorship.

records.speaker: Mr. JAMESON
records.sentence: We sincerely hope there will not be occasion for calling in extra munitions to defend law and order in this country, but we are bound to take precautions, bearing in mind above all things the sacredness of property and the liberty of the subject.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "liberty of the subject" is a classical invocation of freedom from arbitrary interference and state oppression, here opposed to the threat of militarised state force. The subject is being freed from violation by extra munitions and unchecked state power.

records.speaker: Mr. MACQUISTEN
records.sentence: I believe that if you want to make a true and a real system of education in this country it will be done by diminishing State control and by endeavouring, as far as possible, to allow freedom, in which the human soul and intellect blossom.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom in question is freedom from State control over education, which will allow the human soul and intellect to blossom—a classic negative liberty framing: freedom from governmental interference with education.

records.speaker: Mr. ASQUITH
records.sentence: In the whole history of political map-making I suppose that no territory has presented greater difficulty, to those who were trying to adjust the claims of the various populations within it on the basis of liberty and self-government, than Hungary.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty and self-government are being invoked as the basis for adjusting territorial claims—Hungary's populations are being freed to govern themselves, a capacity/empowerment to exercise self-determination.

records.speaker: Viscountess ASTOR
records.sentence: The appeal sometimes comes disguised in the name of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses how an appeal (presumably a problematic or disguised one) presents itself under the name of freedom, without specifying what freedom from or to what is being invoked. The reference is to the rhetorical or deceptive use of "freedom" as a label, not a substantive claim about liberation from interference or empowerment to act.

records.speaker: Sir E. WILD
records.sentence:
per 100 will be at liberty to
oppose the Clause.
records.haiku_rationale: Members are permitted to oppose the Clause; this is parliamentary procedure describing who is entitled to speak/vote procedurally, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. GEORGE BARNES
records.sentence: But in the mind of every single one of us there was no doubt as to our own country, or any other country where freedom had broadened down to representative institutions, that the conventions were to be submitted to those representative authorities.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (expanded democratic representation) is enabled in countries with representative institutions that broaden citizens' capacity for self-governance and political participation.

records.speaker: Sir J. D. REES
records.sentence: Under any circumstances, is it for any foreign Government to accord complete freedom to the Government of the King of Kings?
records.haiku_rationale: A foreign government is being freed (to act, to govern) from external constraint or interference by according it "complete freedom"—an empowerment or grant of autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. FORD
records.sentence: One old gentleman, whom I remember in a former constituency which, I admit, I did not quite succeed in winning, said to me, "Freedom is the gift of God, and there fore Free Trade is the gift of God.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from state restrictions on trade; the sentence invokes freedom as a divine value opposed to mercantilism and state interference in commerce.

records.speaker: Mr. KIDD
records.sentence: They may take an entirely false view of the value of their services, but, looking to the large wage they enjoyed then, and looking, above all, to the freedom they enjoyed together with that large wage, these factors sufficiently explain why domestic service to-day is not so congenial and attractive as it was in other days.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom enjoyed together with large wage in domestic service — a nostalgic reference to perceived material conditions and autonomy/well-being of the past that made the work attractive, expressing capacity or state of comfort rather than freedom from specific interference.

records.speaker: Mr. NEIL MACLEAN
records.sentence: That is an innovation, and if it had been carried into practice many years ago there would have been greater freedom, and there might also have been better relationships between this country and other parts of the world.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: international relations and domestic policy outcomes. From-or-to what: the speaker suggests removing obstacles to better relationships between countries and improving conditions—a general invocation of freedom as absence of constraint on national/diplomatic action, without specifying what would be freed from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. JOHNSTONE
records.sentence: The first is the one that is dealt with in this Bill, the question of spiritual freedom;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to "spiritual freedom" as a topic being dealt with in a Bill, but does not specify what spiritual freedom is being freed from or to—it is a bare invocation without substantive clarification of whether it concerns freedom from state/religious interference or empowerment to practice religion.

records.speaker: Viscount WOLMER
records.sentence:
The third and most important fact is, that it is estab-
lishment on the basis of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as a foundational principle for establishment without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. G. BARNES
records.sentence:
For my part, I am pleased to think that a man, after having spent the major portion of a long life in struggling for the freedom
of his own people, now that that has been achieved, has turned his attention and his talents to the freedom of other smaller and even more helpless people.
records.haiku_rationale: Positive liberty: the sentence celebrates a man's transition from securing his people's freedom (national self-determination/empowerment to govern) to securing freedom for other peoples, emphasizing the achievement and exercise of political independence and self-governance for peoples.

records.speaker: Mr. G. BALFOUR
records.sentence: Upon that liberty depends the volume of employment which gives work to the people of this country.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty (presumably economic/commercial liberty) enables or produces employment and work—a positive capacity to act and generate outcomes.

records.speaker: Mr. CLYNES
records.sentence:
I think it will become commonly known in the constituencies that no matter what individual initiative a Member may display, no matter how full of honesty of purpose and of anxiety to serve his constituents, when he comes here he is
simply fixed as a small item in the general mosaic of Government purpose, and that he is totally deprived of any kind of individual freedom as representing his constituency.
records.haiku_rationale: A member of parliament is deprived of freedom (the capacity to act independently and represent constituents according to personal judgment) by subordination to collective party/government discipline.

records.speaker: Colonel P. WILLIAMS
records.sentence: Are they at liberty to cut their loss in Australia, or have they entered into long-dated contracts for the conveyance of the metal to this country, thereby compelling them to carry on their business further than merely receiving the concentrates in Australia?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to cut their loss" is parliamentary procedural usage meaning "permitted/able to"; this is not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value against interference or as empowerment, but rather a formulaic parliamentary expression asking whether they are free (permitted) to make a business decision.

records.speaker: Captain DIXON
records.sentence: I am at liberty to say that I met Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: Speaker uses "at liberty to" as parliamentary procedure/idiom meaning "permitted to" or "able to"; this is not making a claim about liberty-as-a-value but rather ordinary parliamentary speech formula.

records.speaker: Mr. DEVLIN
records.sentence: Their aspirations for liberty were an outrage upon what he conceived to be freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" and "freedom" as political causes/values in opposition—what one group's aspirations for liberty the speaker sees as an outrage against his conception of freedom. This is a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause opposed to a rival vision of freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. R. McNEILL
records.sentence: In other words, he entirely repudiates the idea that they get the freedom which they require under this Treaty, but it gives them the means of getting it later on.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contrasts freedom (as a state or condition) with the means to obtain it later, presenting both what is currently denied (negative liberty—freedom from constraint) and what is being enabled (positive liberty—the capacity or means to achieve freedom in the future).

records.speaker: Mr. MONTAGU
records.sentence: My position would have been untenable without that freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to a freedom that sustained Mr. Montagu's political position, but does not specify what he was freed from or freed to do—the object and direction of the freedom are entirely context-dependent and absent from this isolated remark.

records.speaker: The POSTMASTER-GENERAL
records.sentence: The only Dominion which has entered upon any wireless project of its own is Australia, whose representative at the Imperial meetings of last year reserved to the Commonwealth Government full freedom of action to decide in what manner it would co-operate in the Imperial wireless scheme.
records.haiku_rationale: The Commonwealth Government is empowered to make its own decision about how to participate in the Imperial wireless scheme; "full freedom of action" grants capacity to choose its own course of action regarding cooperation.

records.speaker: Mr. MACOUISTEN
records.sentence:
Therefore it is right that you should give to the small individual, the man who wants to get a start in life for himself, the opportunity to
have greater freedom in fixing his own working hours.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is arguing for granting individuals the opportunity/capacity to autonomously determine their own working hours, an empowerment to self-govern one's labor conditions.

records.speaker: Mr. JOHNSTONE
records.sentence: Members who have moved this Bill is to give to the individual the fullest possible amount of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The individual is being freed to act; the Bill aims to empower individuals with the fullest possible freedom of action, a capacity or opportunity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. CLYNES
records.sentence:
It is a lamentable fact that Ireland now is more full of fear from certain groups of gunmen,
and in that fear is disabled from exercising the degree of freedom which the Treaty to establish the Free State intended to confer upon the Irish people.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence identifies what is being freed—the Irish people's capacity to exercise freedom (self-governance)—and identifies the barrier: they are disabled from this by fear imposed by gunmen violence. The Treaty intended to confer (grant, empower) upon Ireland the freedom to govern itself; fear from violence prevents them from exercising this capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. TREVELYAN THOMSON
records.sentence: I say, you allow this appalling overcrowding to continue, and children to grow up, with impoverished health and unable to get the necessary freedom and fresh air, to produce a decent manhood and a decent womanhood, you are piling up for the State a legacy of certain ill-health for which you will have to pay dearly in the future.
records.haiku_rationale: Children need freedom from impoverished health conditions and overcrowding constraints (negative liberty from deprivation) to gain the capacity to produce decent manhood/womanhood (positive liberty as empowerment), but the sentence emphasizes the enabling of these future capacities through removal of material obstacles.

records.speaker: Colonel WEDGWOOD
records.sentence: As India progresses towards freedom—and, in spite of this House of Commons, India is progressing towards freedom;
records.haiku_rationale: India is being freed from colonial rule and imperial control, progressing towards self-determination and independence.

records.speaker: Mr. FOOT
records.sentence: Amendment was carried—and whether we agreed with it or not we should all, I think, approve the right of this House to govern entirely our own taxation—the mischief would be that we should wipe out at once the main part of our system of Colonial Preference, and the argument against Colonial Preference as established in this country now is that it deprives this House of its proper freedom and of the power of deciding what taxation there shall be upon one commodity or another.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "proper freedom" and "power of deciding" what taxation to apply—framing these as capacities that the House has been deprived of by Colonial Preference. This is freedom-to (make policy choices) rather than freedom-from (interference).

records.speaker: Mr. WATERSON
records.sentence: I trust that in quoting that telegram again I shall not be taking too much liberty, but I feel justified in re-reading it because of its importance, and as a means of drawing attention to the fact that there were certain manufacturers, wholesale distributors and retailers of sugar who had gone so far as to prepare for a reduction of the tax.
records.haiku_rationale: Mr. Waterson is using "taking too much liberty" as a parliamentary procedural phrase meaning he is permitted or allowed to repeat a telegram; this is a formulaic expression for obtaining rhetorical leave to act, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Sir A. MOND
records.sentence: They are ready to waive the penny rate, and I want Parliament to give me that liberty which will enable me to work in conjunction with them.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker seeks "liberty" (permission/empowerment) to work in conjunction with others—freedom to act and cooperate, not freedom from interference with an existing activity.

records.speaker: Mr. MALONE
records.sentence: whether, while leaving complete freedom to editors in regard to comments in editorial columns, political notes, and elsewhere, he will support legislation to prohibit the publication in the public Press of these misleading reports;
records.haiku_rationale: This sentence contrasts "complete freedom to editors" (freedom from interference with editorial discretion) against "support legislation to prohibit" certain publications, raising ambiguous whether the speaker prioritizes the negative liberty of editors or seeks to constrain it through law.

records.speaker: Mr. THOMSON
records.sentence: We want more freedom and elasticity, and I suggest that local authorities should have a more free hand than they have had in the past, and should be allowed to work out their own salvation.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being empowered/granted capacity to work out their own salvation—this is positive liberty, an enabling of self-governance and autonomous action.

records.speaker: Mr. H. H. SPENCER
records.sentence:
I took the liberty of saying a few words on Monday
night on the question of dye work and I pointed out that we were paying twice as much for certain dye work as we ought to do in the textile industry.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of saying" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning the speaker assumed permission to speak; it is not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. JOHNSTON
records.sentence: May I crave the liberty of a few moments of the time of this House to make a personal observation or two upon the statement we have just heard from the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "crave the liberty of a few moments" as parliamentary idiom requesting permission to speak—a procedural courtesy rather than a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Viscountess ASTOR
records.sentence: Paul knew where true freedom lay.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is a vague philosophical assertion about Paul's understanding of freedom's location, but does not specify what is being freed or from-or-to what, making it impossible to determine whether freedom is invoked as capacity (positive) or non-interference (negative).

records.speaker: Mr. GALBRAITH
records.sentence: Members who support this Measure have no desire to place unfair burdens upon a, very deserving class of the community, and as regards that point, too, I reserve to myself full freedom when the Bill is in Committee.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to vote independently on amendments in Committee without prior commitment; this is parliamentary procedural liberty to act according to one's judgment.

records.speaker: Mr. R. MURRAY
records.sentence: of its additional trade—not of its profits while the lazy, slow, non-progressive and inefficient firm, which did not produce up to this pre-War level, was at liberty to draw from that pool 7½ per cent.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "was at liberty to draw" is parliamentary procedural language indicating permission or entitlement, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. W. GREENWOOD
records.sentence: We are often told, especially from the other side, that if there is one thing more than another that ought to he taxed, it is the luxuries which people buy, and I may say, in regard to that, that I missed something from the Chancellor of the Exchequer's statement, but, first of all, I should be very glad if the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, when he is at liberty, will listen to this point.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty" is parliamentary procedural language meaning "available" or "able to attend to," not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Sir G. HAMILTON
records.sentence: I have always believed in liberty, and if this Resolution means that you are going to combine the so-called professional workers so that you will have them in one big trade union and if there is a strike or dispute you are going to stop them from earning their salary whether they want to work, or not, I am against it.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes liberty as opposition to a scheme that would compel workers to stop earning their salary against their will in a labour dispute — the freedom being claimed is workers' freedom from coercive interference with their choice to continue working.

records.speaker: Mr. STEWART
records.sentence: While I want that freedom for myself, I want.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and does not specify what freedom is being discussed or what its object and direction are; "freedom for myself" lacks sufficient context to determine whether it refers to freedom from interference or freedom to act.

records.speaker: Mr. WILLIAM GRAHAM
records.sentence: We must recognise the broad fact that in the common interest at present, even from the selfish point of view of getting anything in the nature of reparations, the maximum freedom of interchange is essential, and accordingly we must, to do our duty in this country as part of our policy in dealing with unemployment in the State, look beyond the State to these larger measures of fiscal freedom, and see that we play our part in making a contribution to them.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom of interchange" and "fiscal freedom" as capabilities or opportunities necessary for economic coordination and solving unemployment, treating freedom as a positive capacity to act economically rather than a constraint on interference.

records.speaker: Mr. MacDONALD
records.sentence: Meanwhile, whatever gives freedom and variety to thought and earnestness to men's interests in the world, must contribute to a good end.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: thought and men's earnestness in their interests. Freed from: restrictions or constraints that inhibit mental and intellectual engagement. The sentence invokes freedom as a general enabling condition for flourishing.

records.speaker: Mr. BRIGGS
records.sentence: One of the first principles of happiness is freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a bare invocation of "freedom" as a general principle of human happiness, without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what.

records.speaker: Sir JOHN SIMON
records.sentence: that any Member of this elected body enjoys the privilege of freedom from arrest.
records.haiku_rationale: Members of the elected body are freed from arrest—a freedom from interference with their person by agents of state detention.

records.speaker: Mr. GRAHAM
records.sentence: I cannot to-night make a definite statement as to what form any change in the administrative Regulations will take, but we are very sincerely desirous that, subject to the conditions I have tried to lay down in the earlier part of my speech, we should give the greatest measure of freedom, and I hope, perhaps at an early date, to be able to make some definite statement on that point.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker expresses desire to give "the greatest measure of freedom" to some party (presumably local authorities or an administrative body) subject to stated conditions—an empowerment to act or govern, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. BECKER
records.sentence: It is an absolute restriction on the liberty, not so much of the people who buy, but of the young and small men who are trying to build up businesses, and I do ask the House to pass the Bill at this stage and also to give it a Second Reading.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker identifies a restriction being imposed on the liberty of young and small businessmen to build up their businesses—a constraint on their capacity to engage in commercial enterprise and economic activity.

records.speaker: Mr. AYLES
records.sentence:
asked the Prime Minister whether he is aware that the
present Hungarian regime, which was formally recognised in the name of the Supreme Council on 20th November, 1919, was recognised on certain conditions, one of which was that the Hungarian Government shall secure to the Hungarian citizen full civil rights, including freedom of the Press, freedom of assembly, the free expression of political opinion, and universal suffrage resting on an impartial, secret, and democratic basis;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence specifies multiple freedoms—press, assembly, expression—as civil rights to be secured to Hungarian citizens. These are paradigmatic negative liberties: freedom from interference with press, assembly, and political expression.

records.speaker: Sir PHILIP SASSOON
records.sentence: I think they are really doing so if, in their desire to placate the Liberty party, they are sacrificing the interests of the Empire to acquire virtue in that party's eyes.
records.haiku_rationale: The reference to "Liberty party" is a proper noun denoting a political faction; "liberty" here is not being used to make a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value but rather as part of the name of a party, and the sentence concerns political strategy and sacrifice of imperial interests.

records.speaker: Mr. FISHER
records.sentence: I quite agree that this House is perfectly at liberty to reject or modify the conclusions of the Conference.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to reject or modify" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning the House has the procedural right or permission to take certain actions—it does not invoke liberty-as-a-value but rather refers to whether Parliament is permitted (by rules, convention, or constitutional arrangement) to act.

records.speaker: The LORD PRIVY SEAL
records.sentence: The Prime Minister is asking for this Government—minority Government, as it is, neither more nor less—the freedom and right, in relation to treaties that all other Governments have exercised.
records.haiku_rationale: The government is being empowered to exercise the capacity to negotiate and sign treaties—a prerogative that other governments possess. This is freedom to act (to exercise treaty-making authority), not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: The LORD PRIVY SEAL
records.sentence: First, Northern Ireland was given freedom for an independent existence outside the Free State.
records.haiku_rationale: Northern Ireland is empowered to govern itself independently, separated from the Free State—this is positive liberty, the capacity/right to self-determination.

records.speaker: Sir F. HALL
records.sentence: I am perfectly at liberty, until I am called to order by Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking parliamentary procedure: the ability to speak until formally constrained by the Speaker ("called to order"), not making a claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. ASQUITH
records.sentence: I observe that there was greater freedom, at any rate, a warmer temperature in the atmosphere in which he found himself yesterday.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a metaphorical use of "freedom" referring to a warmer atmospheric or rhetorical climate during a previous day; it does not substantively claim liberty as a value or make any assertion about freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. SAKLATVALA
records.sentence: asked the Under-Secretary of State for India to what extent the sovereign States of India of the importance of Hyderabad, Mysore, Kashmir, and Bhopal have freedom in their internal affairs, such as the appointment of their Ministers, including the Chief Minister, and the succession to their thrones in consonance with the traditions and religion of the peoples concerned;
records.haiku_rationale: The question asks about the extent to which Indian sovereign states have freedom in their internal affairs—specifically the appointment of ministers and succession decisions. This concerns empowerment to self-govern and decide matters according to their own traditions, which is positive liberty (freedom to exercise governance).

records.speaker: Mr. SCURR
records.sentence: I think one of the most priceless possessions of this country is that there is absolute freedom of speech not only in this country but in every part of the Empire which owes allegiance to the British Crown, and that everyone has the right to advocate any political or economic change, no matter how absurd it may appear to some people.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech (the ability to advocate political or economic positions without interference) is a classic negative liberty—freedom from state suppression or restriction of expression.

records.speaker: Mr. THURTLE
records.sentence: That kind of thing is the worst way of dealing with any discontent, or demand for freedom, which may be existing in India.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker opposes certain methods of dealing with "demand for freedom" in India, treating freedom as a value that people seek and that governments can recognize or address — here, freedom from colonial rule or oppression. This invokes liberty as a cause opposed to unjust governance.

records.speaker: Mr. GREAVES-LORD
records.sentence: Any organisation which denies political liberty is bound, in this country, to come to the ground.
records.haiku_rationale: Political liberty refers to freedom from interference with political participation and expression; the speaker is invoking this as a value against organisations that deny such freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. SCRYMGEOUR
records.sentence: It has been suggested that the Secretary of State might himself visit the place, and I would make the further suggestion that the Prime Minister, who is shortly going to receive the freedom of the city, might use his influence with the Secretary of State for War, and thus might make some little practical recognition of what I am very pleased to see the city is going to confer upon him.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "receive the freedom of the city" refers to a ceremonial honor (the Freedom of the City award), not a claim about liberty-as-a-value or freedom from interference or empowerment to act. This is parliamentary procedure language where "freedom" denotes an honorific award.

records.speaker: Mr. SAKLATVALA
records.sentence: As a member of the Communist party I have greater knowledge of what the Communist system of human freedom in the Army and Navy does for the discipline of the men than any member of any other parties.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "human freedom in the Army and Navy" as an effect or feature of the Communist system, claiming it enhances discipline; freedom here is presented as what the system provides or enables for men, making it a positive claim about empowerment to participate or act under Communist discipline.

records.speaker: Mr. CHAMBERLAIN
