records.sentence: That is not quite the liberty that might have been inferred from the speech of the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is discussing what inference or interpretation could be made from another politician's speech—a rhetorical or logical liberty being taken, not a substantive claim about freedom from or capacity to do something.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY
records.sentence: Arising out of the last answer, may we take it that this change of policy will be met on our part by the greatest possible political liberty being given in the circumstances?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker asks for "greatest possible political liberty being given," meaning empowerment or capacity granted to govern/act politically in circumstances, not mere absence of interference—it concerns enabling political agency and self-governance.

records.speaker: Mr. STEPHEN
records.sentence: The United Free Church of Scotland had to pay its price for its freedom;
records.haiku_rationale: The United Free Church of Scotland is freed from (institutional constraint or subordination), but the sentence frames this as having required payment of a price—a capacity gained through historical struggle, suggesting empowerment to act independently.

records.speaker: Mr. WILLIAMS
records.sentence: We restrict his liberty, but we do it in the interests of the community and of other persons who are not verminous.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses restricting someone's liberty (freedom from interference with their actions), justified on grounds of community welfare and protection of others.

records.speaker: Mr. LEES-SMITH
records.sentence: The Minister of Health will be aware that, when he determined to base his Bill upon the contributory principle, he at that moment automatically decided that there would be shut out from it that vast number of people who are just as poor as those who work in mills and factories, just as much in need of assistance and of freedom from financial anxiety, but who will not be able to get the benefits because they are not wage-earners working for an employer.
records.haiku_rationale: People are freed from financial anxiety (a source of distress and want); welfare benefits provide the means to achieve this freedom.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY
records.sentence: Wansey Bayly, representing the Workers' Liberty and Employment League—I do not know what this body is—and Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence mentions "Workers' Liberty and Employment League" as a proper noun (the name of an organization), and contains no substantive claim about liberty as a value or concept being freed from or to something.

records.speaker: Mr. AMMON
records.sentence: One can imagine the freedom of discussion in the Cabinet.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of discussion—the capacity to engage in discussion within the Cabinet—is negative liberty: freedom from interference with debate and deliberation.

records.speaker: Sir B. FALLE
records.sentence:
Let us not forget even now—and this is the opinion of almost every man who takes the trouble to visualise the Navy—that the
Royal Navy is not merely our sure shield—it is the bed-rock—for the safety, security, and freedom of this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom from interference/threat — the Royal Navy protects the country's security and freedom, understood as protection from external invasion and subjugation. This is freedom from foreign domination and attack.

records.speaker: Sir H. SLESSER
records.sentence: In the good old days, when people were more careful than they are now about the liberty of the subject, they would never have tolerated this sort of thing, and I ask the House to reject the Clause on the ground that, just like the Clauses which we have cither forced the Government to drop or on which we have defeated the Government when they have tried to carry them through, this Clause is a most dangerous invasion of the liberty of the subject.
records.haiku_rationale: The subject is being freed from invasive government interference (unwanted Clauses); liberty here means freedom from state encroachment on the individual's rights and protections.

records.speaker: Mr. RAMSAY MacDONALD
records.sentence: Society is going to protect its very delicate fabric, which does not like to be kicked and beaten and coerced, by having liberty preserved to it.
records.haiku_rationale: Society is freed from coercion (kicking, beating, forcing) through having liberty preserved—liberty here means freedom from external interference with the social fabric.

records.speaker: The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to the MINISTRY of HEALTH
records.sentence: He expressed, I think, an individual view when he said that it would be far better to leave committees and authorities to do just as they liked, to spend as much money as they liked, and even to mal-administer their affairs if they liked, provided they had freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Committees and authorities are freed to govern themselves (spend money, administer affairs) as they choose—empowering local bodies to act without central constraint—which is positive liberty (freedom to govern).

records.speaker: Lieut.-Commander BURNEY
records.sentence: Nobody wishes to restrict the freedom of purchase by the people of this country, but we do want to give to our manufacturers that same service by State aid which is given by every country in the world, and which will enable them to avail themselves of these new methods of manufacture.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contains "freedom of purchase" — a negative liberty claim about freedom from interference with commercial choice. The second clause about "State aid" to enable manufacturers to compete represents positive liberty (empowerment to act). The sentence mixes both: protecting purchase freedom (negative) while granting manufacturers enabling capacity (positive).

records.speaker: Mr. MONTAGUE
records.sentence: The Liberal Free Trader believes in commercial freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Commercial freedom is a freedom from trade restrictions and state interference in commerce — freedom of contract and trade.

records.speaker: Mr. ALEXANDER
records.sentence: He was careful to point out to the Committee on a previous occasion that there was no violation of the most-favoured-nation Clause in the Anglo-German Treaty, because he said we took particular care to put into the treaty with Germany such words as would make it certain that we held ourselves at liberty to safeguard our industries.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of liberty is the capacity "to safeguard our industries" — freedom is empowerment granted via treaty language enabling Britain to protect its industries, not freedom from interference with some existing right.

records.speaker: Dr. SHIELS
records.sentence: I do not want to take up any more time, because there are other speakers, but I hope that I have said sufficient to show that while, as I say, we welcome as much freedom as is consistent with the public interest, we do not think it desirable to menace the public safety by accepting the principle which has been put forward in the Amendment.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses "freedom" that is permissible "as much as is consistent with the public interest," framing freedom as a value to be balanced against public safety concerns, but does not specify what freedom from or freedom to do; this is a general invocation of liberty as a cause weighed against state interests.

records.speaker: Mr. AMERY
records.sentence:
The League has asked us to continue our policy of granting large liberty in cultural matters to the Kurdish popu-
lation.
records.haiku_rationale: The Kurds are being granted liberty (empowerment) to pursue their own cultural affairs with minimal state interference—the freedom being granted is self-governance in cultural matters.

records.speaker: Sir J. SIMON
records.sentence: I said I hoped he would indicate to any of his colleagues or friends that they were at liberty to attend if they liked.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to attend" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning someone is permitted or free to choose to attend; it does not engage substantive claims about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Viscountess ASTOR
records.sentence: The Minister used the argument that you ought not to interfere with individual liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes individual liberty as a principle against interference or constraint—a negative liberty argument that individuals should be free from governmental or external interference.

records.speaker: Mr. HILTON YOUNG
records.sentence: Secondly, I think it is recognised, with that freedom which one would expect, that one has also to consider the interests of a great people, the people of Russia.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as a rhetorical value—the freedom with which one can consider international interests—as opposed to constraint or dogmatism; this is a general value claim about liberty in political discussion, not a specific claim about what is freed from-or-to what.

records.speaker: Mr. WILLIAM ADAMSON
records.sentence: The Minister of Labour said that this Bill would give the men freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: The men are freed to choose (enabled capacity) — this is empowerment to exercise agency in selecting options, not merely freedom from interference with choice.

records.speaker: Mr. WILLIAM ADAMSON
records.sentence:
Would he be prepared
to test that by a ballot of the men, as to whether they want this freedom of choice?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is asking whether workers want "freedom of choice" regarding some matter (likely union or employment terms)—the capacity to choose among options rather than have a choice imposed on them. This is freedom TO exercise choice capacity.

records.speaker: Dr. WATTS
records.sentence: It is a method of restoring liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "liberty" as a cause or value being restored, without specifying whether it concerns freedom from interference or empowerment to act; the abstract framing and absence of a specific object of liberty makes the direction (negative or positive) indeterminate from this sentence alone.

records.speaker: Mr. MACQUISTEN
records.sentence: These Regulations are for the purpose of giving the men peace and liberty to carry on their business.
records.haiku_rationale: The men are being freed to carry on their business—liberty here is capacity/empowerment to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Captain BENN
records.sentence: What does that indicate but a desire to alter the law as regards freedom of speech?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is discussing freedom of speech, which is a negative liberty—freedom from interference with the act of speaking.

records.speaker: Sir H. SLESSER
records.sentence: I appeal to the Home Secretary to say that while certain Regulations for controlling the price of coal may be necessary these Regulations which deal with liberty of opinion and speech and movement are now unnecessary and need not be repeated.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker argues that regulations controlling liberty of opinion, speech, and movement are unnecessary and should not be repeated—invoking freedom from government interference with expression and movement.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Colonel JAMES
records.sentence: Scrymgeour) said that if we upheld the liberty of the subject all these restrictions on liberty would be at once removed.
records.haiku_rationale: The liberty of the subject is being freed from restrictions/interference with liberty itself; this invokes negative liberty as opposition to constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. GROVES
records.sentence: I should have liked to dilate upon this from my own point of view, because I feel that the development of local life in this country for many centuries past has been the centre from which the great theory of freedom and democracy has been built up.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" rhetorically as a foundational value of democratic development in local life, without specifying what one is freed from or to do; it is a general historical claim about freedom as a causal force in national political theory rather than a claim about a specific object of freedom or a capacity to act.

records.speaker: Mr. WILLIAM GRAHAM
records.sentence: The House knows that under existing conditions there is a great deal of freedom left to the British Broadcastng Company, though, of course, it is subject to a certain amount of regulation at the hands of the Postmaster-General, and to Rules that this House has laid down, in terms of the licence of the great monopoly which it works.
records.haiku_rationale: The broadcasting company is left with "freedom" (discretionary space) under existing regulation—it denotes the scope for autonomous action remaining to the company despite regulatory constraints, a capacity or domain of autonomous operation.

records.speaker: Captain BENN
records.sentence: In fact, by Clause 7 of this Bill, we are tying the hands of future Parliaments, and, although these preferences do not, except in the case of motor cars, represent anything of any importance to the Dominions, they excite hopes in the first place, and, secondly, so far as they are not a sheer illusion and almost a mockery, they foster the growth of interests there which will fetter our freedom at home.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom at home" being fettered by commercial interests fostered abroad—a constraint on Britain's capacity to act freely in its own economic and political affairs.

records.speaker: Mr. MONTAGUE
records.sentence: I believe in individual liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: A bare invocation of individual liberty as a value, without specification of what is being freed or from what constraint. The sentence does not disambiguate between capacity to act versus freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. KIRKWOOD
records.sentence: They were at liberty to come, and that was during the War.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to come" is a formulaic parliamentary expression meaning "permitted to come" or "able to come"; this describes a permission or lack of constraint on action, but is not making a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value against tyranny or interference.

records.speaker: Sir JOSEPH NALL
records.sentence: I am perfectly at liberty to make use, and he observed that the statements in that letter of mine were in every respect contrary to the facts.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning permission or the absence of constraint to take an action (here, to make use of something), not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. JONES
records.sentence: For that reason this particular meeting gets ample protection and freedom to hold its meetings.
records.haiku_rationale: A meeting is being freed to hold its meetings—i.e., given capacity and opportunity to assemble and conduct proceedings without obstruction.

records.speaker: Dr. LITTLE
records.sentence: The theological colleges, through the Bishop of Gloucester, who knows them, of course, extremely well, roundly say that they will not remain in the University if these regulations controlling their freedom are enforced.
records.haiku_rationale: Theological colleges are fighting against regulations that control their freedom—i.e., freedom from external constraints on their operations and governance as institutions.

records.speaker: Dr. LITTLE
records.sentence: It is in the interests of freedom, the freedom of the University, the freedom of the schools of the University, and the freedom of the students, especially of external students, that I beg to move that the House reject the Bill.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being invoked—freedom of the University, freedom of its schools, and freedom of students—refers to institutional and educational autonomy from external interference or control, specifically resisting the constraint imposed by the Bill.

records.speaker: Mr. HURD
records.sentence: May I ask whether at the present moment it would not be desirable to put forward the suggestion that there should be two quarantine stations near the ports, one in the North and one in the South, to which animals for export could be sent for a sufficient period to ensure freedom from disease.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses ensuring animals' freedom from disease through quarantine procedures—a state of being free from a natural condition (disease), not freedom from political interference or human constraint. This is not a claim about liberty-as-a-value in Berlin's political philosophy sense.

records.speaker: Mr. WESTWOOD
records.sentence: While I am prepared to admit that the police do look after the lives of people, and sometimes look after personal liberty, I beg to submit that they are chiefly occupied in defending property and looking after property and, for the life of me, I cannot see why the tenant should have to pay for the cost of protecting the owners' property.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "personal liberty" as something the police should protect people from interference regarding (threat to person rather than property), contrasting it with property protection—negative liberty understood as freedom from interference with one's person.

records.speaker: Captain BENN
records.sentence: No Member of this House, whatever may be thought of this Schedule, is at liberty to move Amendments to redistribute these burdens, beccause the Rules of the House do not permit of that being done during the Report stage.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to move Amendments" is parliamentary procedure language describing what parliamentary rules permit or prohibit—not a claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. W. BAKER
records.sentence: I believe the Under-Secretary is endeavouring to hold the balance very fairly indeed, and my great hope to-night is that the criticisms from this side of the House will be accepted as an endeavour to strengthen his hands against those interested persons who are anxious to obtain freedom in order to thwart the Government in Kenya.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as something "interested persons" desire in order "to thwart the Government in Kenya"—freedom here is the capacity or opportunity to act against the Government, making it an instance of positive liberty (empowerment to act).

records.speaker: Mr. BARR
records.sentence: In my opinion Protestantism is not to win its way by repression at all, but by giving a fuller freedom to all;
records.haiku_rationale: Protestantism is to be freed (empowered) to win its way by granting fuller freedom (non-interference) to all people.

records.speaker: Mr. HARDIE
records.sentence: Where is the freedom?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as a rhetorical challenge, without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what—the context is missing from this single sentence.

records.speaker: Mr. HARDIE
records.sentence: "Freedom" is a word that is running all ways.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is a meta-comment on the word "freedom" itself—observing that the term is ambiguous and used in multiple directions—without specifying what is actually being freed, from what, or to what.

records.speaker: Viscount SANDON
records.sentence: I know that to secure freedom from their civil duties in order to put in the necessary training at what might be very inconvenient times would entail extra expenditure, but I would take that extra expenditure from the money that is spent on the existing Regular Army, and devote it to the requirements of the Territorial Army.
records.haiku_rationale: Territorial Army soldiers are being freed from civil duties (normal civilian obligations) in order to undertake military training—this describes freedom from interference with their availability for defence preparations.

records.speaker: Mr. TREVELYAN
records.sentence: It is not freedom for the local education authorities;
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns freedom to act (not being constrained by external rules) granted to local education authorities as institutional bodies—a question of their empowerment or capacity to govern themselves.

records.speaker: Mr. TREVELYAN
records.sentence: It is freedom to the inferior local authorities to go on giving an inadequate supply of these things, but it is a restriction on the better authorities and an attempt to make them give a less good supply.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns freedom/restriction on local authorities to set supply levels: inferior authorities gain freedom to provide inadequate supply (negative liberty—absence of constraint), while better authorities face restriction on their capacity to provide superior supply (positive liberty—empowerment constrained).

records.speaker: Mr. TREVELYAN
records.sentence: This is done, I understand, in the name of freedom for the local authority.
records.haiku_rationale: The local authority is being freed (empowered) to govern/manage itself, granted capacity to act independently rather than protected from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. MORGAN JONES
records.sentence: I am prepared to grant that there is an age at which a person ought to have perfect freedom to make the decision whether he can or cannot join the Army.
records.haiku_rationale: A person granted the capacity to make their own decision whether to join the Army — empowered agency over a major life choice.

records.speaker: Mr. WHEATLEY
records.sentence: In setting up the Free State in Ireland we did not in regard to the 25,000 troops, or whatever was the size of the Army which we allowed those free people to organise, while we were granting them their so-called liberty, go the length of suggesting to them that if we required to use the Army against Ireland in the future, we would retain the power to make them pay for it whilst we were using it against them.
records.haiku_rationale: Granting the Free State the liberty to organise its own Army represents freedom to self-govern and exercise autonomous control—a positive liberty of empowerment, not merely freedom from external interference.

records.speaker: Mr. HARNEY
records.sentence: That is individual liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual liberty is invoked as a general principle opposed to state control; the specific object of freedom (what is being freed and from what) is not specified in this bare statement.

records.speaker: Sir L. WORTHINGTON-EVANS
records.sentence: This Bill will restore to him his freedom and that is why all that jeering which is organised from the top is not going to save you when you get down—[ Interruption ]—to the country.
records.haiku_rationale: The Bill restores freedom to a person (freedom from some prior constraint or deprivation); this is empowerment or restoration of capacity, making it positive liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. DIXEY

But, at any rate, on the present occasion it is not necessary for any party in the House to troop outside to decide what it shall do, and we shall all of us in every part of the House be
at liberty to go our several ways without any accusation of tactics.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to go our several ways" is a procedural idiom describing MPs' freedom to vote according to their conscience without party discipline, a matter of parliamentary procedure and courtesy rather than a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. SPEAKER
records.sentence: I have not had an opportunity, since this question was raised, of referring to past Rulings, but I have always understood that, although questions might be addressed either to the Prime Minister's Department or to some other Department, that particular Department was always at liberty to transfer questions to some other Department if it thought that they were more concerned.
records.haiku_rationale: A Department was at liberty to transfer questions—this is parliamentary procedure language describing what a body is permitted to do within standing orders, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Major CHURCH
records.sentence: I hope they will be given the fullest freedom to develop their own ideas and to do what they like with the R 100.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is the capacity to develop ideas and make decisions about the R 100; this names empowerment to act without constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. MESSER
records.sentence: Member for Lancaster belongs, in exercising freedom of speech to such an extent that it prevented others from speaking.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses freedom of speech as a liberty that can be exercised to excess, preventing others from exercising the same freedom. The object of freedom is speech; the constraint is interference with others' right to speak.

records.speaker: Mr. MACQUISTEN
records.sentence: We lost the freedom of Parliament because the Irish were so troublesome that we introduced the Closure.
records.haiku_rationale: Parliament lost freedom from interference in its operations (the ability to conduct business without procedural constraints) — the Closure rules restrict Parliament's former unrestricted debating rights, a negative liberty concept.

records.speaker: Earl WINTERTON
records.sentence: The Secretary of State, helped by the methods of attack of some rather unskilful critics, perhaps even on this side of the House as well, has tried to mix up this matter of India's fiscal freedom with the question of the steps that have been taken by successive Governments in India to encourage the production and consumption of Indian goods.
records.haiku_rationale: India's fiscal freedom is freedom from imperial interference in its tariff and trade policy—a freedom FROM constraint on India's autonomous economic decision-making.

records.speaker: Mr. FLINT
records.sentence: In that new spirit of freedom the Economic Conference is to meet again, and we may hope that in that spirit new ties will be formed, for their loyalty is undoubted.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as a rhetorical value to describe a spirit of international economic cooperation among nations, not specifying freedom from or to any particular constraint or capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. RUNCIMAN
records.sentence: It is within the limits of that freedom that we ask the House to give us these powers, and I can assure the House that they will not be abused, because we are just as much alive to the delicacy of British industry and commerce as any hon.
records.haiku_rationale: British industry and commerce are freed to operate without interference—Mr. Runciman is requesting powers while assuring they will not be abused, seeking room for industrial/commercial action within constitutional limits.

records.speaker: Mr. JONES
records.sentence: At what point is this freedom to stop?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asks when a specific freedom (unnamed in the excerpt) ceases to apply; without the antecedent context, we cannot determine whether this refers to freedom from interference or freedom to act.

records.speaker: Mr. JONES
records.sentence: In such circumstances as these, by resignation they will not only regain that freedom which they desire, but they will add to the respect of the electors for the Government of this land.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being regained through resignation is freedom from electoral disrespect or loss of public confidence—a freedom from constraint on the government's standing and authority. This concerns removal of interference or encumbrance, not empowerment to do something new.

records.speaker: Mr. KINGSLEY GRIFFITH
records.sentence: Members are quite at liberty to argue, if they can persuade themselves of the fact, that you can tax food without raising its price.
records.haiku_rationale: Members are at liberty to argue without interference — this is parliamentary procedure language describing freedom of debate from constraint, not a substantive claim about capacity or empowerment.

records.speaker: Mr. COCKS
records.sentence: If these conditions are not fulfilled on both sides, she must have liberty to re-arm and the result must be to increase the burden of armaments and the menace and danger of war.
records.haiku_rationale: A country (she) is being freed to re-arm — empowered to undertake rearmament without external constraint or agreement.

records.speaker: Sir J. GILMOUR
records.sentence: On the other hand, I have got what is generally termed a gentleman's agreement, given with great freedom, and I believe with entire honesty.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "given with great freedom" modifies how an agreement was made (with voluntary, uninhibited intent), not a claim about liberty-as-a-value regarding freedom from interference or empowerment to act.

records.speaker: Sir H. YOUNG
records.sentence: That is one benefit from the new scheme, namely, a greater sense of freedom and initiative for local authorities.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being empowered (granted capacity and discretion) to exercise initiative and self-direction under the new scheme—this is positive liberty, the freedom/power to act rather than freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. CHURCHILL
records.sentence: Friend will forgive me, this bleak Budget, at any rate the assurance of financial solvency, and we have a weapon of unequalled, almost unprecedented, power in a country like ours which is quitting Free Trade after so many generations—the weapon of fiscal freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Fiscal freedom is the freedom from the constraints of Free Trade tariff policy, empowering the country to pursue independent trade policy without interference from prior commitments.

records.speaker: Mr. MACQUISTEN
records.sentence: What a terrible infringement of liberty they are.
records.haiku_rationale: A general rhetorical invocation of "liberty" as a value being infringed—what is being freed is unspecified, but the invocation opposes some interference or restriction as a matter of principle, characteristic of negative liberty discourse.

records.speaker: Mr. de ROTHSCHILD
records.sentence: Up to now the prosperity of the British Empire and of this country has been founded on the readiness of primary producers to let Britain have their raw materials in exchange for manufactures, but it does appear from several reports from Canada that Canadian copper interests are now pressing for some scheme to be adopted at Ottawa to restrict British manufacturers from the freedom of purchasing their raw material in copper from the United States as they have done in the past.
records.haiku_rationale: British manufacturers are being restricted from freedom of purchasing raw materials (copper) from the United States—this is freedom from interference in trade and commercial contract.

records.speaker: Mr. BALDWIN
records.sentence: If they feel the industry would be advantaged by having special representatives of their own they are at liberty to go out, and we shall only be too pleased to take any advice from anyone competent to offer it to us.
records.haiku_rationale: Being "at liberty to go out" refers to whether representatives are permitted to act—a procedural permission to participate, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Sir JOHN WARD LAW-MILNE
records.sentence: I can say so with the more freedom because I was the last witness before the Joint Committee on the Bill of 1919, and I said at that time, speaking for certain opinions held in India, that we thought that the reforms went too far and too fast.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker claims freedom (latitude/ease) to make a particular statement because of his prior role as a witness; "freedom" here operates as permission or lack of constraint to express an opinion, a rhetorical invocation of liberty as release from impediment to speech.

records.speaker: The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER
records.sentence: After a long period of depression we have recovered our freedom in monetary matters.
records.haiku_rationale: The government has recovered its freedom/capacity in monetary matters—moving from constraint (depression, possibly tied to gold standard or fiscal restriction) to an enabled condition where it can now act independently in monetary policy.

records.speaker: Mr. WILLIAMS
records.sentence: The deprivation of liberty in school is not the same as deprivation of liberty in a place where people are put because they have offended against the community and are subject to a degree of restraint which is not true of the ordinary school.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is discussing the removal of freedom (from restraint/interference) in two different contexts: school versus criminal detention. The object of freedom being discussed is freedom from restraint, and the speaker is comparing how much non-interference (freedom from constraint) exists in each setting.

records.speaker: Sir H. SAMUEL
records.sentence: When we accepted that, on the condition we made for full freedom of speech and vote, these hon.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech and the right to vote are named as conditions accepted, specifying freedom from interference with these political capacities.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: freedom both fiscally and politically.
records.haiku_rationale: This is ambiguous—"freedom both fiscally and politically" does not specify whether it refers to freedom from fiscal/political constraint or capacity to act fiscally/politically.

records.speaker: Sir ROBERT HORNE
records.sentence: It has enabled to be carried out the greatest conversion scheme which the world has ever known, and while there are directions in which I could not entirely agree with, and would even take the liberty of criticising some of the authorities who manage our finances, I would desire to-day to pay my meed of admiration to the skill with which these great operations have been conducted.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of criticising" is a parliamentary idiom meaning the speaker permitted himself to make a criticism; it does not invoke liberty as a political value but rather as a conversational courtesy.

records.speaker: Mr. LEONARD
records.sentence: If it be the case that the settlement of the problem in these four items of activity would break the back of unemployment, what we want is more freedom of trade, because these activities thrive according to the extent to which commodities are moved about the world.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker advocates for freedom of trade—removal of interference with commercial exchange and commodity movement—to enable economic activities to flourish and reduce unemployment.

records.speaker: Mr. HOROBIN
records.sentence: It is as if someone were to say "the calculus of variations is a very difficult branch of mathematics, and therefore I am quite at liberty to pretend that two and two make six.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is not making a substantive claim about liberty as a value; "at liberty to" is a rhetorical, idiomatic expression meaning "permitted" or "entitled" in a procedural/conversational sense, used to illustrate logical absurdity in an argument.

records.speaker: Sir R. HORNE
records.sentence: Would he put restrictions to-day upon private enterprises who were desirous of raising their fares in order to meet their charges, and, if he would, what would become of the freedom of private enterprise?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom of private enterprise" — the capacity or opportunity for private businesses to set their own fares without state restriction. This is freedom-to (act/set terms), not freedom-from in the sense of classical civil liberties.

records.speaker: Mr. BUCHAN
records.sentence: There is a great deal of nonsense talked about freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is making a meta-claim about discourse on freedom itself, without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what. The sentence identifies no specific object of liberty or direction of freedom.

records.speaker: Sir STAFFORD CRIPPS
records.sentence: It has to do with one of the great basic conceptions of our constitutional liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "constitutional liberty" as a foundational principle without specifying whether it concerns freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Vice-Admiral G. CAMPBELL
records.sentence: I am going to take the liberty of suggesting one or two ways in which I consider that further economies might be-effected.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of suggesting" is parliamentary procedural language indicating polite permission to speak, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. CHRISTIE
records.sentence: and gallant Gentleman, but it is obvious that when he has got his way the farmer will have to give up a great deal of his freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The farmer's freedom is being constrained or removed—a loss of non-interference with his economic activities and conduct. This is negative liberty being taken away.

records.speaker: Major NATHAN
records.sentence: Let Germany show a response to the public opinion of the world, and let her enshrine liberty firmly in her own country.
records.haiku_rationale: Germany is empowered to establish (enshrine) liberty within its own territory; the speaker calls for Germany to secure and institutionalize liberty in the nation.

records.speaker: Mr. JONES
records.sentence:
May we take it that the Japanese forces are at liberty now to
occupy the whole of Chinese territory without incurring any prospect of protest from the other Powers at Geneva?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to occupy" describes whether Japanese forces are free from constraint or interference from other Powers at Geneva in occupying Chinese territory—the object of freedom is military occupation, and the question asks whether they face freedom FROM potential protest/interference.

records.speaker: Sir H. CROFT
records.sentence: I should not be at liberty to discuss the question of raising prices with the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is used in procedural parliamentary language meaning "permitted by the rules to" rather than as a substantive claim about freedom or rights being valued.

records.speaker: Mr. HORE-BELISHA
records.sentence: Friend has on a number of occasions expressed the view of His Majesty's Government that, although a return to the Gold standard might be our ultimate objective when proper conditions were assured, we must reserve complete liberty to choose both our own time and parity.
records.haiku_rationale: The government reserves freedom from external constraint to choose the timing and terms of return to the Gold standard—a capacity to act autonomously in economic policy.

records.speaker: Mr. JANNER
records.sentence: Heligoland, and was for that given the freedom of the island.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence grants an empowered status (freedom of the island) to enable the person to act within or govern Heligoland — a positive liberty of capacity or privilege.

records.speaker: Mr. MAINWARING
records.sentence: The conscience of the country is certain to respond to the appeal now made, which is: "Do we as a people believe that we ought to give freedom to a certain number of people to make the means which can set millions of people killing each other in various parts of the world?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asks whether the country should grant (positive empowerment to) freedom to armaments manufacturers to produce weapons, juxtaposed against the consequence of enabling mass killing. The core phrase "give freedom to a certain number of people to make" describes granting permission/capacity—positive liberty.

records.speaker: Sir J. WALKER SMITH
records.sentence: From that moment all the freedom, elasticity and good will that attaches to the present joint councils will disappear.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker warns that procedural flexibility and goodwill will be lost if a change occurs to joint councils; "freedom" here names scope for discretionary action and adaptability within an institutional arrangement, not freedom from external interference.

records.speaker: Mr. SMITH
records.sentence: Member talked about the freedom of the individual, but I would remind him that in many cases the freedom of the individual has to be limited for the benefit of the whole.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual freedom is being limited (constrained in its exercise) for collective benefit, framing the tension between non-interference with individual choice and social welfare.

records.speaker: Mr. EMRYS-EVANS
records.sentence: He spoke with vast knowledge and with great authority, but it seems to me that freedom of choice leads us towards the attitude of mind of a mediator;
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of choice is a negative liberty: it names the freedom from interference in making decisions, or the capacity to choose among options without constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. COOPER
records.sentence: Next year should we ask the House to Vote more money, the House will be at liberty to turn it down.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is a procedural expression meaning the House will be permitted or have the opportunity to reject the funding request—an instance of parliamentary practice language, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. BURNETT
records.sentence: I received a pamphlet a day or two ago from a society which calls itself the Freedom Association.
records.haiku_rationale: This sentence reports receipt of a pamphlet from an organization with "Freedom Association" in its proper name; the word "freedom" appears as part of a proper noun and does not make a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Major LLOYD GEORGE
records.sentence:
Let them do that—and after all that is what they were returned here to do—let them get on with the job, instead of wasting their
time upon Bills of this sort, and let them remember in doing so that no State can survive which substitutes fear for freedom and force for persuasion.
records.haiku_rationale: A state survives by maintaining freedom (as opposed to fear) and using persuasion (as opposed to force); freedom here is understood as the absence of state interference and coercion—a foundational negative liberty valued as essential to state legitimacy.

records.speaker: Mr. SKELTON
records.sentence: Friend knows that he is perfectly at liberty to ask the Secretary of State to consider the suitability of the sentence, and so forth.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to ask" is parliamentary procedure language meaning permitted or able to make a request; it does not invoke liberty as a value against interference or as empowerment for self-governance.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: These are the interferences with liberty which they always impute to the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: Interference with liberty (not specified what form—speech, movement, contract, etc.), implying something is being freed from constraint or obstruction.

records.speaker: Mr. LOGAN
records.sentence: We give people freedom to enunciate policy, but we have no right to allow anybody to preach sedition.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to enunciate policy is positive liberty—the capacity to articulate views—but the sentence's normative claim emphasizes restraint from allowing sedition, invoking negative liberty constraints. The speaker grants one freedom while denying another.

records.speaker: Mr. GEORGE BALFOUR
records.sentence: I make no complaint of that, however, and I have no right as a concessionaire to say that my interest must be regarded as a prior right coming before the rights of individual property and individual liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual liberty is invoked as a right opposed to claims that private commercial interests (as a concessionaire) should take priority over it—a claim about freedom from interference with individual property and personal autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. SPEAKER
records.sentence: Of course, the Committee are quite at liberty to do what they like with the Bill provided they do not alter it altogether.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to do what they like" refers to parliamentary procedure—the Committee's procedural authority to handle the Bill according to standing orders, not a substantive claim about political freedom or empowerment. This is a formulaic procedural expression.

records.speaker: Captain ELLISTON
records.sentence: and whether, in view of the fact that this meat cannot be examined on arrival as to its freedom from disease, he will take steps to include it in the schedule of prohibited meat under the Public Health (Imported Food) Regulations?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "freedom from disease" refers to the quality or state of meat being uncontaminated or uninfected—a property of the meat itself, not a liberty-as-value claim about agents' freedom to act or from interference. This is descriptive language about safety, not a normative claim about liberty.

records.speaker: Sir F. ACLAND
records.sentence: I say, trust your teachers, give them freedom and they will do little harm even if they do happen to belong to one particular party or another.
records.haiku_rationale: Teachers are being freed (given capacity/empowerment) to act without interference in their professional judgment regarding party affiliation—this is about enabling them to operate freely, not about protecting them from a specific restriction.

records.speaker: Sir F. ACLAND
records.sentence: If we can get real freedom for our schools though an intermediate system of education, it will be tremendously worth while taking more pains with the training of teachers and giving them a chance of using their freedom better.
records.haiku_rationale: Teachers are being freed to use their professional judgment and discretion in their work—a capacity to act autonomously—rather than being freed from external constraint; this is empowerment to exercise pedagogical choice.

records.speaker: Mr. LAMBERT
records.sentence: Friend has great difficulties to face and I can assure him that the agriculturists will give him support if he recovers his freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as a cause opposed to difficulties facing a friend, using it as a rhetorical appeal for support — freedom from constraints or oppression.

records.speaker: Mr. KINGSLEY GRIFFITH
records.sentence: People who are not ordinarily concerned with politics are gravely concerned with this question of liberty, as all will have realised who read the recent magnificent Rectorial Address of General Smuts.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "liberty" as a general cause of concern and value without specifying what freedom is being protected from interference or what capacity is being enabled.

records.speaker: Mr. MACQUISTEN
records.sentence: We want absolute liberty of speech so that everyone is able to have their grievances ventilated, and I should be the last person to support anything which would be likely to prevent free expression of opinion.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech and free expression of opinion—individuals are freed from interference with their ability to voice grievances and express views.

records.speaker: Mr. LYONS
records.sentence: But everyone knows that, in order to preserve liberty and public order, there must be certain safeguards, and a right to search in certain circumstances becomes essential.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker argues that safeguards and search rights are essential to preserve liberty from disorder and threat—liberty is being defended from interference by lawlessness/chaos, not expanded or empowered.

records.speaker: Brigadier-General CRITCHLEY
records.sentence: On the question of profit from the totalisator, while it is negligible if it runs from 10 to 12 meetings a night, will begin to assume large proportions if you run 100 races a day as you are at liberty to do under the present Bill.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to do" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning "permitted/able to" and does not invoke liberty-as-a-value in the sense of freedom from interference or empowerment as a substantive principle.

records.speaker: Captain ARTHUR EVANS
records.sentence: I believe in liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: A bare rhetorical invocation of "liberty" as a value without specification of what is being freed or from what; insufficient context to determine whether negative (freedom from interference) or positive (empowerment to act) liberty is meant.

records.speaker: Captain EVANS
records.sentence:
I realise, of course, that political liberty is affected by the Incitement to Sedition Bill and that the kind of liberty which we are now
discussing is of a more domestic nature, but I think that it is a kind of liberty to which the average person pays more heed than he does to any other kind of liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking "political liberty" and "the kind of liberty which we are now discussing" as domestic matters to which ordinary people pay attention, in contrast with political liberty affected by sedition law. Without specification of what constraint or capacity defines "this kind of liberty," the sentence treats liberty as a general value opposing potential infringement but does not clearly articulate the specific object of freedom (from-or-to what). The phrasing is rhetorical and under-specified.

records.speaker: Miss HORSBRUGH
records.sentence: It seems strange that those who urge the preservation of the economic liberty of the subject should not be able to find time, perhaps in a sentence, to refer to the liberties that have been restored to more than 900,000 people in this country who have had restored to them the chance to work and earn their own livelihood instead of being dependent on an allowance from the State.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence emphasizes freedom FROM economic dependence on the State through restoration of employment opportunity and self-sufficiency — this is negative liberty against state interference in economic choice, though the "chance to work" also carries an enabling dimension of positive liberty (capacity to earn livelihood).

records.speaker: Mr. HOLDSWORTH
records.sentence: They had the courage to express, in the so-called freedom of speech of the Labour party, their real, honest belief in Socialism, and as a result they now find themselves here.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech—the absence of interference with political expression—is being invoked as what allowed Labour party members to express socialist beliefs.

records.speaker: Mr. MORGAN JONES
records.sentence: Grateful certainly, but satisfied, no, because it is an essential part of freedom as we understand it that people should be adequately equipped for the business of self-government in all its manifestations.
records.haiku_rationale: People must be adequately equipped (enabled capacity) for self-government, which is framed as part of freedom—this is empowerment to govern oneself, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. RHYS DAVIES
records.sentence:
Indeed, many people, not only in
India but in this country, have sacrificed a great deal to try to secure for the Indian people greater freedom than they now possess.
records.haiku_rationale: The Indian people are being freed to/for greater autonomy and self-governance, not from interference with a specific activity. This is empowerment to self-rule.

records.speaker: Mr. CHURCHILL
records.sentence: I took the liberty of borrowing—I had almost said of purloining—his actual copy in order to refresh my own memory, and I have my hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of borrowing" is parliamentary procedure language where "at liberty" / "took the liberty" means "ventured to" or "permitted myself to"—not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. MORGAN JONES
records.sentence: We have been hoping that some day, and we hope soon, the people of India will necessarily be given full power and be free to discuss foreign affairs with the same degree of freedom as Canada, Australia, South Africa or any of the other Dominions.
records.haiku_rationale: India being "given full power and be free to discuss foreign affairs" — the object of freedom is the capacity to conduct foreign policy independently as a sovereign nation, framed as empowerment to self-govern, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Sir K. WOOD
records.sentence:
It will be generally agreed that there is nothing that offends against the liberty of the subject in this provision and that anyone who makes persistent telephone calls without reasonable cause
and causes annoyance should be liable to be proceeded against.
records.haiku_rationale: The liberty of the subject is being protected from interference by those making persistent telephone calls causing annoyance; legal liability ensures freedom from harassment rather than granting capacity to act.

records.speaker: The ATTORNEY-GENERAL
records.sentence: I have pointed out the difficulties of dealing with this matter in the Way proposed in the third Sub-section of the Amendment, but, on the other hand, the Government do recognise that there should be a certain freedom, on the part of the companies or firms who carry on businesses or professions in India, to choose their technical or professional advisers.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of companies to choose their professional advisers—a capacity or empowerment to select agents, not a freedom from interference with selection itself.

records.speaker: Miss RATHBONE
records.sentence: Gentleman say whether there is any evidence of serious sedition in the Gold Coast or Nigeria which makes such drastic restrictions on the liberty of the Press necessary?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker questions restrictions imposed on the liberty (freedom) of the Press, treating press freedom as a value that should not be restricted unless justified by serious sedition.

records.speaker: Sir S. HOARE
records.sentence: Apart from that statutory obligation he is at liberty to decide on what subjects he consults them.
records.haiku_rationale: This is parliamentary procedure language where "at liberty" means permitted or allowed to act; the subject can decide on consultation matters without interference.

records.speaker: Mr. LLOYD GEORGE
records.sentence: In itself it is a notable stand for human freedom that we are celebrating, and, by its success, that stand may yet divert currents of despotism that are sweeping away free institutions in many lands.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "human freedom" and "free institutions" in opposition to "despotism" and threats to liberty across lands—a rhetorical appeal to freedom from tyranny and oppressive regimes.

records.speaker: Colonel WEDGWOOD
records.sentence: I think that in the long run freedom has this enormous advantage over tyranny, that we do get both better information and better confidence in the body politic.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (non-tyranny) is presented as empowering the body politic to achieve better information and confidence in governance—a positive capacity rather than mere absence of constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. McGOVERN
records.sentence: if you had said in 1935, "We will give you the fullest measure of freedom, the right to vote to the whole population of the country;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker describes "fullest measure of freedom" and "the right to vote" as something being granted to the whole population—empowerment to participate in democratic self-governance through voting.

records.speaker: Major MILNER
records.sentence:
Gentleman in paragraph 5 of his reply said:
 In conclusion I would state that His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom feel that the free intercourse on equal terms with the other members of the British Commonwealth which the Irish Free State have enjoyed under the Treaty Settlement, culminating in the Statute of Westminster, is the surest proof of their freedom to work out their own destiny within the Commonwealth.
records.haiku_rationale: The Irish Free State is being empowered to work out its own destiny within the Commonwealth — they are granted the capacity to govern themselves through the freedom conferred by the Treaty and Statute of Westminster.

records.speaker: Mr. KINGSLEY GRIFFITH
records.sentence: We have the same admiration for liberty and freedom of speech, and I believe that these bonds of union should be strong enough to survive any temporary disagreement.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech is being protected from interference; it is treated as a value that bonds nations together in opposition to tyranny.

records.speaker: Captain WALLACE
records.sentence: Member for the Colne Valley stated his case in regard to civil liberty, and I do so with the particular concurrence of my right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence references "civil liberty" as a matter being discussed, but does not substantively explain what is being freed or from what. It is too truncated to determine whether civil liberty is being discussed as protection from interference or as an enabling capacity.

records.speaker: The SECRETARY of STATE for FOREIGN AFFAIRS
records.sentence: It is clearly more convenient for us to do that than if we were cribbed, cabined and confined within the narrow compass of a Supplementary Estimate, and I propose to avail myself of the liberty which has thus been given to me.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is referring to procedural permission granted by parliamentary rules—the liberty to act within a budgetary framework without being constrained to a Supplementary Estimate—rather than claiming a value about freedom from interference or capacity to act on a matter of principle.

records.speaker: Sir K. WOOD
records.sentence: Gentleman ought to have the freedom of the City.
records.haiku_rationale: Gentlemen are being empowered (granted the capacity) to access and participate in the City; this is a grant of opportunity or privilege to act within urban/civic space.

records.speaker: Mr. RUSSELL
records.sentence: But you have to decide between the liberty of the individual to bet and the liberty of the promoter to exploit the betting instinct of others for private gain.
records.haiku_rationale: Two freedoms are in tension: individuals freed from prohibition on betting, versus promoters freed from regulation to exploit others' gambling impulses. Both are framed as freedom from constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. CHURCHILL
records.sentence: Either there will be a melting of hearts and a joining of hands between great nations which will set out upon realising the glorious age of prosperity and freedom which is now within the grasp of the millions of toiling people, or there will be an explosion and a catastrophe the course of which no imagination can measure, and beyond which no human eye can see.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom here is invoked as a rhetorical ideal and ultimate social outcome—a glorious age of "prosperity and freedom" that nations can realize together—opposed to catastrophe and war. The object of freedom is unspecified (freedom from what, or to do what is left implicit), and the sentence presents freedom as an aspirational state or condition to be achieved collectively by "great nations," functioning as part of Churchill's vision of human flourishing rather than as a specific constraint on interference or a specific capacity.

records.speaker: Sir FRANCIS ACLAND
records.sentence: Surely, there ought to be complete freedom in matters of that kind.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "complete freedom" as a general principle opposing constraint in matters unspecified in this excerpt, suggesting freedom from interference, but the sentence lacks specific detail about what is being freed and from what.

records.speaker: Mr. GARRO JONES
records.sentence: We are not discussing whether or not we shall pass the Bill, but whether the Committee are at liberty to reduce the period of years, and we wish to know whether there is anything —absolutely or by implication—in the agreement with Imperial Airways, or the outlined agreement, to prevent us from making a change.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is asking whether the Committee has procedural capacity (empowerment) to reduce the period of years under an agreement with Imperial Airways—whether they are legally enabled to make that change.

records.speaker: Captain CROOKSHANK
records.sentence: As the inquiry is going on, I do not feel at liberty to make any comments on any statements made before it.
records.haiku_rationale: This is parliamentary procedure language: "at liberty to" means permitted/enabled to comment. The speaker is saying they are not permitted (procedurally) to comment while an inquiry is ongoing. This is about parliamentary propriety, not a substantive claim about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Sir S. HOARE
records.sentence: Men who have served as naval ratings are at liberty to enlist in the Territorial Army with the exception of those who, as naval pensioners or naval reservists, will be required in an emergency for service in the Navy.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence uses "at liberty to" as parliamentary procedural language meaning "permitted" or "allowed"—it does not invoke liberty as a value about freedom from interference or capacity for self-direction, but rather describes a formal permission or eligibility rule for military service.

records.speaker: Mr. GALLACHER
records.sentence: It will remain, unless the Arab can get freedom, a key outpost, or as one hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The Arab peoples' freedom is invoked as what is needed in contrast to remaining a colonial outpost—freedom from foreign domination and control.

records.speaker: Sir A. WILSON
records.sentence:
In that report we find these words:
 Our general conclusions are … that the ordinary right of freedom to contract ought not to be withdrawn without some compelling reason.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of contract is being protected from withdrawal/interference—a classic negative liberty claim that freedom from restriction on contractual agreements should not be removed without justification.

records.speaker: The FINANCIAL SECRETARY to the TREASURY
records.sentence: It is in order to preserve our own right, to live our own life, to follow our own ideals of freedom, that we are strengthening our defences.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker claims that preserving the right to live one's own life and follow one's own ideals of freedom requires military strengthening—the freedom being preserved is freedom from external interference/conquest that would prevent the nation from self-determination.

records.speaker: Mr. CHURCHILL
records.sentence: It seems to me that if it were possible to have relations with all the Mediterranean Powers which gave a greater feeling of the freedom and security of the Mediterranean, a feeling that it was, as it were, an area which was not to be disturbed by the storms of war, there would be another very great and essential step forward to the securing of world peace and also, it might well be, to the reinforced action of the League of Nations.
records.haiku_rationale: The "freedom and security of the Mediterranean" refers to the collective region being freed from disturbance by war—a freedom from interference and threat, not empowerment to act.

records.speaker: Mr. MORGAN JONES
records.sentence: This is really a question of the freedom of all candidates to approach the electorate in the way that seems to them best.
records.haiku_rationale: Candidates are freed from interference in their choice of how to approach the electorate—freedom of action/movement in electoral campaigning.

records.speaker: Mr. LOGAN
records.sentence:
What is the use of speaking of liberty if our men and women starve, and why talk about religion when in your everyday actions

you fail to put Christian principles into operation?
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: the ability to exercise liberty and religion as meaningful values. From-or-to what: the speaker argues liberty is valueless when people starve; he is critiquing formal liberty as insufficient without material conditions (food, livelihood) that enable people to actually exercise it meaningfully.

records.speaker: Colonel WEDGWOOD
records.sentence: You have equally vocal throughout the same countries a passionate desire for freedom and for justice.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence expresses rhetorical invocation of "freedom" as an abstract value and cause (paired with "justice"), without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what. It is a general statement about human aspiration rather than a claim about liberty as freedom from or capacity to do something specific.

records.speaker: Sir Robert Young
records.sentence: There are thousands of refugees from Germany, from Poland, from Russia and from other dictator countries, who might find homes in liberty-loving lands within the British Empire, where freedom of conscience, liberty of speech and citizenship will not be denied them.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence names specific freedoms being protected from interference: freedom of conscience and liberty of speech—what refugees are freed from denial of these protections in the British Empire.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: The War left many evil legacies in this country, but the two worst and the most dangerous to freedom, at least I think so, were these: One is propaganda.
records.haiku_rationale: Propaganda is identified as dangerous to freedom itself—presenting it as an obstacle to the speaker's (undefined) conception of freedom, likely the absence of manipulation and control over thought and belief.

records.speaker: Dr. Burgin
records.sentence: The demand was less than half the normal, and it is certain that without the schemes, and the severe restrictions imposed by the Tramp Shipping Administrative Committee upon the freedom of owners to offer tonnage in the market, the freight market would have slumped to most disastrous levels.
records.haiku_rationale: Owners are being freed from restrictions on their ability to offer tonnage in the market—this is freedom from interference with commercial transaction and trade.

records.speaker: Sir Francis Acland
records.sentence: Even if there were any power given to the Chancellor to deal with a certain part of our debt in a certain way, that could be made entirely of no effect by the Chancellor's complete freedom to deal with our total debt from year to year in practically any way he wishes.
records.haiku_rationale: The Chancellor's "freedom to deal with our total debt" names his capacity or empowerment to act (to handle debt in various ways), which is a positive liberty — the freedom to do something rather than freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Sir Stafford Cripps
records.sentence: War, if it is engaged in, will be for the protection of the property and interests of the few and will not be for the winning of greater freedom for the use of the common people, either here or in other countries.
records.haiku_rationale: The common people are being denied freedom to use (or enjoy) their capacities/opportunities; the war protects the few's property rather than winning expanded freedoms or capacities for ordinary people.

records.speaker: Mr. Magnay
records.sentence:
It is true that he suggested a period of seven years and that in this case the period is five years, but altogether the extensions

of the powers of the Commissioner are immense and I do not imagine that anything but good can result from the freedom which the present Commissioner will enjoy compared with the previous Commissioner.
records.haiku_rationale: The Commissioner is being freed to exercise expanded powers (extensions of authority), representing an enabling capacity or empowerment to act with greater scope than the previous Commissioner.

records.speaker: Mr. Westwood
records.sentence: Greater freedom will require to be applied even as far as the leaders are concerned and the instruction that they are to give.
records.haiku_rationale: Greater freedom (enabling capacity) is to be applied/extended to leaders in the instruction they are to give, suggesting empowerment to act with less constraint.

records.speaker: Captain Balfour
records.sentence: Bearing in mind the theoretical freedom of the Crown to send for whomsoever it likes, but usually for the Leader of the Opposition, to form a Government in the event of the defeat of the Government in office, then in the event of Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence describes the Crown's freedom to send for any person (whomsoever it likes) to form a government—an empowerment or discretionary capacity to choose whom to call, not freedom from interference with an existing activity.

records.speaker: The Lord Advocate
records.sentence:
It is interesting also to remember that by the Treaty of Northampton of 1327, which is frequently referred to during elections and by-elections in Scotland, provision was made for the restoration by England to Scotland of all documents
 touching the freedom of Scotland, 
and it is in a sense in fulfilment of that Treaty that some at least of the documents scheduled in this Bill are now being sent back to the custody which they should never have left.
records.haiku_rationale: Scotland's "freedom" here refers to its capacity for self-governance and national independence restored through recovery of historical documents that had been taken, not freedom from interference in a specific activity.

records.speaker: Mrs. Tate
records.sentence: We are only asking the House to recognise the fact that where a marriage has in actual fact broken down the country can give freedom to the partners.
records.haiku_rationale: The country is empowered to grant partners freedom (divorce/release) from a broken marriage—this is about enabling capacity to act (exit a failed marriage), not merely removing interference with existing freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Pickthorn
records.sentence: Another effect of increasing the importance of the Leader of the Opposition would be, I think, to diminish the freedom of choice of Prime Minister.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns the Prime Minister's capacity to make a choice freely (what choices are available to them); increasing the Opposition Leader's power would reduce that capacity or range of options—this is about freedom TO act (or the constraint on one's empowered agency).

records.speaker: The Postmaster-General
records.sentence: I understand that members of the staff of the British Broadcasting Corporation have full liberty to belong to any trade union for which they are eligible, and that it is the policy of the corporation to secure that the conditions of employment of its staff are in every case at least as good as those commonly obtaining in the case of comparable workers.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being described is the right of BBC staff to join trade unions without interference — a classic negative liberty of association and collective representation, protected from corporate restriction.

records.speaker: Mr. Attlee
records.sentence: There are in other parts of the world people who now attack liberty and profess to despise it.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty itself is being attacked and despised as a cause/value opposed to tyranny—a rhetorical invocation of freedom from oppression and coercion.

records.speaker: Mr. Attlee
records.sentence: We shall show them that liberty and democracy are better than autocracy and tyranny by the fact of our success in working our own institutions.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a valued cause (opposed to autocracy and tyranny), defined implicitly by capacity to work one's own democratic institutions—freedom to self-govern and choose one's system.

records.speaker: Mr. Churchill
records.sentence: Long may it be the function of the Monarchy, sustained as it will be by Parliament and by the masses of the nation, to give that element of unity, of the present with the past, which, when all is said and done, is the greatest hope of our freedom in the future.
records.haiku_rationale: The Monarchy and Parliament sustain a unifying force that provides the nation's greatest hope for freedom in the future — freedom understood as a collective national capacity or condition preserved through institutional continuity and unity.

records.speaker: Sir John Wardlaw-Milne
records.sentence: Members on this side of the House who held the view then as they do still and who have expressed it publicly in the days of Free Trade, that the only way of bringing about real freedom in trade was to introduce some measure of Protection.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom in/of trade is being freed from the constraints of unrestricted free trade through protective measures, enabling domestic industry to act and compete—a capacity to govern economic policy.

records.speaker: Mr. Cooper
records.sentence:
But until that time comes, I submit that no case has been


made out for a sudden and violent revolution in our industrial world, and I hope that that dreadful eventuality will never arise, and that meanwhile we shall never be driven to go away from our present system of freedom and private enterprise.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom and private enterprise" as a system opposed to revolutionary change and upheaval—a rhetorical appeal to liberty as a cause against coercive interference with the existing economic order.

records.speaker: Sir J. Simon
records.sentence: If the taxpayer in some cases thinks he should get an even higher figure, he will be at liberty to apply for it.
records.haiku_rationale: A taxpayer having the procedural right (at liberty) to apply for a higher figure is being granted an opportunity or capacity to take action; "at liberty to apply" denotes empowerment to pursue a course of conduct.

records.speaker: Mr. Burgin
records.sentence: Holds-worth) has said, it is a point to deal with trespass and a point to deal with liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "liberty" as a general value or principle in opposition to trespass, but does not specify what is being freed, from what interference, or to what capacity; the reference is too abstract and contextually insufficient to determine whether it is about freedom from state/property interference or about empowerment to act.

records.speaker: Sir S. Hoare
records.sentence: Between 400 and 500 men, each of whom is serving a sentence of at least six months are trained at Wakefield under conditions of greater freedom and responsibility than would be practicable in any ordinary mixed prison.
records.haiku_rationale: Prisoners are being given greater freedom and responsibility (relaxed constraints on movement and autonomy) to enable them to function better in a specialized training program; this is positive liberty—empowerment to act and take responsibility within the prison context.

records.speaker: Mr. Gallacher
records.sentence: Friend who expresses in all his being the desire for freedom and movement, the desire to raise his face to the skies, and to shout to the mountains.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "freedom and movement" and the vivid imagery of raising one's face and shouting express freedom from oppression and constraint—a romantic invocation of liberation from the restraints of tyranny or subjugation.

records.speaker: Mr. Loftus
records.sentence: I hope that head teachers will have freedom to try experiments and that their enthusiasm will not be withered and trapped or the whole spirit of the thing destroyed.
records.haiku_rationale: Head teachers are being freed to conduct educational experiments—they are empowered with the capacity and opportunity to try new approaches without administrative constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Dalton
records.sentence: It is now recognised pretty generally that a certain freedom of movement of the exchanges is most desirable at times of instability of trade such as that through which we are now passing.
records.haiku_rationale: Exchange markets are being freed from (or allowed) flexibility of movement, viewed as a capacity to respond to economic conditions—this invokes freedom as an enabling capacity rather than protection from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Benn
records.sentence: " He wants complete freedom, and the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and does not specify what "complete freedom" means or from-or-to what the freedom pertains.

records.speaker: Mr. Speaker
records.sentence: Gentleman the Minister for the Co-ordination of Defence has suggested to him, he is at liberty to do so, but he will see the difficulty.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to do so" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning the Minister is permitted to act in a certain way; it does not engage substantive claims about liberty-as-a-value or freedom from interference with rights and capacities.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Colonel Muirhead
records.sentence: Members wish to adopt that course in this case, and care to bring forward specific cases and specific information or evidence, they are, of course, at liberty to do so, and the Secretary of State will give consideration to the cases submitted to him, as any Minister gives consideration to cases submitted to him by hon.
records.haiku_rationale: Members are permitted to bring forward specific cases; "at liberty to do so" is a parliamentary procedural phrase meaning they have the opportunity/permission to act in this manner.

records.speaker: Mr. Boothby
records.sentence: Tyranny is bad in any form, and in my opinion the main menace of Socialism is the threat to the freedom of the individual, and I believe that in that opinion I have behind me the support of the vast majority of the people of this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The individual is being freed from the threat of Socialist tyranny and constraints on personal autonomy; this invokes freedom from interference with individual agency, a core negative liberty concern.

records.speaker: Mr. Mabane
records.sentence: It has recognised that if work is not available then means must be devised whereby the unemployed may be able to maintain themselves at the same time as they retain their freedom of action.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being retained is freedom of action—freedom from interference with the unemployed's ability to act and direct their own affairs—while simultaneously being materially supported through devised means.

records.speaker: Mr. MacNeill Weir
records.sentence: " That was a defence of the liberty of unlicensed printing.
