records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is referencing the word "liberty" as used by fellaheen (Egyptian peasants), but provides no substantive claim about what is being freed from or to what—it is a mere mention or citation of the word without evaluating liberty as a value.

records.speaker: Sir Robert Young
records.sentence: whether this notice applies to agricultural and colliery workers resident there and, if so, whether they will be at liberty to return to their homes in other parts of the country, unless alternative accommodation is provided for them, seeing many of them are governed by the Essential Work Order.
records.haiku_rationale: The object is freedom of movement (ability to return to homes); workers are constrained by the Essential Work Order, and the question is whether they will be freed from this constraint to return home unless alternative accommodation is provided.

records.speaker: The Secretary of State for the Colonies
records.sentence: Even political development of itself may react upon the social and economic welfare of a whole community, by releasing potentialities for self-reliance and self-help which were kept suppressed by too little political liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Political development releases potentialities for self-reliance and self-help that were suppressed by too little political liberty — the speaker values liberty as removal of suppression, enabling people to act for themselves.

records.speaker: Sir Ian Fraser
records.sentence:
We stood up against the Government—and it is


supremely important to the Members of this Committee who cherish the freedom and independence of broadcasting to encourage the Governors and give them powers to enable them if need be to stand up against Governments.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence frames "freedom and independence of broadcasting" as freedom from governmental interference or control, coupled with granting empowering "powers to enable" broadcasters to resist government pressure—a mixed claim combining negative liberty (non-interference) with positive liberty (institutional capacity to resist).

records.speaker: Mr. Morrison
records.sentence: In Italy and the ex-enemy satellite States, the authorities will be required by the Peace Treaties to secure to all persons under their jurisdiction human rights and the fundamental freedoms.
records.haiku_rationale: The authorities are empowered to secure human rights and fundamental freedoms to all persons—this is a capacity/obligation to ensure people possess substantive rights and freedoms, not merely freedom from interference with a specific liberty like speech or press.

records.speaker: Mr. R. S. Hudson
records.sentence: We had a certain amount of discussion on this upstairs and we on this side of the House believe that if this particular restriction on the liberty of the Minister to make grants for the reconditioning and building of cottages is retained, it will, in effect, destroy a considerable part of the value of the Bill.
records.haiku_rationale: The restriction on the Minister's liberty to make grants is being opposed; the speaker objects to constraints on the Minister's capacity to act (make discretionary grants for cottages).

records.speaker: Professor Savory
records.sentence:
This Christian, Polish culture,


with all its natural features—adherence to Christian morality, respect for the human being and his natural rights, deep love of personal and natural freedom—constitutes, I am glad to say, the supreme obstacle to the aim of merging Poland into the expanding Communist  bloc  of States, under the leadership of the U.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "personal and natural freedom" as a cultural and moral value opposed to Communist domination—freedom from subjection to external control and merger into the Communist bloc.

records.speaker: Mr. Leslie Hale
records.sentence: Manningham-Buller), who occupied a short, ephemeral and undistinguished office in a still-born Government and who was put up to open this Debate, did not even stay to hear what the Liberty Party had to say about the matter.
records.haiku_rationale: The "Liberty Party" is a proper noun (a political party name), not a claim about the value or concept of liberty itself.

records.speaker: Sir Waldron Smithers
records.sentence: If this Government were to pass an Act that the sun should rise in the West and set in the East, we should say that they were mad, but it is an equally flagrant breach of the natural law to deprive men, unduly, of their freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Men are being freed from undue deprivation of their freedom—a double appeal to negative liberty: freedom from governmental interference with natural liberty.

records.speaker: Major Poole
records.sentence: One was with freedom, and he tried to show that the Tory Party had always been in the forefront in the application of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The Tory Party is credited with being in the forefront of "application of freedom" — a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a political cause/value without specifying the particular freedoms involved or whether these are freedoms from interference or capacities to act.

records.speaker: Wing-Commander Robinson
records.sentence: I feel I would be rather out of Order if I followed on a good many of them, especially his dissertation on freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is referring to parliamentary procedure ("be out of Order") and notes the preceding speaker's dissertation on freedom only as a contextual reference, without making a substantive claim about what freedom is or what it should free someone from-or-to.

records.speaker: Mr. Burke
records.sentence: They are limited, and that limits very severely the number of programmes, and the amount of freedom, there can be.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker identifies a constraint on "freedom" (unspecified in type) imposed by resource limitations; this concerns removal of non-interference or capacity to act broadly, but the object of freedom is left unspecified.

records.speaker: Mr. Derek Walker-Smith
records.sentence: I believe that in the quality and character of the programmes put forward they are serving the cause of freedom and democracy.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as a cause being served by the quality of broadcast programmes—freedom here is opposed to tyranny and unfree governance, making this a rhetorical invocation of negative liberty (freedom from oppressive control).

records.speaker: Sir S. Cripps
records.sentence: Although this statement and offer were not effective in bringing about agreement with, or, indeed, between, the Indian communities, it did, nevertheless, have the effect of encouraging all parties in India to look for an early realisation of their freedom, either by the path of unitary central government or the other path which envisaged a possible division.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is national self-determination and self-government for Indian communities; they are freed to realize political autonomy, either through unified governance or partition—an empowerment to govern themselves rather than freedom from specific external constraints.

records.speaker: Mr. Creech Jones
records.sentence: They are allowed the greatest possible freedom of movement.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of movement is freedom from interference with one's right to move or travel.

records.speaker: Mr. Symonds
records.sentence: Everyone is given his freedom to go away.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence describes capacity or permission to depart—freedom to move oneself away from a place.

records.speaker: Mr. Dugdale
records.sentence: He asked about the question of liberty boats.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a reference to naval vessels (liberty boats) used to give sailors shore leave; it is not making a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Major Legge-Bourke
records.sentence: Members who have been very critical of them, and who intend to be critical of them during this Debate, to try to see these things in the light of reality, and to realise that there is no greater freedom in this world than the freedom to change one's mind when one feels one has to.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes freedom to change one's mind as a capacity or opportunity to exercise judgment and alter one's views—an empowered ability to act according to one's reason, not merely absence of constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Oliver Stanley
records.sentence: I cannot help feeling sometimes that if only company promoters of the past had enjoyed the same amount of freedom of accountancy as the Chancellor of the Exchequer has at the present day, very few of them, if any, would ever have enjoyed His Majesty's hospitality.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom of accountancy" as a freedom from constraint or interference in accounting practices, comparing what company promoters lacked in the past to what the Chancellor currently enjoys—a negative liberty interpretation of freedom from regulatory or procedural restrictions on accounting methods.

records.speaker: Captain Crookshank
records.sentence: Gentleman was not at liberty to have any conversation with anybody concerned.
records.haiku_rationale: A gentleman was prohibited from having conversation with certain persons—this concerns freedom from interference with associative/communicative action, expressed in the negative ("not at liberty to").

records.speaker: Mr. Mitchison
records.sentence: What is being done here is to preserve, for the merchant, the liberty he has in that respect.
records.haiku_rationale: The merchant's liberty (freedom to conduct commerce without interference) is being preserved from restriction.

records.speaker: Mr. Brown
records.sentence: He is not merely not in favour of liberty for the rest of us, but is specially opposed to liberty for himself.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes liberty as freedom from interference—both he (the subject) and "the rest of us" are not being granted freedom from external constraint or oppression, and he actively opposes such freedom. This is a rhetorical invocation of liberty as non-interference opposed to tyranny or domination.

records.speaker: Mr. Creech Jones
records.sentence: My latest report on 6th May states that 29 Jews and 214 Arabs were still at liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: A report stating that individuals "were still at liberty" in a context of detention/confinement — this is parliamentary procedure language meaning they were not in custody or confined, freedom from physical restraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Derek Walker-Smith
records.sentence: The question is this: is the world, after the sweat and agony of war, to reach a state of freedom, democracy and the politics of plenty?
records.haiku_rationale: The world is being asked to reach "freedom" — a state of liberation from the constraint of war, scarcity, and presumably tyranny — without specifying what freedom FROM or freedom TO do with specific capacities or opportunities.

records.speaker: Mr. William Ross
records.sentence: She has won this freedom.

papers, to which a contribution was made on the freedom of the Press by the Party opposite—

records.speaker: Mr. Turton
records.sentence: He has said that there must not be over-centralisation in nationalisation proposals, that a certain amount of freedom must be given to a Commission.

records.speaker: Mr. Creech Jones
records.sentence: I am convinced that in this modern age, with its forces of nationalism and freedom, its economic changes, its spread of education, and the political and social awakening which is going on, we must adjust ourselves to a much quicker tempo of constitutional development than would have seemed practicable a few years ago.

records.speaker: Mr. J. S. C. Reid
records.sentence: I go on to ask him just how this freedom of choice is to work?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker questions how "freedom of choice" will function—that is, how the capacity to choose among options will be operationally enabled or exercised.

records.speaker: Mr. Davies
records.sentence: But when I lose my own personal individual liberty, life is meaningless.
records.haiku_rationale: Personal individual liberty is being freed from interference or constraint; the speaker asserts that loss of freedom from such constraint renders life meaningless.

records.speaker: Viscount Hinchingbrooke
records.sentence: He is prepared to see the people of this country go through fire, provided that at the end they achieve some sort of economic freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Boyd-Carpenter
records.sentence: Paget) appears to believe, that it is in the interests of liberty to take legislative power away from the elected representatives of the people and hand that power over to the Executive, argues a paradoxically of mind.

records.speaker: Lord Willoughby de Eresby

records.speaker: Mr. J. S. C. Reid
records.sentence: I must say that I was a little nauseated by his remarks about liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Byers
records.sentence:
I quoted the words,
 In the name of defence of liberty our liberties may be destroyed.

records.speaker: Sir John Mellor
records.sentence:
The Parliamentary Secretary, on behalf of the then Minister, replied:
 Subject to their Statutory functions and duties the National Coal Board have the same liberty as any other employer to make such payments to their employees as they consider proper and in such manner as they see fit, and I regret that I have no information on the points raised by the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The National Coal Board is granted freedom to determine wage payments to employees without interference with their decisions—a freedom from constraint to act as an employer sees fit.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence:
Let those who tell me that this might bring the Government down remember this, my


last word on this issue—better that the Government should meet their doom than that individual freedom should perish in the British Isles.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual freedom (negative liberty understood as freedom from tyrannical or oppressive government control) is being asserted as a value that must be preserved even at the cost of governmental collapse.

records.speaker: Captain Crookshank
records.sentence: Speaker some liberty of action.

records.speaker: Mr. Peart
records.sentence:
I remember some past words of the present Colonial Secretary:
 You cannot talk about political freedom until you end economic servitude.

records.speaker: Mr. Churchill
records.sentence:
When there is an ancient community built up across the generations,
 Where Freedom broadens slowly down From precedent to precedent", 
it is not right that all should be liable to be swept away by the desperate measures of a small set of discredited men.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being invoked as the characteristic good of an ancient community that develops gradually through precedent and custom—a rhetorical appeal to liberty as opposed to its destruction by tyranny ("desperate measures of a small set of discredited men"). This is negative liberty: the freedom of a community from arbitrary interference with its inherited constitutional order.

records.speaker: The Secretary of State for Air
records.sentence: For the first time, a great nation like our own, not subjected to defeat or even to the threat of force, but because it believes it is doing the right thing, has freely and voluntarily come forward with legislation which has as its immediate object the granting, not of partial freedom or partial independence but complete freedom and complete independence.
records.haiku_rationale: A nation (unnamed, but contextually India) is being granted complete freedom and complete independence — empowerment to govern itself, not merely removal of external constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Fletcher
records.sentence: They cannot ask both for greater financial assistance from the Exchequer and also, at the same time, greater freedom from central control.
records.haiku_rationale: Entities are being freed from central control (a constraint on local autonomy). The "freedom from" language targets removal of interference with decision-making authority.

records.speaker: Sir W. Smithers
records.sentence: The Socialists boast of freedom, but today Britain is one great concentration camp.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" as a value opposed to totalitarian constraint ("concentration camp"), claiming that Socialist policies have removed liberty from British people—a rhetorical claim about freedom from state interference and oppression.

records.sentence: Gentleman has not really told us why—to give definitions in any order which can be debated by the representatives of the people concerned with their liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Bevin
records.sentence: The Arabs, having found their freedom, need it.
records.haiku_rationale: The Arabs are freed from colonial rule/external domination and need to exercise that independence/self-governance; this is positive liberty — empowerment to govern themselves.

records.speaker: Mr. Mallalieu
records.sentence: We believe that in that way it would be possible to secure freedom in the sense that we on this side of the House mean;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "freedom" in an abstract, evaluative sense without specifying what is being freed or from-to what. The phrase "in that way" and "in the sense that we...mean" signal a deliberative conception but do not clarify whether freedom here refers to capacity/empowerment (positive) or absence of interference (negative).

records.speaker: Dr. Stephen Taylor

records.speaker: Mr. H. Morrison

Industrial civil servants, numbering nearly 400,000, are already allowed a very considerable measure of freedom as regards political


and civic activities;

records.speaker: Mr. Lang
records.sentence: The thing to do is to come together on a fundamental belief in the liberty of the subject, in basic freedom and, as I think, in spiritual values.

records.sentence: The first dire mistake that was made—and it was made by those who really desire freedom—was when they departed from those principles which had been laid down in that Charter.

records.speaker: Sir H. Lucas-Tooth
records.sentence: No doubt, the underlying reasons for this judge-made rule have been that effective enforcement would be contrary to English ideas of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom here refers to freedom from interference with a legal principle; the substantive object is protection from enforcement that would violate what English tradition regards as non-interference rights.

records.speaker: Mr. Robens
records.sentence: This Clause ensures the utmost flexibility, and it gives the two parties complete freedom to get on with the job of deciding between themselves what they want for the industry.
records.haiku_rationale: The parties are being freed from constraints on their capacity to decide and negotiate matters internally affecting the industry—freedom to exercise choice and agency in collective decision-making.

records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "no new freedom" here functions as a rhetorical claim about unchanging universal principles (freedom and truth are not subject to innovation or modern invention), not a substantive argument about freedom from or capacity to do something specific. records.speaker: Sir J. Anderson

records.sentence: Gentlemen to realise what is the connection in the terms of the economics of aircraft operation, between the freedom from accidents and the deficit, the bill for which we are being asked to approve now.

records.sentence: It was undoubtedly a landmark in the annals of human freedom, but there was a paradox in that declaration.

records.sentence: When that point is reached, let us be strong in the fact that our Government in Malaya rests on social justice to the people and to their political freedom.

records.sentence: To give some help to the smaller establishments by this new freedom, will the right hon.

records.sentence: I am going to speak later particularly about the supply of meat, and I shall take the liberty of reminding the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "take the liberty of" as a parliamentary courtesy phrase meaning "allow myself to" or "permit myself to" — a conventional formulation with no substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Henry Usborne
records.sentence: if it is possible for the cultural freedoms and legitimate aspirations of the minorities to be adequately safeguarded—if these problems can be solved within this group of allied nations, then we will have discovered, at long last, the pattern of global peace.
records.haiku_rationale: The "cultural freedoms" of minorities are being safeguarded/protected from interference, and the "legitimate aspirations" are being enabled or accommodated within a framework; the sentence treats freedom as a precondition for peace but does not specify whether the emphasis is on removal of constraints or empowerment to pursue aspirations.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence:
By our policy in Asia and other

parts of the world we have given wide scope to those national aspirations, with the result that it is recognised by millions today that the extension of freedom is the policy of the democracies, and that Communist support of nationalist movements is only a part of a design to enslave the whole world and bring it under Communist dictatorship;
records.haiku_rationale: National aspirations are being freed (empowered to express themselves) through democratic policy that extends freedom to colonial/post-colonial territories, contrasted with Communist designs to enslave—this is positive liberty framed as enabling self-determination and self-governance capacity.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: In the Second World War he became Prime Minister again and led his country into the fight for democracy and freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The country is being freed from tyranny/oppression through participation in war for "democracy and freedom" — a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a value opposed to enemy tyranny and domination.

records.speaker: Mr. Sorensen
records.sentence: They, I am quite certain, are also in their own way making their own contribution to the freedom and the peace of the world.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence uses "freedom" as a general value or end-state ("freedom and peace of the world") without specifying what is being freed or freed from what, or what capacity is being enabled; it is a rhetorical invocation of freedom as a cause or aspiration rather than a substantive claim about either negative liberty (freedom from interference) or positive liberty (empowerment to act).

records.speaker: Mr. John McKay
records.sentence: Therefore, taking all these things into consideration, this is a wise thing to do at the moment, to keep our hands upon the country and not to give absolute freedom in a way which would lead to industrial disputes, perhaps unnecessarily, and other evils of which we well know.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker opposes giving "absolute freedom" to industry/workers because it would lead to industrial disputes and social harms; freedom here means freedom from government restraint or regulation to act as one wishes.

records.speaker: Mr. Paget
records.sentence: The test is who prefers the liberty and who prefers the votes.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contrasts two preferences—liberty versus votes—without specifying what liberty means or what is being freed from or to what. The reference is too abstract and contextually opaque to determine whether liberty here means freedom from interference or empowerment/capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. Boyd-Carpenter
records.sentence: I should like to say a word on the subject of liberty, on which so much has been said this afternoon, so much, indeed, that one might almost parody a famous remark and observe: "Liberty, liberty, what nonsense has been talked in thy name!
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is making a meta-rhetorical observation about how the concept of liberty has been invoked loosely in debate, parodying a famous phrase to critique the proliferation of rhetorical appeals to liberty without substantive grounding.

records.speaker: Mr. Paget
records.sentence: Friend the Member for Ardwick was in favour of the idea of providing this religious freedom by creating a new crime, guilt or innocence of which should be decided not by a jury or by a judge but by the public prosecutor.
records.haiku_rationale: Religious freedom is freedom from interference with religious belief and practice; the sentence is critiquing a proposal to restrict this through prosecutorial power.

records.speaker: Mr. Gibson
records.sentence:
I support the Bill on the general principle that there ought to be complete freedom to express one's thought, to preach one's philosophy and to try to persuade others to accept it in whatever way one feels that can best be done, so long as one does not take away from others the right also to express their point of view,


to organise themselves and to give their opinions in the quarter where they can be effective, which is mainly in this House.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to express thought, preach philosophy, and persuade others—freedom from interference with speech and expression. The speaker invokes this as a general principle opposing restrictions on the ability to voice opinions in Parliament and public discourse.

records.speaker: Mr. Deputy-Speaker
records.sentence:
The Minister is perfectly at liberty to answer any question

on this specific Order, but not on the point as to whether other Orders may or may not be laid before Christmas.
records.haiku_rationale: The Minister is permitted to exercise his parliamentary right to answer questions about a specific procedural matter; this is parliamentary procedure language about what the Minister is procedurally allowed to do, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Davies
records.sentence:
There is Cabinet responsibility, which is recognised, and there is a certain freedom of expression allowed in this country, and


nobody knows that better than the right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of expression is a freedom from interference with speech, a core negative liberty.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: The United Kingdom and the United States are found acting in concert, because they are both nurtured in freedom and democracy.
records.haiku_rationale: Both countries are described as "nurtured in freedom and democracy" — freedom here serves as a foundational value and characteristic that shapes their political culture and identity, not as a claim about freedom from interference or freedom to act specifically.

records.speaker: Mr. S. N. Evans
records.sentence: The great rallying cry of the French Revolution was, "Liberty, equality, fraternity.
records.haiku_rationale: Rhetorical invocation of "liberty" as a historical rallying cry of the French Revolution, presented as an ideal cause opposed to the ancien régime.

records.speaker: Mr. Webb
records.sentence: The House well knows that our desire is to give the consumer and the housewife the maximum freedom of choice, and we are determined, as rapidly as possible, to evolve a system which will do that and yet carry out the long-term obligations I have mentioned.
records.haiku_rationale: Consumers and housewives are being granted capacity to choose among options (maximum freedom of choice) — this is empowerment to act in the market, not mere freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. M. MacMillan
records.sentence: and gallant Member is not at liberty to misrepresent what I said.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker uses "at liberty" as parliamentary procedure language meaning the Member is not permitted or allowed to misrepresent the speaker's words; this is about parliamentary constraint, not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Gage
records.sentence: I am sure that on the whole that makes for greater liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "greater liberty" as a value being promoted, but the sentence does not specify what is being freed or from-or-to what; it lacks the concrete object and context needed to distinguish whether this refers to negative liberty (freedom from interference) or positive liberty (empowered capacity).

records.speaker: Sir William Darling
records.sentence: and anyone who interferes with the liberty of printing, interferes with human freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns freedom from interference with the act of printing—a classic negative liberty claim protecting non-interference with a fundamental mode of expression.

records.speaker: Mr. Thorneycroft
records.sentence: My answer to that is one which I can express on behalf of the free hauliers of this country—give them the freedom for which they ask in this Bill and they will look after the C licence holders.
records.haiku_rationale: Free hauliers are being freed from restrictions on their operating capacity, requesting the ability (freedom/power) to operate their haulage business without existing regulatory constraints (C licences), thereby enabling them to compete and provide services.

records.speaker: Dr. Summerskill
records.sentence: Gentleman to allow us certain freedom of action in the field of very difficult cases.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker requests freedom of action (discretionary capacity to decide) from a Gentleman, in the context of handling difficult cases—this is freedom TO act with flexibility, not freedom FROM interference with a pre-existing liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. J. N. Browne
records.sentence: There was then, as there will be today, a sincere and honest conflict between the belief in the value of corporate attendance and the importance of freedom of personal religion and choice.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with personal religious belief and choice; this is negative liberty protecting the individual conscience against external constraint or coercion.

records.speaker: Sir R. Acland
records.sentence: The Ecclesiastical Committee of this House referred back the Measure so that the bishops could be given rather greater liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The bishops are being given greater liberty (empowerment/freedom) to do something — they are being enabled or granted expanded capacity, not being freed from a specific interference or restraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Ede
records.sentence: We are now getting a very clear idea of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence makes no substantive claim about what freedom consists of or what is being freed from or to; it is a bare invocation of the concept without specifying the object, constraint, or capacity involved.

records.speaker: Mr. Brook
records.sentence: That policy has given the working man, for the first time, real freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Working man is freed to act or live with enhanced capacity/welfare (real freedom gained through policy enabling change in condition).

records.speaker: Mr. Jennings
records.sentence:
Major Milner, you ruled that an Amendment was not being accepted because it


was out of order, and I took the liberty of asking you whether you would allow a full and comprehensive discussion on this subject.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning "ventured to" or "presumed to"—not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Churchill
records.sentence: Do I understand that we are at liberty, Sir, to debate the Question which you put to us?
records.haiku_rationale: Parliamentary procedure: "at liberty to" is an idiom meaning "permitted/able to proceed", not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennox-Boyd
records.sentence: The Secretary of State has recently written a book which he has called "Restatement of Liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to a book title—"Restatement of Liberty"—as a proper noun/named work, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value or freedom from/to something.

records.speaker: Mr. Fraser
records.sentence: and so the farmer now has the freedom to apply for a certificate.
records.haiku_rationale: The farmer is freed (enabled) to apply for a certificate — acquiring new capacity/opportunity through regulatory permission.

records.speaker: Mr. Eden
records.sentence: But I say that in all parts of Germany west of the Iron Curtain it has a chance, at any rate, given a Parliamentary system, freedom and the life which we believe every nation should enjoy.
records.haiku_rationale: Nations west of the Iron Curtain are freed from totalitarian control to enjoy democratic self-governance and the conditions of free life (parliamentary system, freedom). This asserts empowerment toward self-governance and dignity.

records.speaker: Mr. Cahir Healy
records.sentence: Farmers should have more freedom to work out their own problems, and these problems are both agricultural and national.
records.haiku_rationale: Farmers are being freed to work out their own problems (capacity/empowerment to act autonomously), not from external interference with a pre-existing activity.

records.speaker: Mr. Bing
records.sentence: otherwise, there will be no freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of choice is freedom from interference with the ability to choose; it names non-interference with choice itself as the object of freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Dugdale
records.sentence: They were great men and they made a great experiment—to give the white South Africans freedom to rule over very large numbers of their black fellow-countrymen.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence describes granting white South Africans capacity/power to rule over Black populations—an empowerment or authorization to exercise dominion, which is positive liberty (freedom to act as governors).

records.speaker: Mr. Ivor Owen Thomas
records.sentence: Would the Minister explain whether under the proposed freedom to sell such houses any limitation is to be laid down as to their purchase by people other than those living in them?
records.haiku_rationale: The "freedom to sell houses" refers to the capacity or opportunity granted to householders to sell their properties—empowering them to take market action, which is a capacity TO act rather than freedom FROM interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Tom Brown
records.sentence: Oft-times in this House when we discuss humanitarian questions we take the liberty of quoting from the Old Book.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "take the liberty of" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning "permit ourselves to" or "make bold to," not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Eden
records.sentence: We think it right that the armistice should be agreed first and then there will be full freedom for any investigation.
records.haiku_rationale: Investigation (the object of freedom) is being freed from constraints/hindrance — there will be no obstruction to conducting it after the armistice is agreed.

records.speaker: Mr. E. Shinwell
records.sentence: While no one on this side of the House wishes to interfere with the freedom of the Press, can we be assured that there is no one on the other side of the House who wishes to interfere with the freedom of men and women to join a trade union and not be deprived of employment because they do so?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asserts freedom of the press (negative liberty — freedom from interference with the press) and freedom to join a trade union without losing employment (negative liberty — freedom from interference with this choice and its consequences).

records.speaker: Sir T. Moore
records.sentence: In any case, why should we force back men who fight for freedom into slavery, if not to death?
records.haiku_rationale: Men are being freed from slavery/death (forced repatriation) — this invokes freedom FROM oppressive constraint, a negative liberty concern about non-interference with those resisting totalitarian domination.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennox-Boyd
records.sentence: I hope that all who will still be condemned—as they, not unnaturally, regard it—to the limitation on their freedom of movement will realise that this is a first step in giving back freedom to road haulage, and that it must be looked at in the light of the whole story.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to "limitation on their freedom of movement" (negative liberty: freedom from interference with movement) and contrasts it with "giving back freedom to road haulage" (negative liberty: freedom from state interference in commercial activity).

records.speaker: Mr. A. Fenner Brockway
records.sentence: It would not be too much to say that the Universal Declaration of Human Rights adopted by the United Nations is one of the great six human documents for liberty since the beginning of time.
records.haiku_rationale: A rhetorical invocation of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights as an historical document advancing liberty-as-a-cause against oppression; what is being freed is humanity broadly, from tyranny and denial of fundamental rights.

records.speaker: Rev. Llywelyn Williams
records.sentence: Member opposite using such words as "freedom" or "enterprise," I instinctively look for the vested interests which are camouflaged by such terms.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is critiquing the rhetorical use of the word "freedom" as a disguise for vested interests; no substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value is made—only skepticism about the term's deployment as propaganda.

records.speaker: Mr. McNeil
records.sentence: I do not know that I am at liberty to quote the name of the firm.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is parliamentary procedure language meaning "permitted" or "able"; it does not substantively invoke liberty as a political or moral value, but rather describes a practical entitlement to perform an action (quoting a firm name).

records.speaker: Mr. Joynson-Hicks
records.sentence: We had been discussing the possibility of obtaining greater freedom in the industry, and I was suggesting that it would be a good thing if we could get together to discuss whether, as a first step.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is operating with less constraint in industry; speakers seek freedom from regulatory or operational constraints to enable business action and cooperation.

records.speaker: Miss Burton
records.sentence: and if the latter, will he give the names of public houses where there is a greater freedom of choice than in the State public houses of Carlisle?
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of choice in selecting public houses is a capacity enabling consumers to patronize different establishments, exemplifying empowerment to decide among alternatives.

records.speaker: The Secretary of State for the Home Department
records.sentence: The discussion in Committee showed very clearly that in this matter, as always, whether discussing visiting Forces, cinemas or practically any subject to which we may turn, there is a conflict between freedom of expression and the danger that freedom will be abused—a conflict which it is not easy to resolve.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom of expression (negative liberty: freedom from interference with expression) and acknowledges tension with preventing abuse, but does not resolve whether the speaker favours enabling capacity or constraining interference—it simply names the conflict as difficult.

records.speaker: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Fuel and Power
records.sentence: They felt that the Ridley Committee and the attitude which we adopted towards the question of freedom of choice was not strong enough, and one of them wanted to reinforce it with sanctions and the other with compulsion.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of choice is being defended against proposals to reinforce it with sanctions and compulsion, framing liberty as freedom from constraint/interference in making decisions.

records.speaker: Mr. Cledwyn Hughes
records.sentence: If the Minister studies the records, he will find that Valley is an ideal airfield for this purpose for it has a remarkable history of freedom from fog.
records.haiku_rationale: The airfield is being characterized by its freedom from fog—a physical/meteorological absence, not a political or personal freedom from interference or coercion.

records.speaker: Mr. Vaughan-Morgan
records.sentence: Gentleman spoke so much about his new friend, Lord Horder, and the Fellowship for Freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: No substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value is being made; "Fellowship for Freedom" is a proper noun (organization name) mentioned incidentally in political gossip.

records.speaker: Mr. Fisher
records.sentence: If that were to happen, through the bonds, light as they are, which still bind the Empire together, we might find that this little island, which taught the world the art of freedom, might teach it too the art of economic unity and expansion.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "taught the world the art of freedom" uses "freedom" as a historical and moral ideal—Britain's exemplary legacy of liberty—without specifying either what is being freed or from what constraint or to what capacity. The sentence invokes freedom rhetorically as a value Britain embodies, not as a substantive claim about removal of interference or empowerment to act.

records.speaker: Mr. Boyd-Carpenter
records.sentence: We have gone out of our way to offer to discuss with them the way to use this new freedom which, as hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is about how to use a newly granted freedom—specifically the capacity or empowerment to do something with that freedom, rather than freedom from interference. The speaker is discussing a positive enablement or opportunity.

records.speaker: Mr. Fletcher
records.sentence: My question is: Now that the Treasury are giving the local authorities this measure of freedom but are still providing funds to the Public Works Loan Board for the benefit of local authorities who still want to adopt the old procedure, is it or is not intended that, as in the last five years, any local authority which gets loan sanction from the Treasury and the other Government Departments concerned can then automatically get the capital it wants from the Public Works Loan Board?
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being given "freedom" to raise capital through direct borrowing rather than via the Public Works Loan Board—an expanded capacity or empowerment to act autonomously in financial matters.

records.speaker: Viscount Hinchingbrooke
records.sentence:
First, Section 3 (2) of the 1947 Act imposed on the Commission the duty to allow any person desiring transport of


his goods the freedom to choose the service most suitable to his needs.
records.haiku_rationale: A person is freed to choose which transport service to use for their goods—an empowerment of capacity to select the option most suitable to their needs.

records.speaker: Mr. Morrison
records.sentence: The Minister makes a great song and dance about the alleged freedom of the railways—given under the revised Bill—in regard to the making of charges.
records.haiku_rationale: The railways' freedom to make charges (set their own pricing) without government interference represents the capacity and authority to act independently in a commercial domain—a positive liberty of empowerment.

records.speaker: Mr. Poole
records.sentence: Indeed, he never intended it, because Tory Party policy pamphlets for the 1950 and 1951 Elections both said that the present freedom of C licences would remain untouched.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with the issuance or operation of C licences; the Tory Party promised not to restrict or alter the existing non-interference in this licensing matter.

records.speaker: Mr. Macmillan
records.sentence: The principle of freedom and the principle of order have often come into conflict.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom as an abstract principle opposed to order in a general philosophical claim, without specifying what is being freed or from-or-to what.

records.speaker: Mr. Davies
records.sentence: While we welcome this freedom which is given to the railway companies, we would warn the Minister that it will be very difficult to operate and it is fraught with many administrative problems.
records.haiku_rationale: Railway companies are being granted freedom (empowerment/capacity) to operate under new terms, shifting from prior regulatory constraint to expanded operational discretion.

records.speaker: Mr. Edward Davies
records.sentence: As far as the new freedom for the railway companies is concerned, the fears of his hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The railway companies are being freed (empowered) to make decisions without previous restrictions or state control.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennox-Boyd
records.sentence:
We believe that the freedom that they are now to exercise will help them in

coming to worth-while agreements among each other and with their co-operators in the field of transport.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to exercise (capacity to negotiate and reach agreements in transport) is being freed — empowered to act, from constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Simon
records.sentence:
The feeling that has been marked throughout the debate is that what we value even more than the wealth and prosperity of this industry is our tradition of freedom and of civil


liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes a tradition of "freedom and of civil liberty" as a value held above material wealth, expressing opposition to interference with foundational personal and civic freedoms.

records.speaker: Mr. Crossman
records.sentence: In addition to the Legion there are no fewer than 3,500 policemen, and in my opinion there is virtually no genuine political liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Political liberty—the absence of interference with genuine democratic participation and expression—is being withheld by the pervasive police and military presence, framing it as freedom from oppressive state control.

records.speaker: Mr. Rodgers
records.sentence: It took centuries of hard struggle to arrive at such freedom of the Press as we now enjoy, and I myself believe that the freedom of the air is vital to the continuance of the freedom of the Press itself.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of the press and freedom of the air are both freedoms from interference with communication and broadcasting; they name spaces protected from state or private control and censorship.

records.speaker: Mr. Thomas
records.sentence: Where these students are entrusted with freedom it is not abused, but in the very exceptional case.
records.haiku_rationale: Students are entrusted with freedom (capacity to act without constraint), and the speaker is claiming this empowered freedom is not abused in normal cases.

records.speaker: The Attorney-General
records.sentence: I am not, of course at liberty to quote the speech made by a noble and learned Lord who sat on the Woolsack during the previous Government—[HON.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning "permitted" or "able" in the practical sense—the speaker cannot quote the speech due to parliamentary rules or conventions, not a statement about freedom as a political value.

records.speaker: Dr. Horace King
records.sentence: We are inclined to take British freedom too much for granted.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes British freedom as an abstract value that people fail to appreciate; it does not specify what is being freed or from what constraint or toward what capacity, making the substance of the freedom claim indeterminate.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennox-Boyd
records.sentence: We are dealing here with Amendments to a Lords Amendment which is itself designed to give greater freedom of choice to the Commission in selecting vehicles which they wish to retain.
records.haiku_rationale: The Commission is being freed to choose among vehicles; it concerns empowering the Commission with discretion/capacity to select, not removing interference from an existing freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Driberg
records.sentence:
and what representations have been made by Her Majesty's Government in respect of this

and other recent similar infringements of human and legal rights and religious freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Religious freedom is being infringed; the sentence protests against interference with freedom of religion, a paradigmatic negative liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. A. Fenner Brockway
records.sentence:
I take the view that issues of liberty are important, even if they affect only one individual, but in this instance it is an

illustration of a power which is applied in other cases as well, and therefore becomes of greater importance.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as an abstract value in matters of principle affecting individuals, but the sentence does not specify what freedom is being discussed (from interference or toward capacity), making the specific object of liberty unclear.

records.speaker: Mr. Rodgers
records.sentence: Gentleman knows very little than attempt to curb the freedom of the Press by the establishment of a statutory Press Council.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of the press from government interference (via statutory regulation); curbing freedom means removing this non-interference protection.

records.speaker: Dr. Hill
records.sentence: Freedom has brought them into the shops in good quantity, and I see no reason for thinking price control would make them cheaper than they are.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from price controls has enabled goods to be brought into shops in good quantity—freedom from restrictive intervention in the market, with the consequence being market availability.

records.speaker: Mr. Brockway
records.sentence: The peace treaties with Italy, with Hungary, with Roumania, with Bulgaria and with Finland all accept the Charter of the United Nations and the essential freedoms in this Declaration.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker identifies "essential freedoms" recognized in the UN Charter and Declaration of Human Rights, which characteristically protect freedom from interference with civil and political rights (speech, conscience, association, etc.).

records.speaker: Mr. Snow
records.sentence: He wrote to what he considered to be one of the biggest cycle agency factors in the country, and I take the liberty of quoting their name because they are a responsible company—Halfords—and asked what was the position about brake equipment.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a parliamentary procedure phrase—"I take the liberty of quoting their name"—meaning the speaker is exercising a conventional parliamentary permission to cite a company name, not making a claim about liberty as a value or freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. H. Macmillan
records.sentence: Some local authorities prefer to give their tenants freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: Tenants are being empowered/enabled to choose (among housing options or arrangements offered by local authorities), a capacity for decision-making.

records.speaker: The Minister of Housing and Local Government
records.sentence: Now that freedom to build under licence has been greatly extended and the price of pre-war houses is declining, we do not think that this control, which imposes a real hardship on many owner-occupiers, can any longer be justified.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom being freed is the capacity to build; it is positive liberty — the granting of permission/empowerment to undertake building activities (formerly restricted by license requirements, now extended). The sentence argues this enabling capacity should extend to relaxing controls on house sales that impose hardship.

records.speaker: Mr. Thorneycroft
records.sentence: This Question refers to the general review, but I have already said that the purpose of getting freedom to make moderate adjustments in tariffs is to free the way for the removal of the quota restrictions.
records.haiku_rationale: Getting freedom to make moderate adjustments in tariffs empowers economic policy-makers to have the capacity to adjust tariffs; this is freedom TO act (make adjustments), not freedom FROM interference.

records.speaker: Captain Duncan
records.sentence: In any form of scheme involving complete freedom, will my hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "complete freedom" in the context of a hypothetical scheme, but provides insufficient specification of what is being freed, from what, or to what—the clause ends without completing the thought.

records.speaker: Mrs. Hill
records.sentence: What the housewife appreciates today is the fact that freedom of choice has been given by the Government.
records.haiku_rationale: Housewives are given (enabled/empowered by Government) freedom to choose—an enabling capacity rather than freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Frank McLeavy
records.sentence: I speak as a Methodist, conscious of the fight which Nonconformists have had to establish their right to freedom of religious thought and worship in the days long ago.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: religious thought and worship; from what: interference/restriction by those in power who did not permit Nonconformists to exercise these rights. "Freedom of religious thought and worship" is freedom from interference with conscience and practice.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: We are spending millions of pounds, shown in the Estimates every year, to defend freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as a cause or ideal that is being defended through government expenditure, without specifying whether this refers to freedom from interference or capacity to act; it is a rhetorical appeal to liberty as a value without sufficient detail to determine Berlin's distinction.

records.speaker: Lieut.-Colonel Bromley-Davenport
records.sentence: Could we not allow our troops a little more freedom to fire off some more mortar bombs in the direction of this indiscriminate night firing, which has consistently been going on against our men?
records.haiku_rationale: Troops are being freed from operational constraints to engage in mortar fire—a capacity to act enabled by relaxing military rules of engagement.

records.speaker: Mr. Dryden Brook
records.sentence: That conception of freedom means the freedom of the strong to exploit the weak.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker identifies a negative conception of freedom—absence of restraint on the strong—but critically: what is being "freed" is the strong's capacity to exploit, which is portrayed as a vice or injustice, not a liberty to be celebrated.

records.speaker: Mr. Cyril Bence
records.sentence: The Liberty ship, as was rightly said by my hon.
records.haiku_rationale: This refers to the Liberty ship, a proper noun naming a class of merchant vessel from World War II, not a claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Harold Davies
records.sentence: the freedom of India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon;
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon; from-to what: independence from British colonial rule, empowerment to self-governance.

records.speaker: Captain Duncan
records.sentence: I agree that there is a case for exclusive rights in line slaughtering, but the whole idea of greater freedom of slaughtering in the future was that there should be greater facilities for all.
records.haiku_rationale: The freedom being discussed is freedom to slaughter (an economic/occupational activity), and the speaker frames it as enhanced capacity or facilities enabling all to slaughter—a positive liberty sense of expanded opportunity and empowerment.

records.speaker: Sir D. Maxwell Fyfe
records.sentence: I intended to say "life or liberty," I beg the right hark.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "life or liberty" as a classical rhetorical pair representing fundamental values opposed to state interference or deprivation; the object of freedom is life and liberty itself, from threats/violation by the state.

records.speaker: Mr. Crouch
records.sentence: Millions of men and women are unaware of the freedom which we enjoyed 15 or 20 years ago.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker contrasts past freedom (negative liberty from interference or constraint) with present unawareness, implying that men and women have lost freedoms they previously enjoyed—a loss of freedom from some form of control or restriction.

records.speaker: Dr. H. Morgan
records.sentence: about four, five or six are involved in relation to personal liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking "personal liberty" as a value in relation to a count of cases, without specifying what is being freed or from/to what—the referent is unclear from this fragment.

records.speaker: Mr. C. R. Hobson
records.sentence: There is nothing to prevent that little country from being given its freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: A country is being empowered to self-govern; "given its freedom" means granted the capacity to govern itself independently.

records.speaker: Mr. Raymond Gower
records.sentence: It has an almost unequalled record of freedom from strikes and trade disputes, and for providing a very quick turn-round for ships.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to freedom from strikes and trade disputes—freedom from interference with normal operations, a classic negative liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Thomas Williams
records.sentence: As one writer put it, it is the fruit of a blind plunge into freedom which allowed no breathing space for proper adjustment of production and marketing policy to the new conditions.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker characterizes "freedom" as an uncontrolled capacity that permitted actors to plunge forward without restraint or adjustment to economic conditions; freedom is presented as the enabling of unregulated action (a positive capacity) that lacked proper constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Nicholls
records.sentence: I want now to refer to the general position of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is a bare invocation of "freedom" without specifying what is being freed, from what constraint, or to what capacity, making it impossible to distinguish between freedom from interference and freedom to act on the basis of this excerpt alone.

records.speaker: Mr. Fienburgh
records.sentence: Many controls are not restrictive but, rather, are productive of even greater freedom for other people.
records.haiku_rationale: Controls are being freed from a claim of pure restriction; they are productive of (enable) greater freedom for others — a claim that intervention creates positive liberty for beneficiaries.

records.speaker: Mr. H. Hynd
records.sentence: asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs when it is proposed that this country will declare its acceptance of the clause about right of individual petition in the Council of Europe's Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed is the individual's right to petition; what is being freed to is recourse to the Council of Europe's human rights mechanism. This concerns empowering individuals with a procedural capacity to seek redress through an international body.

records.speaker: Mr. John Edwards
records.sentence: Nehru and all his planning people are doing their best, as I understand it, to step up the pace of their development, but without having to forgo the kind of freedoms which the Indian Government think essential.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is praising India's ability to pursue development while maintaining "the kind of freedoms" (civil and political liberties) that the Indian Government regards as essential, i.e., freedom from interference with those liberties despite economic development pressures.

records.speaker: Mr. MacPherson
records.sentence: We are in the very serious dilemma of, on the one hand trying to prohibit what most people would agree to be an evil, and, on the other, trying to avoid those restrictions upon ordinary freedom as to matters of the mind, self-expression, and so on, which can be so easily imposed by this kind of legislation.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes freedom from restrictions on matters of the mind and self-expression—classic negative liberty concerns—in tension with legitimate prohibition of acknowledged evils.

records.speaker: Mr. Thomas Fraser
records.sentence: Brown, was having her freedom to buy her television set on hire-purchase terms restricted because the Treasury were compelling local authorities to have water supplies on hire purchase.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence focuses on restricting someone's capacity to purchase a television set via hire-purchase terms—an economic choice or transaction opportunity—which is being removed by government policy.

records.speaker: Mr. Jay
records.sentence: Is it part of the functions of the Chancellor of the Duchy to consult the Chancellor of the Exchequer before putting up expensive and misleading posters in the country about prosperity and Conservative freedom and so forth?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "Conservative freedom" is deployed rhetorically as a partisan political slogan without specifying what is being freed or from/to what; the sentence does not make a substantive claim about liberty as a value but rather invokes it mockingly within a question about administrative procedure and government spending.

records.speaker: Mr. Gerald Nabarro
records.sentence: Friend the Chancellor believes, as I believe, that Conservative freedom works.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "Conservative freedom" as a rhetorical ideal contrasted with other political systems, but does not specify what is being freed (from or to what), making it a bare invocation of freedom as a cause without substantive content about the object or direction of liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Davies
records.sentence: Initiative is smothered under this party of a property-owning democracy which was going to give a fillip to initiative and freedom for the small man.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom for the small man (i.e., ordinary person) is being freed from the smothering restraint imposed by the property-owning democracy system—this is freedom from governmental or institutional interference constraining economic or entrepreneurial activity.

records.speaker: Vice-Admiral John Hughes Hallett
records.sentence: Of course, if wages and all other forms of income could be fixed by law and, as a corollary, labour were controlled as well, there is not the slightest doubt that one could achieve full employment and have stable prices at the same time, and pay one's way, but the price would be a wholly unacceptable surrender of individual liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual liberty is being sacrificed (surrendered) to state control over wages, income, and labour—the freedom from economic coercion and state direction of work and livelihood.

records.speaker: Mr. Speaker
records.sentence: Lady finds any material in it for further interrogation, she is quite at liberty to put down further Questions.
records.haiku_rationale: A Member "at liberty to put down Questions" describes a procedural permission to take an action within parliamentary rules; this is parliamentary protocol language, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: The Financial Secretary to the Treasury
records.sentence: For some years past, local authorities have had freedom to borrow where they wish, and as to about 30 per cent.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being empowered with the capacity to borrow from any source they choose, rather than being freed from interference with an existing activity.

records.speaker: Mr. Willey
records.sentence: Griffiths) says something about Tory freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contains a bare, unspecified reference to "Tory freedom" without indicating what is being freed from or to, or what object of freedom is at stake.

records.speaker: Mr. F. Maclean
records.sentence: As to the second part, any soldier is at liberty to seek private medical treatment at his own expense in off-duty hours.
records.haiku_rationale: A soldier is permitted to seek private medical treatment (object of freedom: accessing medical services), freed from prohibition/restriction during off-duty hours.

records.speaker: Mr. McInnes
records.sentence: Ross) said, we hear much about Tory freedom and how it functions.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "Tory freedom" as a political catchphrase being discussed, apparently to criticise how it "functions" in practice—a rhetorical opposition to actual freedom from interference or tyranny, without specifying what concrete freedom (from what or to what) is at issue.

records.speaker: Mr. Dugdale
records.sentence: That is what the Government want to do, and it is in order that they may do that that we are having to keep Cyprus without any date set for her freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Cyprus is being freed from (or toward) independence/self-determination; the speaker argues the Government withholds a date for Cyprus's freedom in order to achieve their own political objectives.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennox-Boyd
records.sentence: —abuse of the freedom of which my right hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" in the context of identifying an "abuse" of it—a rhetorical opposition to the proper exercise of freedom, likely freedom from unjust interference. The reference is to a right hon. colleague's freedom being misused or exploited.

records.speaker: Mr. Airey Neave
records.sentence: It says, in paragraph 6, that it is to a certain extent lacking in freedom of manoeuvre, compared with industry, in the matter of salaries.
records.haiku_rationale: Public sector salaries are restricted compared to industry; the sentence identifies freedom of action in setting salaries as lacking, i.e., constrained by rules or external limits.

records.speaker: Mr. D. Jones
records.sentence: If the Government's new policy in relation to subsidies is to be effective, it demands for local authorities the greatest measure of freedom in their financial arrangements.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being freed/empowered to manage their financial arrangements (to make independent financial decisions) rather than freed from interference—the emphasis is on capacity and discretion to act.

records.speaker: Mr. Fisher
records.sentence: This, of course, depends upon what you mean by Press freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "Press freedom" as a concept requiring definitional clarification, but does not itself specify what is being freed from or what enables the freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Godfrey Nicholson
records.sentence: It is also very moving to find that, although complete freedom has been attained, there is no thought of breaking the link with this country.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker refers to "complete freedom" as a state that has been "attained," suggesting the empowerment of a nation (likely the context is decolonization) to govern itself independently, which is a capacity to act rather than absence of constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. E. G. Willis
records.sentence: He is not the millionaire that the Press represents him to be in view of the fact that he has to give up his liberty and sign away his freedom for six years to earn it.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker refers to giving up one's liberty and signing away one's freedom (from not being bound by contract) as a constraint—freedom from contractual obligation is being removed or surrendered as the cost of earning money.

records.speaker: Mr. Shepherd
records.sentence: Therefore, I say that while our objective ought to be a free economy in which we have the widest possible measure of freedom for our citizens—I believe that by people pursuing their business relatively unhampered they will achieve the best for society as a whole—I would not say that one must rush and try to gather all the freedoms at once.
records.haiku_rationale: Citizens are freed from interference with their business pursuits (unhampered economic activity), which are presumed to benefit society—this is freedom from constraint on economic action.

records.speaker: Mr. Creech Jones
records.sentence: If, therefore, the Bill succeeds in giving the Secretary of State greater freedom of choice in appointments, so that men with wide public service and experience may be considered for some of the appointments, the Bill is all to the good.
records.haiku_rationale: The Secretary of State is being freed (empowered) to make appointments with greater discretion in selecting men with broad public service experience—this is about enabling a capacity to choose, not removing interference.

records.speaker: Mr. H. Brooke
records.sentence: They have at all times wished for their freedom to do so;
records.haiku_rationale: The Speaker (acting subject) is freed to do something unspecified—the antecedent action is contextually bound. This is a capacity or opportunity being asserted, not freedom from interference with a named activity. The "freedom to do so" suggests empowerment or permission.

records.speaker: Mr. Gordon Walker
records.sentence: If the Amendment is rejected, that chance will be destroyed, and we shall retain our feeling that this is wrong and our liberty to put it right when the chance comes to us to do so.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker asserts liberty (capacity/opportunity) to put right what he views as wrong—a future power to act on grievance when circumstances permit.

records.speaker: Mr. Lloyd
records.sentence: There is another matter in the approach of many people to this problem which I think is disturbing, and that is the indifference they seem to show to the freedom of choice or opinion which is allowed to individual Greek Cypriots, in the pressure that can be applied by the refusal of the Church to baptise, marry or bury people who are opposed to Enosis.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: individual Greek Cypriots' choice/opinion. From what: pressure via church refusal of sacraments. This names freedom from interference with one's ability to hold and express an opinion without coercive religious sanction.

records.speaker: Mr. Dodds-Parker
records.sentence: We believe that it is with the Commonwealth and with the United States of America that freedom in the world, as we understand it, and economic progress must be based.
records.haiku_rationale: What is freed: "freedom in the world" (generalized). From/to: freedom is opposed to an unstated contrary condition and is framed as something that "must be based" on alliance with Commonwealth and US—an enabling or foundational condition for freedom rather than removal of interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Maitland
records.sentence:
It is one thing to say, "We want somehow to feel Greek and to have freedom of movement," but it is another thing to say, "We want to be terrorised and we want our young men and women


shot down in the streets or at the altar to attain that end.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of movement is a freedom from interference with one's capacity to travel or move about; the speaker frames this as desirable, contrasting it with wanting to be terrorised and have young people killed—making the object of negative liberty explicit (movement itself) and its context a negative liberty claim.

records.speaker: Mr. Gaitskell
records.sentence:
This is what she writes:
 …At a moment when our moral authority and leadership are most directly needed to meet this most brutal assault on freedom we find ourselves bereft of both by our own Government's action.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence opposes a "brutal assault on freedom" — i.e., freedom from forceful interference/oppression. The moral complaint is about defending freedom from violation, a classic negative liberty concern.

records.speaker: Mr. P. Williams
records.sentence: Will he not agree that whatever Resolutions and recommendations may have been passed by the United Nations, there is only one transgressor of international law, and that is the Government which has prevented the freedom of navigation of the Canal?
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of navigation is a negative liberty—it refers to freedom from interference with maritime passage through the Canal, specifically freedom from the blocking action by the Government.

records.speaker: Miss Jennie Lee
records.sentence: Is not the fear now abroad, hunger—and there is plenty of material not only of men and women driven by hardship—but of men and women everywhere hungering for liberty, and it is contagious?
records.haiku_rationale: People hungering for liberty (as opposed to hunger and hardship) — liberation from oppressive conditions and the desire for self-determination is being contrasted with material deprivation.

records.speaker: Mr. Lloyd
records.sentence:
The other factor which could not have been foreseen and which has had an impact on the debate has been that the development in the satellites took place


rather more quickly than had been expected or foreseen, that instead of there being a gradual process towards liberalisation, freedom and self-determination, as soon as there came signs of a change in the Soviet Union, the satellites began very quickly to desire to cast off the oppression which they had borne until then.
records.haiku_rationale: The satellites desire to cast off (freedom from) the oppression they had endured; the passage invokes a freedom/self-determination contrasted with Soviet oppression—negative liberty from foreign domination and constraint.

records.speaker: Sir Thomas Moore
records.sentence: I could give many other instances of their qualities—their admiration for Britain, which everyone finds on visits there, their admiration and imitation of our institutions and even our houses of Parliament, and their intense love of freedom which, as we have seen from the incidents of the last few weeks, still persists.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "love of freedom" as a positive attribute persisting in the referenced population, functioning as a rhetorical affirmation of a fundamental value opposed to oppression and tyranny, marking it as negative liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Kenneth Robinson
records.sentence: That seems to me to be a fantastic interference with the rights of free speech and freedom of expression.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes interference with free speech and freedom of expression, which are freedoms from constraints on speaking and expressing oneself.

records.speaker: Mr. Harold Wilson
records.sentence: to give us freedom from the crises that have still been dogging us nearly twelve years after the war and in the easiest world conditions we have known for a generation.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from crises and economic difficulties—negative liberty, freedom from hardship and instability that have persisted since the war.

records.speaker: Mr. Hare
records.sentence: As I said in my Answer, I think that the journalist in question thought that he was at liberty to use General Gale's name.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to use General Gale's name" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning the journalist believed he was permitted or authorized to do something, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Frank Beswick
records.sentence: A constant state of neurotic fear, of suspicion and hatred, is not freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being freed from a constant state of neurotic fear, suspicion, and hatred—an internal and psychological condition that obstructs one's liberty.

records.speaker: Wing Commander Bullus
records.sentence: I can trace no dispute which has arisen in the case of a county council or a rural district council because of the freedom of those authorities from the necessity of having a town's meeting or a town's poll.
records.haiku_rationale: County councils and rural district councils are freed from the requirement to hold town meetings or town polls—a removal of procedural constraint, enabling their autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. Philip Noel-Baker
records.sentence: Hungarian freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Hungarian people are being freed from Soviet domination and oppression—this is a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause opposed to foreign tyranny.

records.speaker: Mr. Stewart
records.sentence: I may say that when we hear of the block grant and the supposed greater freedom which it is to give to local authorities, it does not encourage us to believe that these variations in the opportunity of getting a grammar school education are likely to become less.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being given enhanced capacity (block grant) to govern themselves and allocate resources autonomously — this is empowerment to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Charles Doughty
records.sentence:
Therefore, in the interests of the publicity of justice—that everything


should be done in public and that the Press should, if necessary, be at liberty to report the happenings in their local courts—although I respect the hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "be at liberty to report" concerns freedom from interference with press reporting—a classic negative liberty protecting the Press from constraints on access and publication.

records.speaker: Mr. Fienburgh
records.sentence: It is only a question of a common collective endeavour for the common preservation of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (unspecified object) is being preserved collectively—the freedom in question is not clearly defined as freedom from specific interference or freedom to do something specific, making this a rhetorical invocation of liberty as an abstract cause requiring collective action.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: The temporary use of areas outside territorial waters for gunnery or bombing practice has, as such, never been considered a violation of the principle of freedom of navigation on the high seas and hence no special agreement is called for.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of navigation on the high seas is freedom from interference with ships' passage; the sentence asserts that gunnery practice in certain areas has never violated this negative liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. C. W. Armstroug
records.sentence: A further problem, which faces all Governments to some extent, but perhaps very particularly these emerging Governments, is the relationship between freedom and justice, freedom and security, freedom and progress.
