records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom as a high-level value in tension with justice, security, and progress, without specifying what is being freed or from what constraint—a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause of concern for governments.

records.speaker: The Attorney-General
records.sentence: He is, of course, at liberty to consult, as I understand he has done, any other counsel he wishes, but the only ground for my consulting other counsel would be lack of confidence in the experienced counsel who have appeared for me, and I certainly do not lack that confidence.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to consult" is a parliamentary procedural idiom meaning "entitled/permitted to" rather than a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value; it describes discretionary procedural authorization, not a principle of liberty from interference.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: These included the Eden plan for German reunification in freedom, which was first put forward on behalf of the Western Powers by Sir Anthony Eden at the Berlin Conference in 1954, and the outline Treaty of Assurance.
records.haiku_rationale: Germany is being freed to govern itself/reunify without external constraint (empowerment to self-determination), rather than freed from interference with an existing activity.

records.speaker: Mr. Hare
records.sentence: Our homes, our freedom, our industrial progress, our welfare, all these things depend on the soldier's readiness to come forward.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as a collective good dependent on military readiness, framed as something the nation collectively possesses and wishes to preserve against external threat—a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause opposed to tyranny.

records.speaker: Mr. Kershaw
records.sentence: I take the liberty of assuming that the House will agree with the first part of my Motion, that relating to the liberty of the Press.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "liberty of the Press" refers to freedom of the press from interference with publishing; "took the liberty of assuming" is parliamentary procedural language, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Fletcher
records.sentence: Justice Parker pointed out that the Parliamentary practice which enables us to have these debates on the Budget, which has enshrined the freedom of speech which ensures that a Finance Bill is not passed into law until we have had the opportunities that we cherish so much of criticising every sentence in it, is designed for the protection of the subject.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech is the specific object, understood as freedom FROM interference with parliamentary speech and debate on the Budget; it is a non-interference liberty enshrined in parliamentary practice to protect the subject.

records.speaker: Mr. Lipton
records.sentence: I am now at liberty to name him as Mr.
records.haiku_rationale: Parliamentary procedural use: the speaker is permitted (by debating rules) to name someone; "at liberty to" means "permitted to", not a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Emrys Hughes
records.sentence: If we are in favour of freedom, then they are all entitled to bolt.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with the ability to leave or depart; the sentence invokes liberty as a principle opposed to constraint on movement.

records.speaker: Mr. Butler
records.sentence: and learned Member wishes to put any point before me, he is at liberty to do so at any time of the year, whether the House is sitting or not.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to do so" is parliamentary procedural language denoting permission or absence of restriction on putting a point before the speaker, not a claim about substantive liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mr. Patrick Maitland
records.sentence: The first is that there should be much greater freedom of movement between Greece and Cyprus.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of movement between Greece and Cyprus is freedom from interference with travel and migration—a classic negative liberty.

records.speaker: The Minister of Housing and Local Government and Minister for Welsh Affairs
records.sentence: Anyone is at liberty to reproduce and distribute them.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "at liberty to" is parliamentary procedure language indicating permission or procedural allowance to reproduce and distribute materials, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: We believe in freedom, and we have done a great deal to restore it, but freedom does not mean licence, and rights involve responsibilities.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being affirmed as a value opposed to constraint (licence/unrestricted action) and paired with responsibility, invoking liberty as a cause against tyranny and disorder—a classic rhetorical invocation of negative liberty (freedom from interference and arbitrary rule).

records.speaker: Mr. Lindgren
records.sentence:
The


quarrel has always been on the question of cost, but now this Government claim to act on the basis of freedom for local authorities
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being empowered/granted capacity to act autonomously in making decisions (on cost/spending), not being freed from interference with an existing activity.

records.speaker: Mr. Blackburn
records.sentence: " ft would have been far more honest to do that instead of to pretend that the aim is to give more freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes a pretense that the aim is to give more freedom; the object of freedom is unspecified, and the sentence is evaluating a rhetorical claim rather than articulating a substantive freedom-claim itself.

records.speaker: Mr. Blackburn
records.sentence: It has been going on all this century, but in the past the block grant has been advocated as an economy measure and there has been no pretence of trying to hide it as giving greater freedom to the local authorities.
records.haiku_rationale: Greater freedom is being given to local authorities - they are empowered/enabled to govern and raise funding with less central constraint, representing capacity to act autonomously.

records.speaker: Mr. Michael Stewart
records.sentence: I believe that on this new towns question, the Government have thrown away an opportunity of giving local authorities a real increase in democratic freedom and not an illusory one.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being denied an increase in their capacity to govern themselves democratically—the freedom to make decisions and exercise self-governance.

records.speaker: Mr. Barter
records.sentence: I think it would be fair to say that the sort of freedom desired would be in the acceptance of certain tenders.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom desired through acceptance of tenders—empowerment to proceed with business transactions; capacity granted to act (accept/perform contracts).

records.speaker: Sir F. Soskice
records.sentence: After listening to the speech with which this debate opened, I think that I am right in saying that the Government have, in effect, adopted a kind of half-way house between the proposals contained in the Franks Report and the proposals contained in "Personal Freedom".
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker references a document titled "Personal Freedom" as a policy proposal in a debate. The sentence itself does not argue for or against any substantive conception of freedom; it merely cites a named document in a legislative/policy context.

records.speaker: Mr. Ellis Smith
records.sentence: There was to be freedom for all to take part in the scramble which has gone on, but at last steps are to be taken to deal with inflation.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom being referred to is the capacity/opportunity for all to participate in economic competition and the scramble for resources, which is enabled by removing obstacles (addressing inflation). This is positive liberty: empowerment to act and compete.

records.speaker: Mr. Crossman
records.sentence: We have made it perfectly clear that there shall be a genuine freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker promises "genuine freedom of choice" — the capacity/empowerment of people to choose, which is a positive liberty claim about enabling choice.

records.speaker: Mr. Willis
records.sentence: Members on the other side had a great deal to say about giving the local authorities greater freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities being given greater freedom (scope/capacity to act), freed to exercise discretion and self-governance in their domain.

records.speaker: Mr. Blackburn
records.sentence:
As has been said, Article 9 of the Bill of Rights of 1689 stated:
 The freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any Court or Place out of Parliament.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech and debates in Parliament from impediment or questioning by courts and places outside Parliament—negative liberty protecting non-interference with parliamentary expression.

records.speaker: Mr. Michael Stewart
records.sentence: Jekyll argument of increased freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence makes a passing reference to "increased freedom" as a debating point but does not specify what is being freed, from what constraint, or through what mechanism. The phrase is too bare and context-dependent to determine whether this concerns negative liberty (freedom from interference) or positive liberty (empowerment to act).

records.speaker: Mr. William Hamilton
records.sentence: Friend the Member for Glasgow, Central asked why we should not extend that freedom to the other services;
records.haiku_rationale: The "freedom" being referenced concerns extending non-interference or capacity to "other services," but the sentence is incomplete and does not specify what is being freed (from interference or to act). The referent and the direction of freedom (from or to what) are unclear without fuller context.

records.speaker: The Minister of Transport and Civil Aviation
records.sentence: I thought that on this occasion the House should know that we are doing our best to secure the maximum freedom not only for airlines and air corporations operating from this country, but for all airlines, to traverse the sky as freely and with as much service to the travelling public of the world as can possibly be arranged.
records.haiku_rationale: Airlines and air corporations are being empowered to traverse the sky and provide service to the travelling public — a capacity to act and compete, not merely freedom from restriction.

records.speaker: Mr. Prentice
records.sentence: asked the Minister of Transport and Civil Aviation whether his attention has been drawn to the Cornell-Liberty Safety Car which has been built in the United States of America and which incorporates many new features designed to minimise injuries in the event of accidents;
records.haiku_rationale: Cornell-Liberty is a proper noun (car model name); "liberty" appears incidentally as a product brand and does not make a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value or freedom from/to something.

records.speaker: Mr. Black
records.sentence: Members from the Sunday Freedom Association.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a proper noun reference to an organization name ("Sunday Freedom Association"), not a substantive claim about liberty as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Douglas Jay
records.sentence: If we are to make a success of these industries in the future, we shall have to give them more freedom in their price policies and continue to enable them to borrow for their essential development programmes at reasonable rates of interest.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from constraints on price-setting and borrowing are being granted to industries to enable their development—this is empowerment to act and pursue economic goals, not mere freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Rupert Speir
records.sentence: No one has suggested that the Bill goes too far, and I think that this lack of criticism is rather surprising, because when one is taking steps to put restraints and restrictions on the liberty of the subject one would expect some form of abuse at least from members of the lunatic fringe.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker identifies "restraints and restrictions on the liberty of the subject" as what is being constrained—the freedom from state interference with the individual's conduct and choices. The "lack of criticism" being surprising suggests that when government imposes such restraints, opposition defending liberty from interference is normally expected.

records.speaker: Mr. Mitchison
records.sentence: We hear a great deal about Tory freedom, and about the Government's idea of giving more liberty to local authorities, but those ideas seem to disappear when there is a conflict of interests between private transport undertakings and those of local authorities.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes the Government's stated commitment to giving local authorities "more liberty" (empowerment to govern/act independently), which he alleges is abandoned when private interests conflict with local authority interests.

records.speaker: Mr. G. R. Mitchison
records.sentence: As for Tory freedom, what is the freedom of saying to people, "You can spend money as you like;
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is questioning what "freedom" means when Conservatives simply allow people to spend money as they choose—identifying an enabling capacity (the ability to allocate one's own resources) rather than freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Michael Stewart
records.sentence: As to the other aspects of freedom, that is to say the actual resources to do it, the capacity to do it, this Bill gives them nothing in that direction.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes the bill for failing to provide actual resources and capacity—the positive means—to exercise freedom; what is being freed is people's practical ability to act.

records.speaker: Mr. Lawson
records.sentence: The point now emerges in the words of the gentlemen opposite themselves—this particular Clause is a violation of what they consider to be freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: unspecified (the gentlemen's abstract "freedom"). From-or-to what: from interference by a Clause being voted on. The sentence mentions violation of freedom without specifying the concrete content or domain of that freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Ross
records.sentence: They show that in Lanarkshire, where the Tory hopes were very high, the Government's policy of freedom for Scottish local authorities is scorned by the people.
records.haiku_rationale: Scottish local authorities are freed/empowered to govern themselves and make decisions (capacity to act), not merely freed from interference; this is empowerment to self-govern.

records.speaker: Mr. Willis
records.sentence: One of the carrots dangled before us is that of greater freedom for local authorities, but we have not yet been told what it is.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being offered expanded capacity to govern and act independently (positive liberty empowerment), but the speaker emphasizes that the specific content of this freedom remains undefined.

records.speaker: Mr. Collins
records.sentence: I think that the greater the freedom of trade we have, the better it will be for this country, with the proviso—other things being equal.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of trade (absence of interference/restriction on commercial activity) is what is being freed; it is freedom FROM governmental or external impediment to trading activity.

records.speaker: Mr. Lennox-Boyd
records.sentence: Drawing from this encouragement, if encouragement it can be called, many people are now saying of the League of Colonial Freedom and of similar bodies that there should now be a general inquiry into all Kenya prisons.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "League of Colonial Freedom" as a body expressing political demands, but the operative claim is about a procedural matter—a general inquiry into Kenya prisons—not about freedom as a value or principle. "Freedom" here is part of a proper noun/organization name, not the subject of liberty claims.

records.speaker: Mr. Ridsdale
records.sentence: In view of the fact that we are now ending coal rationing, could it not be possible to allow people freedom to trade both in exports and imports?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is advocating for freedom to trade in exports and imports—enabling people's capacity to engage in trade transactions without state-imposed restrictions.

records.speaker: Mr. Watkinson
records.sentence: It is a difficult problem, because the traditional policy of our shipping is that of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Shipping policy is being freed from government control or restriction—this is freedom in the sense of absence of interference with commercial navigation and maritime trade.

records.speaker: Mr. Page
records.sentence: I wish to give freedom to the employer and employee to make a reasonable arrangement of this sort if they both wish to do so.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to make a contractual arrangement: the speaker is advocating capacity/empowerment for employers and employees to negotiate their own terms, a positive liberty to act rather than freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Clement Davies
records.sentence:
It is well to look back at the position in this House in 1688 when those words were written:
 Freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament, ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech and debates in Parliament is freedom from impeachment or questioning—a protection against interference with parliamentary speech and proceedings.

records.speaker: Miss Joan Vickers
records.sentence: It is worth recalling that of all the territories which have recently been given their freedom, whether they became Dominions or Republics, not one, with the exception of one small State in India, has turned to Communism.
records.haiku_rationale: Territories are freed from imperial control or constraint—given the capacity to govern themselves as independent Dominions or Republics, making them capable of self-determination rather than being subject to external rule.

records.speaker: Sir R. Boothby
records.sentence: All they said, at the end of the communiqué, was that we were struggling for freedom and liberty and the ultimate hopes of mankind;
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom and liberty are invoked rhetorically as abstract causes mankind is struggling for, opposed to oppression/tyranny, without specific content—this is a rhetorical appeal to negative liberty (freedom from oppression) rather than a claim about enabling capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. Wedgwood Bean
records.sentence: They love this country and this House because what we have here represents for them the freedom which they want for their own people.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence describes freedom as a value/condition that people desire for their own people, without specifying whether it is freedom from interference or freedom to act; "freedom which they want" is too generic to disambiguate between negative and positive liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Collins
records.sentence: Will the new regulations avoid a scandal of this kind and provide reasonable freedom for men to write without interference to their Members of Parliament?
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom for men to write without interference to their Members of Parliament is freedom from obstruction of the communicative act, not an empowerment capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. T. Fraser
records.sentence: It has nothing to do with giving the local authorities more freedom, or reducing the amount of paper work between local authorities and the central Government.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities being freed (empowered) to have greater capacity to act independently, without the constraining burden of paperwork and central Government oversight — positive liberty as enabling autonomy and agency.

records.speaker: Mr. James McInnes
records.sentence: There is no freedom in respect of the councillors or the functioning of committees, but purely in administrative work by officials of local government, and a negligible amount of freedom it is.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker claims that "freedom" exists only in the administrative work of local government officials, not in the functioning of councillors or committees—describing a narrow scope of discretion or autonomy (positive liberty) granted to officials in their administrative operations, while emphasizing this freedom is minimal.

records.speaker: Mr. Harold Wilson
records.sentence: In this document "Onwards In Freedom", the Prime Minister repeats his great thought.
records.haiku_rationale: This sentence is a procedural reference to a document title containing the word "freedom" but does not make any substantive claim about liberty as a value or concept; it is merely citing a proper noun/document name.

records.speaker: Mr. Marquand
records.sentence: The whole profession of zeal for freedom is absurd while this is denied.
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: the ability to exercise something substantive (the subject of denial is unspecified in the excerpt, but the speaker criticizes hypocrisy in claiming freedom while denying it to others); from-or-to what: freedom from being denied something, or more fundamentally, freedom from hypocrisy in professing freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Pannell
records.sentence: Nobody would doubt that as we go on we not only want an increasing standard of life but a greater degree of personal freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Personal freedom is being valued as something desired for its own sake, alongside material well-being, without specifying what one is being freed from or to do—making this an abstract invocation of liberty as a general good rather than a concrete claim about non-interference or empowerment.

records.speaker: Mr. Christopher Boyd
records.sentence: Bidgood), and indeed, nearly every other speaker in this debate, has laid great emphasis on the issue of freedom involved in this Bill, to which we are asked to give a Second Reading tonight.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as a general issue at stake in a Bill without specifying what freedom from or to, or what is being freed—it is a bare reference to liberty as a parliamentary value without sufficient context to determine whether it concerns non-interference or empowerment.

records.speaker: Mr. Gordon Walker
records.sentence: Although we must dismiss the attempt to pass the Bill off as a great charter of liberty, it is, none the less, for doctrinaire party reasons, a Measure that will do a great deal of damage to the interests of the nation.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "liberty" rhetorically as a cause/value opposed to what he sees as partisan damage to national interest; the reference to "a great charter of liberty" is a rhetorical dismissal rather than a specific claim about what freedom is being constrained or enabled.

records.speaker: Mr. Mitchison
records.sentence: The farmer is at liberty to turn out practically all the equipment of his modernised farm, so far as it consists of vehicles, and take voters to the poll.
records.haiku_rationale: A farmer is permitted (free from legal prohibition) to use his farm vehicles for the purpose of transporting voters to the polls.

records.speaker: Mr. Bishop
records.sentence: I urge the House to accept that here it is a necessary principle that the public interest must override the feelings of pain and distress that may sometimes be caused to individuals, although the House should do all it can to discourage those newspapers, magazines and other publications that use their present freedom in a way that is unnecessarily distressing to private people.
records.haiku_rationale: The newspapers' "freedom" being discussed is freedom of the press from interference—they have the capacity to use their present liberty but are doing so in ways that cause distress; the speaker urges discouraging such use of this freedom from restraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Norman Dodds
records.sentence: Many have been led to believe that the Bill will contain stronger and better methods of safeguarding the liberty of the individual.
records.haiku_rationale: The individual is being freed (protected) from interference or violation of their rights through stronger safeguarding methods in the Bill—this is negative liberty, the absence of interference with personal liberty.

records.speaker: The Chancellor of the Exchequer
records.sentence: They also played what I acknowledge as a very effective part in the move to bring about in Europe greater freedom of trade.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of trade — removal of barriers and interference with commercial exchange and contract — is freedom from protectionist or regulatory restriction.

records.speaker: Mr. Wilson
records.sentence: For one thing, it is not of the same parity, but what we say is that the Chancellor's freedom to take the necessary measures to expand economy will be limited.
records.haiku_rationale: The Chancellor's capacity to take economic measures to expand the economy is being constrained; freedom refers to empowerment to act (expand economy), not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Viscount Hinchingbrooke
records.sentence: I suggest that is a possible means which might be explored of gaining a certain freedom of manoeuvre for the £ without violently impinging upon our international obligatons.
records.haiku_rationale: The £ (British pound) is being freed from constraint, and the specific object is operational capacity or flexibility ("manoeuvre") — the ability to act in monetary policy without external impediment. This is positive liberty: empowerment or expanded capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. Mitchison
records.sentence: Lindgren) says, what about Tory freedom?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is a rhetorical question that lacks substantive specification of what "Tory freedom" means or what is being freed from or to; it appears to be a bare invocation of freedom as a political term without enough context to identify the specific object or direction of liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Blyton
records.sentence: The Coal Board is not free to fix its prices in the way in which the oil companies are, but it must have that freedom to fix prices if it is to compete on an equal footing.
records.haiku_rationale: The Coal Board is being freed to fix prices (capacity/empowerment to set prices), which would enable it to compete equally with oil companies.

records.speaker: Major Legge-Bourke
records.sentence: I have always felt that the four freedoms of the Atlantic Charter left out one important one, and that was freedom of choice to do the right thing.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker proposes a fifth freedom beyond the Atlantic Charter's four: "freedom of choice to do the right thing"—this is an empowering capacity to make moral choices and act on them, not freedom from interference with an existing practice.

records.speaker: The Prime Minister
records.sentence: By removing a source of bitterness and division it will enable us and our Allies and the people of Cyprus to concentrate on working together for peace and freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as part of a hoped-for outcome ("for peace and freedom") that will result from removing division and enable cooperation—a rhetorical appeal to liberty as a shared cause and value to be collectively pursued, characteristic of negative liberty framing in the context of national/political aspiration.

records.speaker: Dr. King
records.sentence: Today, tens of thousands of people are denied some of that freedom as a condition of their employment, some B.
records.haiku_rationale: People are being denied freedom (unspecified, but contextually likely freedom of association/speech/conscience) as a workplace condition—a case of constraint and non-interference being withheld from them.

records.speaker: Sir R. Robinson
records.sentence: Of course, there have been crimes and crimes have been committed in the name of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Crimes committed "in the name of freedom" refers to acts carried out under the rhetorical banner of freedom as a value against tyranny or oppression, an invocation of liberty as a cause opposed to constraints.

records.speaker: Mr. Brockway
records.sentence: We have the right to ask whether the prisoners will be allowed freedom to collect evidence.
records.haiku_rationale: Prisoners are being freed to collect evidence — a capacity/empowerment to perform an action rather than freedom from interference with an abstract category.

records.speaker: Mr. Moyle
records.sentence: What is the use of talking to people about liberty when they want bread, sustenance and shelter?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence contrasts talking about liberty (negative liberty, freedom from interference) with meeting material needs (sustenance, shelter); it questions the value of abstract freedom when people lack basic welfare, implying that enablement to meet needs takes priority over non-interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Moyle
records.sentence: we cannot talk about the philosophy of democracy and liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a procedural remark about parliamentary discourse (inability to discuss philosophy), not a substantive claim about what liberty means or protects; no specific freedom from interference or empowerment capacity is identified.

records.speaker: Mr. Graham Page
records.sentence: that local authorities, unless they are given freedom of administrative action, will find themselves saddled with the problem families of the district.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are given freedom to act administratively (capacity/empowerment to manage problem families) rather than freed from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Paget
records.sentence: to say that to provide that power is an invasion of civil liberty considering what our law of the subject is, I submit is the highest hypocrisy.
records.haiku_rationale: Civil liberty is being freed from governmental power/interference; the speaker invokes it as a constraint on what government should do.

records.speaker: Mr. F. H. Hayman
records.sentence: I take the liberty of speaking because I was Chairman of the Committee on Opposed Bills which dealt with Leicester Corporation Act, 1956, Sections of which are amended or repealed by this Order.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of speaking" is a parliamentary procedural idiom indicating permission to speak, not a substantive claim about freedom as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Thompson
records.sentence: Questions of the liberty of the subject are involved.
records.haiku_rationale: The liberty of the subject refers to civil liberties and personal freedoms from interference with one's rights and person—a classical negative liberty formulation.

records.speaker: Mr. Philip Bell
records.sentence: He might well say that he intends to accept the child to the family and use that as an instrument to prevent the woman getting her freedom and taking her child to the paramour or the person she hoped to marry.
records.haiku_rationale: A woman's freedom from interference/constraint to leave the family and marry whom she chooses; the sentence describes using custody of a child as an instrument to prevent her exercising this freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Green
records.sentence: Do not let us do anything which in any way restricts freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence opposes restrictions on freedom of choice—an individual's freedom to make decisions without interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Reeves
records.sentence: This can come about only when the State confines itself and its activities to the provision of educational facilities for its people, leaving to the religious bodies and the non-religious bodies freedom to carry out their work in their own way and of making known their deeply held views on such subjects.
records.haiku_rationale: Religious and non-religious bodies are freed from state interference in carrying out their work and expressing their views—freedom to act without state constraints is negative liberty (absence of interference).

records.speaker: Dr. Mabon
records.sentence: The slogan attached to the Bill was "More Freedom for Local Authorities," but in this matter they have lost their freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being freed to (or empowered to) govern themselves and raise funding independently, but the sentence claims they have actually lost that capacity/empowerment under the Bill.

records.speaker: Mr. G. M. Thomson
records.sentence: The Government's case for making this very substantial change was that Scottish local authorities should have much more freedom than they have been given in the past to decide their own pattern of expenditure.
records.haiku_rationale: Scottish local authorities are being empowered to decide their own expenditure patterns—a capacity to act autonomously in budgeting and resource allocation.

records.speaker: Mr. G. M. Thomson
records.sentence: When the general grant was introduced, I believe that all of those authorities—the Minister can correct me if I am wrong—certainly many of them, stated that they would exercise the freedom which the Government had generously given to them.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are given (empowered with) freedom/discretion to exercise choice in how to use government funding—this is capacity to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Jones
records.sentence: Indeed, when last year I made a statement to the effect that normally—always admitting exceptional cases—the Government would expect a firm to develop aircraft out of its own resources, what lay at the back of that statement was a desire to allow customers full freedom of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker intends to allow customers full freedom to choose which aircraft to purchase or use, emphasizing their empowered capacity to select among options in the market.

records.speaker: Mr. Emrys Hughes
records.sentence: The Irish Rebellion resulted in freedom for the Irish Republic and I say that the Irish Republic for which Casement died has a right to these historic documents.
records.haiku_rationale: The Irish Republic is being freed to self-governance and national independence—positive liberty as empowerment of a body to govern itself, contrasted with colonial subjection.

records.speaker: Mr. Maclay
records.sentence:
I would hope that authorities would give


full weight to the importance of giving the greatest possible freedom of choice to their tenants as recommended in the Scottish Housing Handbook.
records.haiku_rationale: Tenants are freed to choose their housing/accommodation options; the speaker urges authorities to enable and empower this capacity to exercise choice.

records.speaker: Mr. Pannell
records.sentence: Lady was trading on chivalry to take that liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is using "took the liberty" as a colloquial expression meaning the lady presumed or was bold enough to do something (likely to make an assumption or take an action), not as a substantive claim about freedom-as-a-value or constraint on action.

records.speaker: Mr. Wood
records.sentence: There is the further important point that the denial of freedom of choice to consumers and the compulsion to use certain fuels rather than others is not only industrially undesirable, but it is also humanly immeasurable and indefinable.
records.haiku_rationale: Consumers are being freed from compulsion to use certain fuels—a denial of freedom of choice in fuel selection represents interference with consumer autonomy.

records.speaker: Mr. Iain Macleod
records.sentence: Member will give me any examples of how he considers the freedom of hon.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence is incomplete and cannot be analyzed for a clear conception of liberty; it cuts off mid-thought after "freedom of hon[orable members]" without specifying either the constraint or empowerment at issue.

records.speaker: The Solicitor-General
records.sentence: We all recognise that it is not enough for the preservation of freedom to have a virile Parliament continuing, as we hope, to recruit able and dedicated men.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "preservation of freedom" as a value that requires more than institutional continuity (a strong Parliament); the object of freedom remains unspecified, but the claim treats freedom as a state or condition to be preserved, not a capacity being enabled.

records.speaker: Mr. William Clark
records.sentence: What we have to do is to try to get true freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "true freedom" as an abstract goal without specifying what people are to be freed from or empowered to do; the sentence is too bare and general to determine whether the underlying concept is negative (freedom from interference) or positive (capacity to act).

records.speaker: Mr. Elwyn Jones
records.sentence:
He has said, in his classic study, "International Law and Human Rights":
 The General Assembly or any other competent organ of the United Nations are authorised to discuss a situation arising from any alleged non-observance by a state or a number of states of their obligation to respect human rights and freedoms.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns the empowerment of UN organs to discuss alleged violations of human rights and freedoms; it describes institutional capacity and authorization rather than freedom from interference with individual rights themselves.

records.speaker: Sir William Robson Brown
records.sentence: Members a freedom of action which they have never had before, and that would be well worth while.
records.haiku_rationale: Members are being given capacity (empowerment) to act—a freedom-to rather than freedom-from. The phrase grants Members the ability to take action they previously lacked.

records.speaker: Mr. Rankin
records.sentence: The primary thing is to look at this from the point of view of the liberty of the individual.
records.haiku_rationale: The individual is being freed from unspecified interference or constraint; this is a rhetorical invocation of personal liberty as a foundational value without specification of what particular freedom is at stake.

records.speaker: Mr. Butler
records.sentence: This is a free country and the more opportunities for freedom of speech, the better things will be.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech is freedom from interference with expression; the clause "opportunities for freedom of speech" reinforces removal of obstacles to speaking.

records.speaker: Mr. Marsh
records.sentence: Gentleman think that this is a desirable state of affairs, that the only way in which a prospective employee can obtain the freedom of choice which both sides want to ensure for employees should be by deliberately agreeing to something in the full knowledge that, the moment he gets the job on that basis, he will dishonour the agreement?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses freedom of choice for employees to select employment terms (enabled capacity to decide), contrasted with the concern that such freedom is undermined by making agreements that will be dishonoured—the substantive object is the capacity to choose one's employment conditions.

records.speaker: Mr. Callaghan
records.sentence: Gresham Cooke)—that it is quite absurd that they should be detained by any civilised State in respect of any crime concerned with freedom or liberty?
records.haiku_rationale: Detention is being lifted as a violation of persons' freedom from unlawful restraint; the speaker opposes state detention as incompatible with liberty.

records.speaker: Mr. Stewart
records.sentence: It is useless to think that we can preserve or pursue liberty by not making laws or regulations.
records.haiku_rationale: The capacity to pursue liberty (positive liberty as a goal) depends on the enabling structures of laws and regulations, not on the absence of legal constraints.

records.speaker: Mr. Brockway
records.sentence:
Will he take steps to see that it is administered in a

way which does not mean that there will be any restriction on liberty of writing?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker opposes restrictions on liberty of writing—a classic negative liberty claim about freedom from interference with the act of writing.

records.speaker: Mr. Graham Page
records.sentence: Committee's Report and the Drew Report they are at liberty to do so.
records.haiku_rationale: Parliamentary procedural phrasing: "at liberty to do so" is an incidental procedural phrase meaning "permitted" or "able", not a substantive claim about liberty as a value.

records.speaker: Mr. Butler
records.sentence: As Leader of the House, I had taken the liberty to acquaint myself of this problem.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is using "taken the liberty" as a parliamentary idiom meaning "permitted myself" or "allowed myself"—this is procedural language about speaking or acting in Parliament, not substantive discussion of liberty as a value to be protected.

records.speaker: Mr. Warbey
records.sentence: If he had listened, he would have realised that what I said was that in a number of countries of the so-called free world the suppression of political freedom was as great as it was in any of the Communist countries.
records.haiku_rationale: Political freedom (understood as freedom from suppression/interference with political participation) is being constrained equally in some Western and Communist countries.

records.speaker: Mr. Parkin
records.sentence: It is a pity, therefore, that the rather ambitious ideas of the Motion, which promises economic stability, political freedom and social security if only we examine this problem properly—and I do not dissent from these aspirations—have finally settled down into a discussion of how best to dispose of minor shares in industry.
records.haiku_rationale: The "political freedom" invoked here is a value-laden aspiration presented as a benefit that would result from examining the problem properly. The specific object of freedom is left unspecified—it is bare political freedom as a desired outcome without clear specification of freedom from what interference or freedom to do what capability. The sentence positions this among "economic stability" and "social security," but does not elaborate what constrains or enables this freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Barnett Janner
records.sentence: The average man considers that his liberty is not only of considerable importance to himself but that an attack upon his personal liberty is a matter of the greatest importance to the community.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes personal liberty as a value to be protected from attack—framing liberty as freedom from interference with an individual's basic rights, a matter of community concern when threatened.

records.speaker: The Solicitor-General
records.sentence: Both are essential contributories to the liberty of the individual.
records.haiku_rationale: The individual is freed from constraint and empowered to act through two essential factors, but the sentence does not specify what is being freed, from what interference, or to what capacity.

records.speaker: Mr. Thomson
records.sentence: It is no longer a question of whether there is to be independence and freedom for the countries of Africa or other members of the former Colonial Territories.
records.haiku_rationale: Countries are freed to govern themselves (independence and freedom granted to African and former colonial territories) — a conferral of positive liberty through empowerment of self-determination.

records.speaker: Mr. Jack Jones
records.sentence: The notion of Tory freedom is an anachronism.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence dismisses a conception of freedom associated with Tories as outdated, without specifying what is being freed or from-or-to what; it makes a rhetorical claim about a political philosophy rather than substantively defining a liberty-value or proposing a concrete freedom.

records.speaker: Mr. Wilson
records.sentence: Here we are again—after eight years of Tory government, Tory freedom breaks down if the wicked trade unions ask for a fair share of the prosperity their members have created.
records.haiku_rationale: Tory freedom (freedom from trade union constraint or regulation) breaks down when unions demand higher wages, so freedom from union interference or constraint is the object being discussed.

records.speaker: Mr. Edwards
records.sentence:
They have discussed their problems here in the Metropolis of a great Empire and Commonwealth, and we have agreed that


Nigeria shall have its freedom without having to win it on the barricades, without the civil war and bloody revolution which many people envisaged as the only way the Africans could win their freedom from this Parliament.
records.haiku_rationale: Nigeria is freed (empowered) to self-govern without external constraint; freedom from Parliament's imperial control is being granted as capacity for autonomous governance.

records.speaker: Mr. Brown
records.sentence: Nevertheless, I believe more strongly than ever that freedom, the democratic way of doing things and the advance to effective social democracy and all we stand for depend upon the answers which we give in this difficult field.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom as a general political ideal being invoked in relation to democracy and social progress; the sentence does not specify what is being freed (from or to what), making it an abstract rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause.

records.speaker: Mr. Bevins
records.sentence: We have complete freedom to decide which contractors shall be investigated and the extent of the investigation.
records.haiku_rationale: Government/parliamentary body is being freed (empowered) to decide which contractors to investigate and the extent thereof—a capacity to act and make choices without constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Turton
records.sentence: Therefore, I suggest that we should now demand freedom to negotiate reciprocal agreements.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is asserting a capacity or empowerment to negotiate reciprocal agreements, i.e., the ability/opportunity to enter into negotiations without constraint.

records.speaker: Mr. Dugdale
records.sentence: We have heard a great deal lately about the Congo, and we have been told that the Congo presents an example of how freedom should not be given too suddenly to a country.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to govern/self-govern is being conferred on a country (Congo) in the form of independence—this is empowerment to act as a sovereign entity, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. S. Silverman
records.sentence:
He put down an Amendment


to the Address in these terms, and was allowed to move it, and a debate took place:
 But humbly represent to your Majesty that, in the present circumstances of the world, the strength of our national defences, and especially of our air defences, is no longer adequate to secure the peace, safety, and freedom of Your Majesty's faithful subjects.
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is "peace, safety, and freedom of Your Majesty's faithful subjects"—freedom from external threats/aggression by means of adequate national defence, where the agent (the nation/Crown) acts to provide security and protection.

records.speaker: The Minister of State, Home Department
records.sentence: All this, the licensing of the drivers and of the cabs, is done to ensure the highest possible standard of safety and freedom from breakdowns and this attitude must have some bearing on the points put by my hon.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from breakdowns: drivers and cabs are being freed from mechanical failures through licensing and safety standards that ensure reliability.

records.speaker: Mr. Ede
records.sentence:
I hope that we shall leave the Bookmakers' Committee and the Levy Board with the freedom the Bill as drafted gives them, because I am certain that any attempt to forecast the amount of money that will


be at the disposal of those who will then have to consider the matter is completely futile at present.
records.haiku_rationale: The Bookmakers' Committee and Levy Board are being given freedom (discretion/empowerment) to make decisions about disposing of money without prior legislative constraints on the amount.

records.speaker: Mr. Ness Edwards
records.sentence: Has he purchased his freedom at too high a price?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker questions whether a person has purchased freedom (autonomy/independence from constraint) at too high a cost—i.e., whether they have achieved self-determination, but possibly at unacceptable cost. This concerns empowerment to act autonomously, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Mr. Philip Holland
records.sentence: In any attempt to be early in this field, the freer swinging stride of the Post Office, run on commercial lines as now but with the greater freedom that this Bill offers, should outstrip the slow, deliberate march of Government consultation and deliberation.
records.haiku_rationale: The Post Office is being freed from (procedural constraints of) slow Government consultation and deliberation, and given greater freedom to operate on commercial lines—enabling it to act more swiftly and decisively.

records.speaker: Mr. Fletcher-Cooke
records.sentence: If we define this as a power conferred by Statute—and these bodies incorporated by Royal Charter do not have their powers conferred directly by Statute—they fear that they will be omitted from this new freedom which is to be given to trustees and persons not being trustees having the statutory power.
