records.haiku_rationale: The liberty of the people is being constituted or formed through Parliament as an institution—a claim about how collective political freedom and self-governance are enabled through democratic representation and parliamentary procedure.

records.speaker: John Home Robertson
records.sentence: Friend the Member for Wallasey (Angela Eagle), will forgive the Scottish Minister with responsibility for fisheries for taking the liberty as a Back-Bench Member in this place of saying something about the peculiar predicament of share fishermen that has arisen recently.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "took the liberty of saying something" is a parliamentary procedural expression meaning the speaker is permitted to speak; it does not make a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Mike O'Brien
records.sentence: The Canadian information commissioner has said that, after Canada's 15 years of freedom of information legislation, although it had strong laws, it had not achieved the cultural change.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from government interference with access to information; the sentence discusses freedom of information as a legal right constraining state secrecy.

records.speaker: David Lock
records.sentence: However, the authority may not know whether the information is accurate, and the cost ceiling for charges made under the freedom of information regime is designed only to cover finding and retrieving the information.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of information is freedom from interference with access to information held by public authorities; the sentence discusses the operational mechanism (cost ceiling) governing this negative liberty.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: 15 (Exempted business),That at this day's sitting, the Freedom of Information Bill may be proceeded with, though opposed, until any hour.
records.haiku_rationale: This is a parliamentary procedure motion granting permission to proceed with debate on the Freedom of Information Bill beyond normal time limits; "at this day's sitting" is procedural language, not a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Richard Shepherd
records.sentence: Having marched through the Lobby on these issues over many years, I believe that deep, deep within the feeling of the House, and certainly within the new generation that marches, marking the changing of the guard for each and every Parliament, there is a desire for true freedom of information that will give us equality with an Executive.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker seeks "freedom of information" that would grant Parliament equal footing with the Executive—this names freedom from Executive secrecy and lack of transparency, a classic negative liberty of access to information without executive obstruction.

records.speaker: Richard Shepherd
records.sentence: I had hoped that the Third Reading of the Freedom of Information Bill would be one of the greatest occasions of my life.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with access to information (held by the state); the "Freedom of Information" bill aims to constrain government power to withhold information, thereby enlarging citizens' capacity to obtain information free from state obstruction.

records.speaker: Tony Wright
records.sentence: The Government themselves say that provision of that type of factual information contributes to more effective policy making, but in their freedom of information provisions, that whole category of information is to be exempt.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference with access to factual information is being constrained; the speaker objects to exempting that category of information from disclosure provisions.

records.speaker: Menzies Campbell
records.sentence: They may not fall within the provisions of the freedom of information legislation, which is rather less vigorous than I should have liked, but I hope that — to enlist the support of those who have an interest in the matter — the Government will be willing to make the information that the reports contain available on a wider basis.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses "freedom of information legislation" — a right to access information free from governmental restriction on disclosure. This is freedom from interference with the citizen's capacity to obtain information.

records.speaker: Archibald Hamilton
records.sentence: What does that mean in the context of freedom of information?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker is invoking "freedom of information" — a specific civil liberty naming freedom from government restriction or secrecy regarding access to information.

records.speaker: George Young
records.sentence: and does not the fate of the Financial Services and Markets Bill and the Freedom of Information Bill disprove that assumption?
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker references the "Freedom of Information Bill" as a legislative object whose fate is being discussed, but the sentence does not make a substantive claim about liberty as a value—it is a rhetorical parliamentary question about whether the bills' outcomes disprove an assumption.

records.speaker: Stephen Byers
records.sentence: The Bill guarantees a publicly owned Post Office, but with the commercial freedoms that will be needed to meet the challenges of the 21st century.
records.haiku_rationale: The Post Office is freed to act commercially (capacity to innovate, compete, manage operations without regulatory constraint), enabling it to meet market challenges.

records.speaker: Jim Murphy
records.sentence: Does he share my view that there is nothing at all patriotic about threatening to incarcerate every asylum seeker while campaigning for the freedom of dictators such as Pinochet?
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "freedom of dictators" refers to freedom from interference with the actions of authoritarian rulers—a rhetorical invocation of liberty as a cause being critiqued. The speaker is attacking the view that one should champion freedom (from constraint) for tyrants.

records.speaker: Theresa May
records.sentence: It is difficult to recruit young people into teaching, but to ensure the future of the profession and to encourage them to enter the profession we need to show them not only the value of teachers, but that they will be treated as professionals and will be given the freedom and flexibility that they need to get on with the job, without constantly being subjected to interference from the bureaucrats in Whitehall.
records.haiku_rationale: Teachers are being freed from bureaucratic interference (constraints on their professional judgment and action), which is freedom FROM interference—a classic negative liberty concern, even though the surface grammar frames it as empowerment ("given the freedom and flexibility").

records.speaker: Richard Shepherd
records.sentence: We made the point when considering the Freedom of Information Bill, and we shall make it again.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to "Freedom of Information Bill" by proper name (a legislative title); it does not make a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value or what is being freed from what.

records.speaker: Peter Hain
records.sentence: In the global age, it is in Britain's national interest to promote British values of freedom, democracy and economic modernisation.
records.haiku_rationale: Britain's national interest is promoted through advancing freedom as a general value—a rhetorical invocation of freedom as a cause to be championed, aligned with democracy and modernization, rather than specifying freedom from particular interference or freedom to do particular things.

records.speaker: Adrian Sanders
records.sentence: The freedoms that local councils need are not necessarily in the Bill, although there is some movement towards that.
records.haiku_rationale: Local councils are being enabled/empowered to govern themselves and make decisions, freed from central constraints to take independent action.

records.speaker: Stephen Byers
records.sentence: Gentleman will know that when we have the Postal Services Bill on the statute book, greater commercial freedom will be given to the Post Office to address those concerns.
records.haiku_rationale: The Post Office is being freed (given "commercial freedom") to act in ways addressing business concerns—this is enablement of capacity/opportunity to compete and manage affairs, not removal of interference.

records.speaker: Peter Lilley
records.sentence: We need time to debate these matters and to test them by amendment, so that we may judge whether the Bill is incompatible with freedom of movement in the EU.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom of movement" which is a core negative liberty—freedom from interference with the ability to move across EU borders. The speaker is asking whether proposed legislation would infringe (constrain) this freedom.

records.speaker: Jeremy Corbyn
records.sentence: Finally, the statements made by Liberty and the Law Society suggest that the Bill is outwith the European convention on human rights.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence references "Liberty" as an organization name (the civil liberties pressure group) and discusses human rights compliance, but does not make a claim about liberty-as-a-value or freedom itself—it merely names an organization and reports its legal position.

records.speaker: Simon Hughes
records.sentence: Freedom of movement between the countries of the European Union is part of the treaty of Rome.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes freedom of movement—a negative liberty protecting people from interference with their ability to travel between EU countries, as guaranteed by treaty rights.

records.speaker: Geoffrey Hoon
records.sentence: There is clearly already competition between the ranges, and the commercial freedom that we expect to be extended will be of benefit to them.
records.haiku_rationale: Commercial actors are being freed to compete in markets — empowered capacity to engage in commerce and innovation without constraints.

records.speaker: George Young
records.sentence: Will she confirm that there are likely to be 118 Lords amendments to the Freedom of Information Bill, 280 amendments to the Countryside and Rights of Way Bill, and 700 amendments to the casually drafted Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Bill?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence mentions "Freedom of Information Bill" as a named legislative act; it does not substantively discuss freedom as a value or claim about what freedoms ought to be protected or enabled.

records.speaker: Eric Forth
records.sentence: As has been said many times, there are about 120 Lords amendments to the Freedom of Information Bill.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence references "Freedom of Information Bill" as a proper noun and legislative title; it does not make a substantive claim about liberty-as-a-value but merely mentions the bill's name in procedural context.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: — (1) Proceedings on Consideration of Lords Amendments to the Freedom of Information Bill shall be completed at today's sitting and shall, if not previously concluded, be brought to a conclusion at midnight.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses parliamentary procedure for concluding legislative proceedings on a specific bill; "Consideration of Lords Amendments" is a procedural step, not a substantive claim about freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: That the following provisions shall apply to the remaining proceedings on the Freedom of Information Bill and the Countryside and Rights of Way Bill: —
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to "Freedom of Information Bill" as a proper noun and parliamentary procedure for legislative proceedings; the word "freedom" appears only as part of a named Act, not as substantive discussion of liberty-as-a-value.

records.speaker: Richard Shepherd
records.sentence: The rituals in question are freedom of speech and the right to represent those who sent us here.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of speech is being protected from interference; the right to represent constituents is a civic capacity/empowerment, making this sentence compound in its liberty claims.

records.speaker: Jack Straw
records.sentence: As for the Freedom of Information Bill, we were famously told in the Conservatives' campaign guide at the general election that such a Bill was of interest only to "left-wing busybodies".
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence discusses freedom of information as a policy enabling access to government information, which is an expansion of citizens' capacity to know and scrutinize government — a positive liberty of empowerment, not merely freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Peter Lilley
records.sentence: It is called the Freedom of Information Bill, but it is largely a restriction of disclosure Bill.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes the bill for claiming to enhance freedom of information (negative liberty—freedom from state suppression of disclosure) but actually restricting what information can be disclosed, thus undermining that non-interference claim.

records.speaker: Robert McCartney
records.sentence: …The spirit of liberty is the spirit which is not too sure that it is right;
records.haiku_rationale: The object of freedom is intellectual humility and openness to doubt; liberty is characterized as freedom from dogmatic certainty, enabling a disposition to question one's own rightness rather than imposing one's will on others.

records.speaker: Nick Hawkins
records.sentence: The Minister is talking about provisions in the Freedom of Information Bill — or Act, as it will become.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to a named act ("Freedom of Information Bill/Act") and does not make a substantive claim about liberty as a value — it merely names legislation in parliamentary procedure.

records.speaker: Robin Cook
records.sentence: At the same time, we in this House are committed to freedom of speech and freedom of expression, and we cannot prevent the Palestinian media from reporting views that are widely expressed in Palestine.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence asserts freedom of speech and freedom of expression—both paradigmatic negative liberties naming freedom from interference with media reporting and expression of views, contrasted with prevention/restriction.

records.speaker: John Gummer
records.sentence: That freedom is crucial, perhaps even more so when we disagree with what those individuals want to do.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from interference in action is being defended as a value that must be protected especially when one disagrees with those actions—the core principle of negative liberty as a constraint on others' power to suppress or control.

records.speaker: Nick Palmer
records.sentence: I accept that a fundamental issue of liberty is at stake and I shall return to that.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes liberty as a fundamental value at stake in an unspecified debate, but does not specify what is being freed, from what constraint, or toward what capacity—the object and direction of liberty remain entirely unspecified.

records.speaker: Peter Luff
records.sentence: They are both moral issues — animal welfare and liberty.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is invoked as a bare moral value in a list with animal welfare, without specification of what freedom is from or to what.

records.speaker: Nigel Evans
records.sentence: The convention holds that children are born with fundamental freedoms and the inherent rights of all human beings.
records.haiku_rationale: Children are understood to possess fundamental freedoms and inherent rights as human beings — a positive account of their essential capacities and dignities as persons, not freedom from specific interference.

records.speaker: John Maples
records.sentence: When we talk about individuals' freedom to behave as they want, we cannot take just the people with whom we agree and dismiss the rest.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom to behave as individuals want: capacity/empowerment of individuals to act as they choose, without constraint based on others' agreement.

records.speaker: Nigel Waterson
records.sentence: Most of us will have received a briefing from the Campaign for Freedom of Information, which has a distinguished record on dealing with such issues over the past six to nine months while the legislation was going through the House.
records.haiku_rationale: The "Campaign for Freedom of Information" is an organizational name; the sentence mentions it but does not make a substantive claim about liberty itself—it merely references an organization's involvement in legislation. The sentence is descriptive, not normative.

records.speaker: David Heath
records.sentence: Why did the Government resist the amendments tabled by me and many others to the Freedom of Information Bill, which would have entrenched in statute the right to information and factual advice provided to Ministers — exactly the core of Lord Phillips's findings?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "Freedom of Information" — a freedom from government interference with access to official information and advice. It is about establishing a right (entrenchment in statute) to prevent interference with access to factual information.

records.speaker: Michael Fabricant
records.sentence: We believe in freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: Bare invocation of "freedom" as a value without specification of what is being freed or from/to what—the sentence is too abstract to disambiguate between negative liberty (freedom from interference) and positive liberty (capacity to act).

records.speaker: Mike O'Brien
records.sentence: In a multicultural society, in which freedom and free trade should not be unnecessarily restrained, some of the arguments were unconvincing.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom and free trade are things that should not be unnecessarily restrained—this expresses negative liberty against interference with commerce and individual action.

records.speaker: Richard Page
records.sentence: Friend's speech led on to the importance of freedom, and that point should be stressed in Committee when the time comes.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence mentions "importance of freedom" as an abstract value to be stressed in debate, without specifying what freedom from or to what, or what capacity/right is at issue.

records.speaker: Barry Gardiner
records.sentence: If there be any virtue in the way that we live, we should proclaim it as a memorial to those who died and as a covenant with those who share our values throughout the world in which we shall continue to live governed by the principles of tolerance, democracy, freedom and the rule of law.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes "freedom" as part of a rhetorical affirmation of liberal-democratic values (alongside tolerance, democracy, and rule of law) that the speaker commits to upholding as a memorial principle and covenant with others. This is a rhetorical invocation of freedom as a cause opposed to what it implicitly rejects—it names freedom as a foundational principle to be preserved and lived by, functioning as a value to be protected from threats, not as an empowering capacity being granted.

records.speaker: Barry Gardiner
records.sentence: In precisely the same way, we must distinguish genuine civil war where freedom fighters are engaged in a military campaign of secession that is fought against a state and its legitimate military and economic targets.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom fighters are being freed from state control (secession), exercising self-determination and independence from an incumbent state's rule.

records.speaker: Bridget Prentice
records.sentence: Most people in this country would agree to sacrifice some of their liberty if it meant greater security.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes liberty as freedom from constraint, weighing it against security; sacrificing liberty here means accepting restrictions on freedom.

records.speaker: Stephen Ladyman
records.sentence: We have seen how the freedom that we have as an individual nation has allowed us to act flexibly and forcefully.
records.haiku_rationale: The nation is freed—empowered with the capacity—to act flexibly and forcefully; this is framed as an ability or opportunity granted to the nation, not as freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Alistair Burt
records.sentence: The Government must look at ways of giving universities more freedom and allowing them greater scope to harness funds from the private sector.
records.haiku_rationale: Universities are being freed to harness private funds and act autonomously—freedom to do/capacity rather than freedom from constraint.

records.speaker: Andrew Tyrie
records.sentence: The Prime Minister wants much greater intervention around the world to impose our notion of justice and freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The Prime Minister seeks freedom/justice (as values to impose externally on other nations), implying enabling or empowering distant peoples to realize these ideals, but the sentence is critical of expansionist intervention and does not specify what is being freed from or enabled to do within those nations.

records.speaker: Bill Wiggin
records.sentence: The Bill is constructive and helpful, and we should all support it because it promotes freedom of choice, freedom of information and freedom from cruelty.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence invokes three distinct freedoms: freedom of choice (capacity to choose), freedom of information (freedom from interference in accessing/sharing information), and freedom from cruelty (freedom from interference via harm). The first is positive liberty (empowerment to choose), while the latter two are negative liberties (non-interference).

records.speaker: Richard Shepherd
records.sentence: What constitutes our sense of freedom and justice, which we extend to all members of our communities and those who reach our shores?
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence articulates "freedom" and "justice" as abstract values that are extended (shared/applied) to all community members and newcomers, without specifying what freedom from or to—it names a general moral commitment rather than a specific object of liberty.

records.speaker: George Osborne
records.sentence: I am happy to confine myself to English law, which has a long history of liberty established by the rule of common law and by decisions of judges and jurists over many centuries, which are in many cases as important as acts of revolution or Acts passed in the House over the centuries.
records.haiku_rationale: Liberty is being invoked as a historical value established through common law and judicial decisions (protection from arbitrary power through institutional constraint), which is a constraining concept—freedom from interference secured by law and institutional precedent, not capacity to do something.

records.speaker: Donald Foster
records.sentence: The Secretary of State was right to speak in his statement about giving further powers to local councils, but I fail to understand why he continues to say that they must earn their additional freedoms.
records.haiku_rationale: Local councils are freed from constraints (enabled to exercise greater powers), but the condition "must earn" suggests empowerment contingent on demonstrated performance.

records.speaker: Simon Hughes
records.sentence: 34 and 35 — with their freedom of information legislation intentions.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of information is freedom from (government) interference with access to official information — a classic negative liberty concerned with non-interference with citizens' ability to obtain public data.

records.speaker: Tony Blair
records.sentence: He seemed to think that, somehow, agreeing to this would mean that our freedom to act as we have done after 11 September would be curtailed.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom from curtailment of Britain's capacity to act militarily/in foreign policy after 9/11; the phrase "freedom to act" emphasizes preserved agency in response to circumstances.

records.speaker: The Reverend Ian Paisley
records.sentence: As Martin McGuinness said:"I apologise to no one for saying that we support and admire the freedom fighters of the IRA.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "freedom fighters" is an evaluative/rhetorical label for IRA members; the sentence expresses support for those characterized as fighting against constraint or occupation, but does not articulate a specific liberty—whether freedom from interference or capacity to act.

records.speaker: Douglas Alexander
records.sentence: Derek Hodgson, then general secretary of the Communication Workers Union, said of the Bill:"It secures the union's major objective of securing a long-term future in the public sector for the post office, and offers the business commercial freedom we believe it needs.
records.haiku_rationale: The Post Office business is being freed to act commercially (to innovate, compete, and operate without public-sector constraints) — this is empowerment/capacity to act, positive liberty.

records.speaker: George Osborne
records.sentence: The Government amendment rests on the fiction that the Government have given the Post Office commercial freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: George Osborne criticizes the claim that the Government granted the Post Office "commercial freedom"—empowerment to act commercially without constraint—which he treats as a false fiction, implying the Post Office lacks genuine capacity to operate independently.

records.speaker: David Chaytor
records.sentence: On any analysis of the structure of secondary education — it is important that we draw the distinction between the operation of faith schools in the primary and secondary sectors — the crux of the matter is that one persons' freedom of choice is another person's denial of choice.
records.haiku_rationale: One person's freedom of choice (to select schools on grounds of faith) is enabled at the expense of another person's denied choice, creating a tension between enabling and constraining aspects of liberty.

records.speaker: Edward Leigh
records.sentence: On the one hand, people have the right to have schools — freedom of association is a fundamental right — but can we be absolutely sure, once the school has been set up, that it will ensure that its pupils are aware of the history of the nation and of the wider community?
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom of association (right to set up schools freely without interference) is being asserted as a fundamental right, but the speaker then questions whether exercising that freedom will ensure educational outcomes aligned with national history awareness.

records.speaker: Ian Gibson
records.sentence: The supporters of the middle way option argue that it would guarantee an improvement in animal welfare and boldly attempt to merge that point with arguments about human liberty and freedom — but we will ignore that one.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker invokes "human liberty and freedom" generically without specifying what is being freed, from what, or to what—it is explicitly dismissed ("we will ignore that one") and serves as a rhetorical reference point against which the speaker declines to engage.

records.speaker: David Rendel
records.sentence: "That is, freedom will be benevolently bestowed on the say-so of the Secretary of State — but only for a few, as only 10 per cent.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (understood as the ability to act or exercise some right) is being bestowed/granted by the Secretary of State to a select few, conditional on their say-so—a positive empowerment that is subject to bureaucratic discretion and limited access.

records.speaker: Bob Blizzard
records.sentence: Having said that, however, we must be careful that rogues cannot take advantage of the greater freedom that the Bill would introduce in the insolvency laws.
records.haiku_rationale: The "greater freedom" refers to increased operational flexibility and scope for action in insolvency proceedings — the ability to do things (take advantage of loopholes) that were previously constrained by law. This is empowerment capacity.

records.speaker: Yvette Cooper
records.sentence: Member for Woodspring set out the traditional, right-wing libertarian view that any action by Government is a restriction on freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence describes a libertarian claim that government action restricts freedom—framing freedom as freedom FROM government interference and coercion.

records.speaker: Yvette Cooper
records.sentence: Friend the Member for Crawley (Laura Moffatt) said, the addiction factor makes debates about freedom of choice rather more complicated.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "freedom of choice" refers to the freedom from interference in one's ability to make choices, which is a classic negative liberty concept.

records.speaker: Evan Harris
records.sentence: I believe that when there is clear evidence of harm, it is reasonable to restrict the liberty of businesses to sell, or at least to advertise, a dangerous product.
records.haiku_rationale: Restricting the liberty (freedom) of businesses to sell or advertise dangerous products — a negative liberty claim about non-interference with commercial action being legitimately curtailed when harm is evident.

records.speaker: Adrian Flook
records.sentence: I find it unfortunate that the Bill will lead to increased censorship, enhance red tape and restrict freedom to make one's own decisions.
records.haiku_rationale: The phrase "restrict freedom to make one's own decisions" identifies the object of freedom as autonomous decision-making capacity — what is being freed is the ability to make personal choices, and what is being restricted is that capacity to act.

records.speaker: Alan Milburn
records.sentence: However, because nicotine is so enormously addictive — as the Royal College of Physicians and others have testified — it is much harder for smokers to exercise an equivalent freedom of choice to give up.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence concerns smokers' capacity to exercise choice to give up smoking, constrained by nicotine addiction. This is positive liberty — the actual ability to exercise a choice to act (quit), not freedom from interference with smoking choices.

records.speaker: Liam Fox
records.sentence: I was frank about the need for a balance, and we accept the restriction of individual freedoms in other areas.
records.haiku_rationale: Individual freedoms (negative liberty to act without interference) are being restricted; the speaker frames accepting such restrictions as a policy stance on the balance between liberty and other values.

records.speaker: George Howarth
records.sentence: It might have been possible for Ministers who are members of the Government's legislative programme committee to have noted the possible threats to academic freedom when the Bill was originally proposed.
records.haiku_rationale: Academic freedom is freedom from interference with scholarly inquiry and teaching—a constraint on ministerial action over academic institutions. This is negative liberty.

records.speaker: Bill Cash
records.sentence: "He could not understand why we would not want commercial freedom for the companies in question.
records.haiku_rationale: The companies are freed to engage in commercial activity (capacity to act without state constraint/regulation).

records.speaker: Estelle Morris
records.sentence: Rather than having a one-size-fits-all approach, we need to acknowledge the truth that different schools are at different stages in school improvement and need different levels of challenge and support, freedoms and responsibilities.
records.haiku_rationale: Schools are being freed from the constraint of one-size-fits-all prescriptive policy in order to pursue school improvement strategies suited to their particular stage and needs.

records.speaker: The Reverend Ian Paisley
records.sentence: The statement concludes:"The IRA is unequivocally committed to the search for freedom, justice and peace in Northern Ireland.
records.haiku_rationale: The IRA is said to be committed to "freedom" as a general political goal and cause in Northern Ireland; the sentence does not specify freedom from what constraint nor freedom to perform what particular action, making the object of freedom under-specified.

records.speaker: Nick Raynsford
records.sentence: I am delighted that the Conservatives have had a death-bed repentance and that they will follow our Government in giving freedoms and flexibilities to local authorities.
records.haiku_rationale: Local authorities are being empowered (given flexibilities and freedoms) to govern and act with greater discretion, a capacity granted by the Government.

records.speaker: David Davis
records.sentence: Gentleman, I shall start with another quotation:XThe idea that you give freedom to the people who are already achieving is quite perverse.
records.haiku_rationale: The speaker criticizes granting freedom/empowerment to people already succeeding as contradictory; the concern is about enabling capacity for those who lack it (positive liberty context), but the sentence invokes "freedom" in a general evaluative rather than substantive sense.

records.speaker: Tony Blair
records.sentence: It was that, if we care about these values of freedom, the rule of law and democracy, we should not flinch from the fight in defending them.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being defended against threat (flinching from fight); the object is freedom as a value opposed to tyranny/threat, a rhetorical invocation of negative liberty (non-interference with the free exercise of democratic and legal rights).

records.speaker: Alan Milburn
records.sentence: Lady knows, sometimes there are land swap deals, but trusts will have considerable freedom to enter into new sorts of contract as well.
records.haiku_rationale: Trusts are being empowered (given the capacity) to enter into new types of contract—positive liberty as expanded agency and opportunity.

records.speaker: John Gummer
records.sentence: The Labour party used to be about the enlargement of freedom and the provision of wider choice on issues on which many people, including many on this side of the House, wished to enforce their own sense of repugnance.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom is being enlarged and choice is being widened—enabling people to exercise their own preferences rather than having others enforce their sense of repugnance. This is positive liberty: the empowerment to act on one's own values and make one's own choices.

records.speaker: Liam Fox
records.sentence: Will they have the freedom to vary pay and conditions for clinical conditions outside the Xagenda for change" arrangements announced by the Secretary of State?
records.haiku_rationale: What is being freed: NHS bodies (hospitals/trusts) to vary pay and conditions for clinical staff; from-or-to: freed to act without constraint from the "Agenda for Change" pay framework.

records.speaker: Siobhain McDonagh
records.sentence: It seems reasonable that the best standard — three stars — should be achieved before that freedom is given.
records.haiku_rationale: Freedom (empowerment to act) is given to local authorities or bodies once they achieve a three-star standard.

records.speaker: Andrew Lansley
records.sentence: Quite what freedom that means for Addenbrooke's, I do not know.
records.haiku_rationale: Addenbrooke's hospital is being freed from operational constraints or bureaucratic control to act more autonomously, making this a reference to institutional empowerment or capacity to govern itself.

records.speaker: Alan Milburn
records.sentence: They will operate under a statutory duty of partnership, and we will introduce legislation to ensure that they will have the freedoms necessary to empower front-line staff and managers to shape local services to meet the local community's needs.
records.haiku_rationale: Front-line staff and managers are being empowered (given the capacity and opportunity) to shape local services to meet community needs—this is freedom to act, not freedom from interference.

records.speaker: Unknown
records.sentence: and why the benefits of the measure outweigh any loss of freedom.
records.haiku_rationale: The sentence refers to "loss of freedom" from some unspecified measure, framing it as a trade-off against benefits; without knowing what specific freedoms (positive or negative) are being curtailed, this is under-specified.

records.speaker: Philip Hammond
records.sentence: The Government say that the Bill is about delivering freedoms and flexibilities to local authorities, but their actions on capital receipts, the associated debt and local authority housing grant demonstrate exactly the opposite as far as prudent, debt-free authorities are concerned.
records.haiku_rationale: The Government claims to deliver "freedoms and flexibilities to local authorities"—empowering them with greater discretionary capacity to act—but the speaker argues their fiscal policies (on capital receipts, debt, housing grant) contradict this by constraining authorities' actual ability to govern themselves.

records.speaker: Philip Hammond
records.sentence: The Government have given us a curious idea of what freedom and flexibility mean.
records.haiku_rationale: Philip Hammond criticizes the Government's conception of "freedom and flexibility" as inadequate or misguided, but the sentence itself does not specify what is being freed or from/to what constraint or capability.
